US President Donald Trump told Fox News on Monday that his options on Iran were “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically, or making a deal.”

The US introduced new rounds of sanctions in August to further isolate the country, but the effort stalled. The campaign, called Operation Economic Outcast, primarily targets countries doing business with Iran.

Iran’s aviation industry has already faced significant restrictions due to years of US sanctions. The sanctions limited Iranian carriers’ ability to purchase new aircraft and obtain spare parts and maintenance services.

This new policy will further strain the sector.

Mr Trump earlier demanded that Tehran “put up the white flag of surrender.” He also threatened to make the Strait of Hormuz US territory.

The US President had also previously threatened that “a whole civilization will die… never to be brought back again.”

However, the war, which he projected to last weeks, has expanded across the region, killed at least 18 US service members and thousands of people in the Middle East, and rattled the global economy.

But Mr Bessent told CNBC that the US president is presently in a “deciding mode,” and that “Very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future.”

He said the war is likely to be over in the coming weeks.

World.title: NCAA directs Air Peace to compensate passengers over delayed Lagos-Enugu flight
World.content:
The Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) has directed Air Peace to prepare a compensation package for passengers affected by a delayed Lagos-Enugu flight after its preliminary investigation found that the airline sent passengers the wrong notification about the disruption.

The flight, scheduled to leave Lagos at 6:45 a.m. on Monday, was rescheduled to 4:50 p.m., leaving passengers at the Murtala Muhammed Airport for several hours.

The development followed a complaint by human rights lawyer Inibehe Effiong, who said the delay caused him to miss a scheduled court appearance in Enugu State.

The NCAA’s Director of Public Affairs and Consumer Protection, Michael Achimugu, said the disruption was linked to the ripple effects of the previous night’s disruptions.

However, he said Air Peace should have informed passengers booked on the Monday morning flight that it had been rescheduled.

Wrong notification

Mr Effiong said he arrived at Terminal One of the Murtala Muhammed Airport, Lagos, at about 5:50 a.m. to board the 6:45 a.m. Air Peace flight after checking in the previous night.

He said he was due to appear in court in Enugu that morning for a case scheduled for a definite hearing.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to him, passengers were kept waiting for about an hour before airline officials announced that the flight had been delayed until 4:50 p.m.

Mr Effiong also questioned why the airline sent another reminder to passengers at about 2:01 a.m. asking them to report for the flight despite the disruption.

He said the delay meant he would miss his court appearance and incur additional transportation and other expenses.

He subsequently criticised the airline and aviation regulators over what he described as poor handling of passengers affected by flight disruptions.

Mr Effiong also cited NCAA data showing that Air Peace recorded 1,330 delayed flights out of 1,864 flights listed by the regulator for August.

NCAA investigates complaint

Responding to Mr Effiong’s complaint on X, Mr Achimugu said the NCAA could not be expected to intervene in a disruption before it occurred, but that passengers could report such incidents to the authority.

He said the regulator would investigate the matter and acknowledged the inconvenience caused to the passengers.

Mr Achimugu later explained that the investigation showed that the Lagos-Enugu flight was affected by disruptions from the previous night.

He said the airline should have notified passengers of the change in schedule.

According to him, a senior management official of Air Peace initially claimed that passengers had been informed.

However, after Mr Effiong shared a screenshot of the message he received, the airline’s station and duty managers confirmed that the message sent to passengers was the one he received and that it had been sent in error.

“The Station Manager and Duty Manager have confirmed that the messages sent out were the ones you received, and that it was done in error,” Mr Achimugu said.

He said the airline officials also acknowledged that passengers should have been informed that the flight had been rescheduled.

Mr Achimugu said Air Peace told the NCAA that the affected passengers had been taken to a hotel and would receive care until boarding time, but added that the regulator was still verifying the claim.

Compensation ordered

Mr Achimugu said the NCAA had directed Air Peace to submit a compensation package for the affected passengers in line with Part 19 of the Nigeria Civil Aviation Regulations 2023.

“Timely and honest information is key, and there was a gap in this regard,” he said, adding that sending the wrong notification could not be treated as a force majeure incident.

He added that the airline would avoid sanctions if it provided the affected passengers with compensation and the required duty of care, but warned that sanctions could follow if it failed to comply.

He stressed that sanctions are not automatically imposed after every flight disruption, noting that the applicable rules determine when and how penalties are applied.

Under Part 19, which governs passengers’ rights and airlines’ obligations, domestic airlines must provide passengers with the reasons for a delay within 30 minutes of the scheduled departure time. The regulations also provide for refreshments and communication assistance after two hours, reimbursement or rerouting beyond three hours, and hotel accommodation and transport when a delay extends from 10 p.m. to 4 a.m. or when the airport is closed.

The regulations also provide for compensation of at least 25 per cent of the fare for eligible domestic cancellations, subject to the conditions and exceptions contained in the rules.

Wider flight delay concerns

The incident comes amid renewed concerns over flight disruptions in Nigeria.

The NCAA’s August 2026 report showed that 15 domestic airlines operated 7,961 flights during the month, of which 4,765 were delayed and 36 were cancelled.

Air Peace was listed with 1,330 delayed flights out of 1,864 flights, representing 71.4 per cent of the flights recorded for the airline in the NCAA’s dataset.

The airline, however, disputed the figures, saying it operated 2,564 flights during the month and that more than 700 of its flights were not captured in the NCAA’s data.

The airline also said internal factors accounted for only about 15 per cent of its delays.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that the NCAA had earlier recorded widespread delays across the domestic aviation sector, with the regulator and airlines attributing the disruptions to a combination of factors, including technical issues, weather, airport restrictions, and other operational challenges.

The regulator has also stressed the need for airlines to maintain realistic schedules, provide adequate operational buffers and comply with passenger protection requirements.

World.title: Netball World Cup Qualifiers: Malawi crush Nigeria 82–22 in Nairobi
World.content:
Nigeria’s national netball team suffered a heavy defeat at the Africa Netball Cup and Netball World Cup Sydney 2027 Qualifiers, losing 82–22 to Malawi in their Pool 2 encounter in Nairobi on Monday.

The result saw Malawi maintain their perfect start to the qualifying campaign and secure their place at the 2027 Netball World Cup in Sydney. According to World Netball, the Africa qualifier is being held in Kenya from 19–26 September, with Nigeria among the 10 participating nations.

Nigeria overwhelmed from the start

The Queens dominated from the opening whistle, racing to a 21–6 lead after the first quarter as the Green Hawks struggled to contain Malawi’s attack, and the gap continued to widen. By half-time, the Malawians had established a 40–11 advantage, leaving Nigeria with a steep task after the interval.

The third quarter proved even more difficult for Nigeria as Malawi scored 23 goals to Nigeria’s three, taking the score to 63–14. The Queens went further to add another 19 goals in the final quarter to complete an emphatic 82–22 victory, a 60-goal winning margin.

Quarter-by-quarter score

1st quarter: Malawi 21–6 Nigeria

2nd quarter: Malawi 40–11 Nigeria

3rd quarter: Malawi 63–14 Nigeria

4th quarter: Malawi 82–22 Nigeria

For Nigeria, the defeat follows their earlier losses to Kenya (61–40) and Uganda (68–30) in Pool 2.

Up next

The Green Hawks of Nigeria battle Zambia next on Tuesday, 22 September 2026. While Pool 2 action concludes with Uganda vs Malawi on Wednesday, 23 September.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to World Netball, South Africa and Uganda had already qualified for Sydney 2027 based on their world ranking, while the Africa qualifier determines which additional teams are invited to the tournament.

World.title: Peace Cup: Young talents seek European breakthrough as scouting event ends
World.content:
Young Nigerian footballers at the inaugural Dominion Peace Cup will have one final opportunity to impress foreign scouts when the scouting tournament ends on Tuesday at the Legacy Pitch of the National Stadium, Surulere, Lagos.

After two days of matches, the players will return to the pitch hoping to deliver performances that could attract the attention of scouts and agents seeking emerging talent for clubs abroad.

Three matches are scheduled for the final day, with Athletic SC facing Dominion Excellence, Coal City taking on Bethel FC, and SCL Nigeria FC playing Goal Getters FC.

The tournament, organised by Dominion Football Club, has brought together teams from different parts of Nigeria, as well as a club from Ghana, in an effort to provide young players with a platform to showcase their abilities.

Several scouts and agents have been monitoring the matches from the sidelines, including representatives linked to clubs in Portugal, Belgium and Turkey.

According to the tournament organiser, Benjamin James, about six scouts are covering the competition, with some working directly for clubs and others operating as agents.

“We don’t just want to bring people to come and spend all day here,” Mr James said. “We want them to know why they are here: to scout our players and see that they are doing well, so you can take them to Europe and market them.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr James said there was no predetermined number of players the scouts were expected to select.

“We cannot specify that we are looking for two or five or six,” he said. “It’s how good the players are. You can market them easily.”

He added that the scout from Turkey, expected to watch the final day, had already provided a list of positions for which the club was looking for players.

Adada Warriors claim biggest win

Adada Warriors recorded the biggest result on Monday, defeating Dominion Excellence 2-0.

Dominion Excellence had earlier defeated Coal City 1-0 on Saturday, while Adada Warriors lost 1-0 to Edel FC.

Edel FC maintained their unbeaten record on Monday after playing out a goalless draw with Glorious Day.

SCL Nigeria FC also secured a 1-0 victory over Bilada, while Eagle Elites defeated Bilada by the same scoreline.

The matches between Bethel FC and Coal City, Athletic SC and Eagle Elites, and Eagle Elites and SCL Nigeria FC ended goalless.

Only four goals were scored across Monday’s five matches, highlighting the competitive nature of the tournament.

Platform for young players

For Dominion FC proprietor, Ogechi Agana, the tournament goes beyond football and is designed to provide young people with opportunities while keeping them productively engaged.

“Football is an international game, and it exposes everybody to great opportunities,” Mrs Agana said.

She expressed hope that the competition would produce players capable of progressing to the international stage.

“We are hoping to produce one or two people who can go on to the international stage,” she said.

With the final three matches scheduled for Tuesday, the players have one last opportunity to make an impression before the scouts leave Lagos.

For some of the participants, the final whistle could therefore mark not just the end of the Peace Cup but the beginning of a possible journey into professional football abroad.

World.title: Bandits continue attacks in Sokoto, Katsina despite local peace deals, military operations
World.content:
Months after many communities in Katsina State entered local peace arrangements with armed groups, renewed attacks, abductions and displacement are testing those arrangements and the security measures meant to protect rural residents.

Across southern Katsina and neighbouring Sokoto State, many people have been killed, kidnapped or forced from their homes in recent weeks. Farmers in some areas are afraid to go to their fields, and livestock have been stolen.

Security agencies have responded with extra deployments, rescue operations and raids on suspected bandit hideouts.

Results vary by location. Some communities report improvements after local negotiations and security operations. Troops have rescued some abducted residents and say they have disrupted planned attacks. Elsewhere, families remain displaced, and the attacks continue.

Casualty and displacement figures remain fluid and often rest on local accounts that are difficult to verify independently. Available evidence does not show that fighters displaced by military operations in Zamfara are driving the renewed violence elsewhere.

Attack after troops blocked bandits’ advance

The pressure is sharpest in the Rabah Local Government Area of Sokoto State.

In the early hours of 7 September, suspected bandits attacked Tofa, killing residents, abducting others and rustling livestock. Reports put the death toll at between seven and 10, while estimates of those abducted ranged from 35 to about 40.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Sokoto police spokesperson Ahmad Rufai confirmed the attack to PREMIUM TIMES, but had not provided final figures when the newspaper reported the incident.

The Tofa attack came about a week after troops said they intercepted armed men advancing towards Ghandi, a community in Rabah. On 30 August, eight farmers were killed, and five were injured in an attack in Ghandi, according to police figures. Days later, Operation FANSAN YAMMA said troops intercepted another group of armed men moving towards the community.

The interception did not prevent the later attack on Tofa. No evidence links the men stopped near Ghandi to those who attacked Tofa.

When PREMIUM TIMES contacted army spokesperson Olaniyi Osoba, he declined to talk discuss military operations over the telephone and invited the reporter to the 8 Division headquarters in Sokoto.

Repeated attacks empty Sokoto communities

Further south in Kebbe Local Government Area, the consequences are clearer.

On 4 September, the police confirmed that five people had been killed and three injured in an attack on Girkau and neighbouring communities the previous day.

The attack followed reports that suspected bandits had demanded ₦40 million from residents of Kebbe town. Mr Rufai confirmed that police were aware of the demand and said the Anti-Kidnapping Unit was investigating.

Girkau later came under another attack.

By mid-September, the Kebbe Local Government Council said it was providing food and cash assistance to 150 households displaced from Ungushi, Girkau, Margai, Kebbe East, Kebbe West and other affected communities.

Council chairman Musa Garba Kuchi said displaced families were taking refuge in Kebbe. The district head of the town, Lawal Margai, also acknowledged that insecurity had forced residents from their communities.

Mr Kuchi said improved security operations had encouraged some residents to return, but the council did not identify the communities or say how many households had returned. At least 150 assisted households remained displaced in Kebbe town.

Displacement without camps

A similar pattern is unfolding across southern Katsina, though much of the displacement is harder to count.

Residents fleeing attacks in Bakori, Funtua, Faskari and Dandume have mostly moved in with relatives rather than gathering in formal camps. Many families have relocated to Dandume town, Funtua, Yan-Kara, Mairuwa, Katsina, Zaria and Kano.

The scattered movement makes the scale less visible.

Reports that as many as 15 communities around Dandume had been deserted have been disputed. Dandume council chairman Bishir Sabiu said no community between Dandume and Funtua had been completely deserted, though he acknowledged the insecurity.

Mr Sabiu confirmed a recent attack on Takalamawa in which three residents were killed, and three were injured. He also said vigilantes and community patrol members killed three suspected attackers.

IOM data

An International Organisation for Migration assessment of attacks between 9 and 14 August in Bakori, Dandume and Jibia recorded 2,723 people affected across 629 households. Of that number, 1,535 people from 218 households were displaced, comprising 697 children, 495 women and 343 men.

The affected settlements included Labo Kankia in Bakori; Magaji Wondo Dansuda, Gyazamar, Bokolo and Unguwar Rimin Jiruwa in Dandume; and Daddara in Jibia.

The assessment does not break the figures down by local government area, so the 1,535 cannot be attributed to Dandume alone.

Peace agreements face test

Several communities had previously participated in local peace arrangements.

On 20 September 2025, representatives of Sabuwa and Dandume reportedly entered a ceasefire with armed groups.

Weeks later, representatives from Bakori, Funtua, Kafur, Malumfashi and Kankara met armed-group leaders at Kakumi in Bakori Local Government Area.

Among the community representatives were Abdurrahman Kandarawa of Bakori and Audu Goya of Funtua. The representatives of the armed groups were reported to include Ado Aleru of Yankuzo in Zamfara, Isiya Kwashen Garwa of Guga Ward in Bakori, Babaro of Gidan Gamji and Iliya Zango Dan Sabau.

The meeting reportedly ended with commitments to end hostilities, restore order and pursue peaceful coexistence.

The Katsina State Government has insisted these arrangements should not be read as negotiations between the government and armed groups.

Governor Dikko Radda described the approach as community-driven peace accords, initiated by communities. He said the government supports efforts to restore peace but continues security operations against groups that remain active.

There were early signs of benefit. In November 2025, the Funtua council chairman said five captives had been released without ransom after the agreement.

By December, however, residents interviewed by PREMIUM TIMES in some rural communities were already questioning whether the arrangements could deliver lasting security as attacks continued.

Reports in early September described killings, abductions and livestock theft across Bakori, Funtua, Faskari and Dandume. In Bakori, residents reported attacks on Gidan Na Kaura, Yar Tukunya, Unguwar Gambo and Gidan Sarkin.

In Faskari, community leader Abubakar Aliyu said security had improved after local negotiations, with some residents returning home and farming and commercial activity resuming.

The agreements were reached with particular communities and commanders, meaning they did not necessarily bind every armed group operating in the affected areas. Establishing whether recent attacks constitute breaches, therefore, requires identifying the attackers and determining whether they or their commanders were parties to the agreements.

The relationship between the local agreements and continuing security operations adds a further layer of complexity.

In September, the police said air and ground operations in Katsina killed seven suspected associates of Ado Aleru, one of the bandits reported to have taken part in the Kakumi meeting.

The development shows how the two approaches can operate simultaneously: communities may pursue agreements with particular armed-group leaders while security agencies continue operations against people they allege are associated with those leaders.

More troops, but attacks continue

The Katsina State Government has responded by reviewing security arrangements in the southern part of the state.

On 9 September, senior security officials met in Funtua to assess conditions across Funtua, Faskari, Sabuwa and Dandume.

Police later deployed additional personnel and an armoured personnel carrier to the zone and announced intensified joint operations, intelligence sharing, rapid response and community policing.

On 14 September, armed men abducted residents from Unguwan Daudu and Unguwan Chibauna in Funtua.

Operation FANSAN YAMMA said troops pursued the attackers, engaged them and rescued 10 captives, comprising three males and seven females, including an infant.

On 17 September, another abduction occurred along the Dandume-Damari axis. Troops responded to a distress call, engaged the attackers and rescued three men, recovering their vehicle.

The military did not identify the attackers or link them to the earlier Funtua abduction.

On 15 September, troops acting on intelligence about a planned attack on communities in Matazu and Kankara raided a suspected hideout.

The military said two suspected fighters were killed, including Abbah Alhassan, whom it described as a known terrorist kingpin.

Two other suspects were arrested around Yantumaki in Dan Musa. According to the military, preliminary interrogation linked them to a commander known as Mannori.

The same military statement said 21 abducted residents were rescued in a separate operation around Fafala and Dandikwa in Kebbi State. Together with the 10 from Funtua, that produced the widely reported figure of 31 rescued captives, though the rescues occurred in separate operations.

Displacement crosses state boundaries

The effects of the violence do not end when families escape an attack.

Three residents, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, separately confirmed to PREMIUM TIMES that people displaced from communities in Tureta Local Government Area of Sokoto State have crossed into neighbouring Zamfara, particularly Gummi, while others have relocated to Tureta town and other locations.

The sources asked not to be named for security reasons.

Their accounts corroborate findings by Daily Trust, which interviewed displaced residents from the affected communities.

Umar Abubakar, a trader from Dan Gulbi, told Daily Trust he fled to Gummi in Zamfara after an attack on his community about three months earlier.

His brother was killed, his provision shop was burnt, and he sold some of his remaining livestock to raise ₦250,000 for six months’ rent for a two-bedroom house in Gummi.

Another displaced resident, Muhd Dan Gulbi, estimated that up to 1,000 people from the area were living in Gummi, some in rented accommodation and others in primary schools and an Eid ground.

In another part of Tureta, a resident of Gidan Kare told the newspaper that most residents had fled into Tureta town after months of attacks. He estimated that 97 per cent of the village had been displaced.

The account named Lofa, Tsamiya and Doma among the affected communities.

Those places also appear among the origins of families assisted by the Centre for Peoples Health, Peace and Progress (3Ps). The organisation said it assisted 106 displaced households, including 397 children, from Doma, Rafin Gero, Tsamiya, Lofa, Dabegi, Jurga, Dakku, Damri and Kuruwa.

The Daily Trust accounts and the 3Ps data cover some of the same communities, making the extent of any overlap unclear. Both, however, document displacement from communities around Tureta, including movement across the Sokoto-Zamfara boundary.

Farmers count cost

Displaced residents and community sources who spoke to PREMIUM TIMES said attacks had separated families from farmland, livestock, businesses and local markets, forcing some residents to depend on casual work after fleeing their communities.

The sources, who requested anonymity because they feared reprisals, described abandoned farms and businesses, livestock losses and difficulties returning to communities where attacks remained a threat.

Their accounts are consistent with those of displaced residents interviewed by Daily Trust.

In Sabon Birni, Abubakar Usman, who fled Tsamaye with his wife and four children, told Daily Trust that he abandoned five farms, two plots of land and a phone-accessories business after an attack on his community.

Another displaced resident, Isa Mai Yadi, said his family abandoned 11 farms.

In Goronyo, a displaced veterinarian said livestock rustling had made it impossible for him to return to his former livelihood.

Other displaced residents described turning to masonry, gathering firewood and grass, or casual farm labour to feed their families.

Housing costs have added another burden.

Displaced residents interviewed in Gummi reported paying between ₦250,000 for six months and ₦500,000 annually for accommodation. In Tureta town, one resident said increased demand had pushed the cost of a three-room house to about ₦100,000 a month.

The figures reflect individual residents’ experiences rather than prevailing rental costs across the affected communities.

There are also allegations of more direct interference with farming.

Mr Mai Yadi alleged that an armed-group leader known as Jamu Baki had for years exercised control over his community and compelled residents to farm and sell seeds and fertiliser to him.

PREMIUM TIMES has not independently corroborated the allegation against Mr Baki.

Elsewhere in the North-west, residents have reported that armed groups impose levies as a condition for accessing farmland. Different groups operate in different places; there is no evidence that the levy demands recorded in Sokoto and Zamfara come from the same network.

Years away from home

PREMIUM TIMES also confirmed through community sources that some families displaced by insecurity in parts of Sokoto have remained away from their communities for several years.

The sources, who requested anonymity for security reasons, said prolonged insecurity and fears of renewed attacks continued to prevent some residents from returning permanently.

Daily Trust separately interviewed residents of a displacement settlement in Goronyo who said some families had been away from their communities for between four and eight years.

At a displaced persons settlement in Goronyo, some residents told Daily Trust they had lived away from their communities for between four and eight years.

The chairman of the 200-housing camp, Yakubu Adamu, said it contained 5,764 residents as of 12 March 2026 and housed people from 19 villages.

Recent attacks are creating new displacement in parts of Sokoto, but they sit alongside a population that has already spent years unable to return home.

Any assessment of improving security must therefore account not only for reductions in attacks, but also for whether people displaced over several years can return safely and rebuild their livelihoods.

Are armed groups moving between states?

Military operations in Zamfara and along adjoining corridors have raised the question of whether pressure in one area is pushing fighters into neighbouring states.

Security agencies have reported intercepting suspected fuel and ammunition suppliers and other logistics networks along corridors linking parts of Zamfara, Katsina and Kaduna, indicating that at least some support networks operate across state boundaries.

Security analyst Yahuza Getso told Daily Trust he believed pressure from operations in Katsina and Zamfara had contributed to the movement of some armed groups into Sokoto.

He said agencies in neighbouring states had increasingly carried out operations at the groups’ hideouts and argued that the resulting pressure had increased movement towards Sokoto.

Mr Getso’s assessment offers one explanation for the changing pattern of violence, but PREMIUM TIMES found no operational evidence linking the perpetrators of the recent Rabah or Kebbe attacks to fighters displaced from Katsina or Zamfara.

Recent attacks inside Zamfara further complicate a simple displacement theory.

On 12 September, six Islamic clerics were abducted along the Dakko-Damri feeder road in Bakura while travelling towards Talata Mafara, according to the Zamfara State Police Command.

The military rejected initial reports that the victims were taken from the residence of former governor Abdul’aziz Yari.

Between 16 and 17 September, communities around Dansadau in Maru came under attack.

Published accounts put the death toll at between 13 and 15; another report said as many as 33 people were feared killed. Residents also described substantial displacement into Dansadau town.

There is no evidence connecting the perpetrators of the Dansadau attacks to the recent violence in Sokoto or southern Katsina.

Accounts that some communities around Dansadau had struggled to access farmland for a prolonged period suggest an established local security crisis rather than, by themselves, evidence of newly arrived fighters.

Tactical gains, unresolved insecurity

Security forces have carried out rescues, arrests, and successful operations across the affected states. Local agreements have brought periods of relative calm to some communities. Recent attacks and displacement, however, show the limits of those gains.

In Tofa, some residents were killed and abducted days after troops reported stopping armed men advancing towards nearby Ghandi. In Kebbe, local authorities are supporting 150 displaced households even as they report that some residents are beginning to return.

In southern Katsina, additional personnel and an armoured vehicle have been deployed while troops continue responding to kidnappings, including the rescues in Funtua and along the Dandume-Damari axis.

In Tureta, displaced residents described another struggle after escaping attacks: finding shelter, feeding their families and surviving without access to the farms, livestock and businesses they left behind.

The repeated rescues show an ability to pursue kidnappers. The recurrence of abductions in the same broader theatre raises a different question: whether additional deployments are preventing attacks or mainly improving the ability of security forces to respond after attacks have already occurred.

The evidence does not show one bandit army sweeping across the North-west. It instead points to interconnected security theatres in which armed groups and their logistical networks can operate across boundaries, while local truces and security operations yield different outcomes from one community to another.

For residents, the measure of progress remains practical: whether attacks are prevented rather than merely answered, whether displaced families can return permanently, whether farmers can cultivate without risking abduction or coercive levies, and whether communities can rebuild the livelihoods they abandoned because of the violence.

World.title: Advancing food security through ONSA AgriShield Initiative, By Chido Onumah
World.content:
AgriShield reflects the Federal Government’s understanding that food security cannot be separated from human security. Military, intelligence and law-enforcement operations create the protective space; agricultural and financial institutions support production; communicators make verified progress visible; and civil society ensures that policy hears the people it affects. Each element reinforces the others. Farmers who feel protected are more likely to return to their fields. Communities that receive credible information are better placed to resist rumours, cooperate with authorities and report threats.

The Federal Government is strengthening the connection between national security and food security through the AgriShield Initiative, led by the National Counter Terrorism Centre in the Office of the National Security Adviser, in partnership with TAG International. The Borno State pilot focuses on a concern that reaches every Nigerian household: farmers must be able to reach their land, cultivate it and bring in the harvest without fear. By explaining the protection being provided and bringing community concerns into government planning, AgriShield supports agricultural recovery, safer livelihoods and a more secure national food supply.

AgriShield is a creative campaign under the NCTC strategic communication programme for counter-terrorism and countering violent extremism. Its central message, “Our Presence is Your Peace,” translates security from operational statistics into everyday outcomes. For a farming family, security means an open road to the farm, crops tended through the season and produce reaching the market. The campaign measures progress by threats removed, harvests secured and ordinary life restored.

This approach is grounded in research. Between June and July, a baseline survey covered 1,409 residents in 18 wards across Maiduguri Metropolitan Council, Jere and Mafa Local Government Areas. Only 17 per cent of respondents were aware of any local action to counter violent extremism, and only about one-third of that group could identify a security-related intervention. Awareness of the NCTC itself was about two per cent. Yet 86 per cent expressed strong interest in information about how government protects them. The findings point to a serious visibility gap: substantial work is being done, but too little of it is understood by the communities it is meant to serve.

The survey also showed why food security provides the right frame for engagement. Unemployment concerned 81 per cent of respondents, the cost of living 70 per cent and food insecurity 57 per cent, while terrorism was named by 29 per cent. About 83 per cent rejected extremist groups and the harm they cause. Government therefore need not convince these communities that violent extremism is destructive. It must demonstrate a credible alternative built around protection, livelihoods, visible delivery and hope, particularly for young people vulnerable to recruitment, irregular migration, drugs and despair.

AgriShield will run initially from October to December in Maiduguri Metropolitan Council, Jere and Mafa. It will combine radio programmes, community town halls, locally performed drama, recorded testimony from farmers and frontline officers, and carefully selected national media content. Four radio stations will carry 24 talk shows and 80 jingle slots in Hausa and Kanuri. Six town hall meetings, two in each local government area, will enable farmers, traditional and religious leaders, young people, women and security representatives to discuss practical concerns directly. An endline survey in December will return to the same wards to measure changes in awareness, trust and public understanding.

The channel mix reflects local evidence. Radio reaches 67 per cent of respondents and is the single most trusted source for 41 per cent. Community and religious leaders form the next most trusted category, while Facebook and TikTok are important for people under 30. AgriShield will therefore use radio for broad reach, credible local voices for trust and short-form digital content for younger audiences. It will also incorporate SMS and telephone engagement so that subsistence farmers are not excluded by limited internet access. Communication will remain two-way: questions and criticism from communities will inform weekly editorial decisions and subsequent messages.

A major strength of the initiative is the breadth of federal institutions that have committed their capabilities to it. At the first inter-agency coordination meeting convened by the NCTC-ONSA on 17 September, the Nigeria Police Force offered its state commands and public-relations network; Defence Headquarters offered its strategic communication structures, monthly briefings, Armed Forces Radio and service platforms; and the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps brought its Agro-Rangers mandate and field presence for the protection of farmers. The State Security Service committed intelligence support and early warning, while the Nigeria Immigration Service highlighted the cross-border dimensions of recruitment and youth migration.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Federal Radio Corporation of Nigeria offered its nationwide broadcast capacity in more than 25 Nigerian languages. The National Orientation Agency placed its 818 structures and over 4,000 personnel at the service of community mobilisation, dialogue, drama and local-language outreach. The Institute for Peace and Conflict Resolution offered state-level peace structures, trained dispute-resolution stakeholders and an early-warning volunteer network. NIRSAL Plc also committed institutional support. These bodies join the NCTC-ONSA in an emerging whole-of-government platform that connects security operations, agricultural resilience, public information, community participation and conflict prevention.

The pilot also relies on partners with strong local knowledge. The Network of Civil Society Organisations in Borno State, which brings together about 200 organisations, will support mobilisation and community delivery. Its grassroots reach complements the NCTC’s continuing engagement with the Partnership Against Violent Extremism network. TAG International provides technical partnership in research, campaign design, content support, monitoring and evaluation. The initiative is also enabled by the Federal Government’s partnership with the United Kingdom Government in strengthening strategic communication, community resilience and counter-terrorism cooperation.

Inter-agency cooperation is itself part of the message. Communities often interpret contradictory statements or isolated agency publicity as evidence of disorganisation. AgriShield establishes a common message platform, nominated communication focal points and a single NCTC clearing house. Operational claims will be verified by the responsible agency before publication, and sensitive information will be escalated through agreed channels. Agencies will appear together at community engagements and amplify verified campaign material through their existing platforms. This arrangement preserves accuracy, protects operations and allows citizens to see a coordinated Federal Government response.

The safeguards are equally important. The campaign will communicate verified operations and results without disclosing itineraries, compromising intelligence or exposing farmers and community messengers to retaliation. Planning will take account of possible extremist backlash, and field engagements will be limited to accessible locations agreed with the responsible security agencies. Local voices will be selected with care because formal gatekeepers are not equally trusted in every ward. Above all, the campaign will avoid exaggerated claims. Public confidence grows when official communication is accurate, timely and matched by visible action on the ground.

AgriShield reflects the Federal Government’s understanding that food security cannot be separated from human security. Military, intelligence and law-enforcement operations create the protective space; agricultural and financial institutions support production; communicators make verified progress visible; and civil society ensures that policy hears the people it affects. Each element reinforces the others. Farmers who feel protected are more likely to return to their fields. Communities that receive credible information are better placed to resist rumours, cooperate with authorities and report threats. Safe cultivation and harvests, in turn, strengthen livelihoods and reduce the economic pressures that violent groups exploit.

Through the NCTC-ONSA, TAG International, participating federal agencies, civil society and local leaders, AgriShield places the farmer at the centre of the national security conversation. The initiative recognises that every safely cultivated field contributes to stability and every protected harvest strengthens Nigeria’s food supply. That is the standard by which the campaign should be judged: credible information, responsive institutions, safer communities and more Nigerians able to produce food without surrendering their land or future to fear.

Chido Onumah is special adviser to the National Security Adviser on Strategic Communication and Civil Society Liaison.

World.title: Ibrahim Shehu Shema at 69: A legacy of service, By Oluwabusola Olawale
World.content:
Shema is widely regarded as one of the finest minds from northern Nigeria — a brilliant statesman and a national asset. He is a catalyst for institutional renewal, strategic vision, and interventions that consistently yield visible and measurable results. His record in both past and present leadership positions stands as clear testimony to his capacity. For the average Katsina resident, he remains a leader of remarkable distinction.

Today, 22 September, Dr Ibrahim Shehu Shema, CON, FNIM, former governor of Katsina State, will mark his 69th birthday. Known for his modesty, Shema consistently avoids discussions of personal or public achievements. For that reason, I take it upon myself each year to write about him — without his prior knowledge — lest he discourage the effort.

Shema is a man of quiet disposition, a leader whose work speaks louder than words. His results introduce him, and his record continues to resonate across Nigeria. It is not uncommon to hear people from diverse backgrounds remark, “Shema performed creditably well as governor.” While this is widely acknowledged, the weight of that truth struck me more deeply when I recently read an article comparing past and present administrations in Katsina State.

The writer emphasised that assessments must be based on verifiable facts rather than conjecture. He commended the incumbent governor, Dikko Umaru Radda, for notable achievements within a short period. Yet he also reminded readers of the contributions of earlier administrations, particularly those of the late Umaru Musa Yar’adua and Ibrahim Shehu Shema.

“When the late Malam Umaru Musa Yar’Adua assumed office from the military administration,” the article noted, “the state faced severe financial constraints, leaving little or no resources for immediate projects. He exercised prudence and patience, mobilising funds and making necessary savings. By the time he left office, Yar’Adua had inscribed his name in the annals of Katsina State’s history through transformative development and the solid foundation he laid for future progress.”

That foundation was further strengthened under Shema, whose tenure is still remembered for its impact across multiple sectors. His leadership style—anchored in humility and results—remains a benchmark for governance in Katsina State.

His successor, Ibrahim Shehu Shema, built upon the foundation laid by the late Umaru Musa Yar’adua, consolidating and expanding the state’s progress. Like Yar’adua, Shema made substantial contributions to the infrastructural and socio-economic development of Katsina State. Indeed, if the projects executed under his administration were removed, Katsina would lose many of the defining features that mark it as a modern urban centre.

Consider, for instance, the absence of the new Government House, the Ring Road, Karkanda Stadium, the Orthopaedic Hospital, KSITM, the Barhim, Sardauna, Fatima Shema, and Makera Housing Estates (comprising about 2,000 housing units), the ICT Institute, and Umaru Musa Yar’adua University. Without these landmark projects, Katsina’s transformation into a thriving capital would be incomplete.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Nearly 12 years after Shema left office, the enduring impact of his administration remains evident. The fact that removing his projects would strip Katsina of its modern character speaks volumes about his vision and leadership. He was a trailblazer in governance and infrastructure, remembered for human-centred policies and projects that left an indelible mark.

To call him a leader of uncommon performance and excellent service is no exaggeration. Recent developments further reinforce this belief. Shema has demonstrated an ability to turn situations around for good in record time. A case in point is his appointment as Chairman of the Governing Board of the Nigerian Shippers Council (NSC) by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu (GCFR). The Council was inaugurated on 19 January, following years of legislative and regulatory challenges.

In 2014, the Federal Government designated the NSC as the economic regulator for Nigeria’s ports through a presidential order, but without enabling legislation from the National Assembly. Efforts by successive assemblies to pass a permanent law faltered amid vested interests. In 2023, however, the Federal Government introduced the Nigeria Port Economic Regulatory Agency (NPERA) Bill under President Tinubu’s leadership. The bill sought to empower NPERA to regulate maritime service providers and set standards among port operators.

The legislation faced repeated delays between the National Assembly and the Presidency. Reflecting on this challenge shortly after his inauguration, Shema remarked at his Abuja residence: “President Tinubu’s passion to reposition Nigeria on the right path cannot be quantified. The President truly means well for this country. I resolved long ago to do my best to ensure his vision for a new Nigeria of renewed hope succeeds.”

Even before the 2023 presidential election, Shema consistently expressed this conviction. His words and actions continue to underscore his commitment to national progress and his reputation as a leader with a “touch of gold.”

True to his words, within three months as Chairman of the Nigerian Shippers Council (NSC), Dr. Ibrahim Shehu Shema leveraged his cordial relationship with the leadership of the National Assembly. On 28 April, the Senate passed the revised Nigeria Port Economic Regulatory Agency (NPERA) Bill during plenary. The bill was subsequently signed into law on 13 August by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, a leader determined to usher Nigeria into a new era of transformation.

Just days later, on 18 August, during a board meeting at NPERA headquarters in Lagos, management and staff gave Shema a heroic welcome. Their gesture symbolised appreciation for the dramatic transformation of the agency within the short period of his assumption of office. His “touch of gold” had already begun to leave a positive imprint, further confirming his reputation as a result-driven and impactful leader.

Shema is widely regarded as one of the finest minds from northern Nigeria — a brilliant statesman and a national asset. He is a catalyst for institutional renewal, strategic vision, and interventions that consistently yield visible and measurable results. His record in both past and present leadership positions stands as clear testimony to his capacity. For the average Katsina resident, he remains a leader of remarkable distinction.

In Katsina’s history, Shema stands out as a governor who ensured the completion of all projects inherited from previous administrations before embarking on new initiatives. His style is defined by a focus on results where others might offer excuses. He sees opportunities where others see challenges, and delivers success where others make promises. Conversations with him on governance reveal a depth of knowledge and vision that is both impressive and instructive. His intellectual prowess and command of issues are often described as a case study in leadership.

Beyond politics, Shema is a respected figurehead for many families outside his immediate household, admired for his integrity and guidance. He rarely criticises or indulges in praise, but he has remained consistent in acknowledging the leadership records of two figures in Nigeria: the late President Umaru Musa Yar’Adua and President Bola Ahmed Tinubu.

Shema often refers to Yar’Adua as his father, leader, and mentor. His commitment to the Yar’Adua family has been unwavering, even after the former president’s passing. For example, ahead of the APC primaries for the 2027 general elections, when some stakeholders urged Shema to contest for the Katsina Central senatorial seat — currently held by Senator Abdulazees Yar’Adua, the late president’s younger brother — he dismissed the idea. Laughing, he remarked: “That must be a joke. How can a member of the Yar’Adua family have interest in a position, and at the same time I desire the same thing? I have a sacred duty to protect the interest of anything that has to do with Yar’Adua.” His actions over the years have consistently reflected this principle.

The second personality he frequently pays glowing tribute to is President Bola Ahmed Tinubu (GCFR). Ahead of the 2023 presidential election, despite not being a member of the ruling APC, Shema pledged uncompromising support for Tinubu and his running mate, Senator Kashim Shettima. Without placing any demands, he directed his political structures to back their candidacy.

According to Shema, President Tinubu is the right leader to steer Nigeria out of difficulty. He often says that the measure of an exceptional leader lies not in doing what is popular, but in doing what is right. “What is popular may not be right. A good leader must have the courage to do what is right against all odds,” he has remarked. In his view, Tinubu exemplifies this courage, prioritising what is right above what is popular, regardless of public perception. Shema repeatedly emphasises that, irrespective of religion or ethnicity, Tinubu is a leader every Nigerian who truly desires the nation’s progress should support wholeheartedly.

“You cannot take away honour and integrity from President Tinubu, and nobody can reverse Nigeria’s misfortunes within just two or three years. Since the advent of democracy in 1999, no individual has impacted lives across the country like Tinubu. God has used him to help many people become what they are today on the national stage.”

Asiwaju, he added, is deeply loyal to his loyalists — though some have unfortunately taken advantage of that loyalty to act against the president’s interests.

“What he did during the burial of the late President Buhari further convinced me that Tinubu is a good man. Despite the challenges he faced during the 2023 presidential election, he sent his presidential aircraft to convey Buhari’s remains from London. He insisted that the body be placed inside the cabin of the aircraft, not in the cargo hold. Tinubu himself chose to fly to Katsina on a chartered flight instead, then travelled by road to Daura and directed key government officials to attend the state burial.”

Despite the difficulties he endured, Tinubu remained committed to Buhari even in death. It is public knowledge that he inherited a failed system of governance, yet he has accepted responsibility without shifting blame—a hallmark of distinguished leadership.

Since early 2025, Shema pledged to mobilise his political structures and devote his strength and resources to support President Tinubu’s re-election. True to his word, on 14 July, he established the Tinubu/Dikko Again 2027 Women and Youth Centre — a political structure unprecedented in the state’s history. The platform, which extends from polling units to wards, local governments, and the state level, is headed by Salisu Yusuf Majigiri, a member of the House of Representatives for Mashi/Dutsi Federal Constituency, as director general.

At the inauguration of the Centre, which drew the crème de la crème of Katsina politics, Governor Malam Umaru Dikko Radda declared: “This is a political structure that can win elections,” pledging his full support.

To my boss, leader, mentor, and father, I cannot say enough about you. I pray that Almighty God keeps you in good health. Happy birthday, sir.

Oluwabusola Olawale is Head of the Media Team in the office of former Governor Ibrahim Shehu Shema.

World.title: Network upgrades are announced, and people still carry two SIMs
World.content:
Nigeria’s telecommunications sector is transforming, with operators promising faster speeds and more reliable networks through the rollout of 4G and 5G technologies. These announcements dominate industry news and fuel hopes of a more connected future.

Yet, in the midst of these advancements, millions of Nigerians continue to rely on two SIM cards in their daily lives. This practice is not just a habit—it’s a practical response to persistent concerns about network coverage, affordability, and the unpredictability of service. The continued popularity of dual SIM usage offers a revealing window into the realities facing mobile users and highlights the gap between cutting-edge ambitions and the challenges encountered on the ground.

Carrying two SIMs: everyday calculations, not just old habits

For most Nigerians, carrying two SIM cards goes far beyond tradition or convenience. It’s a flexible response to the daily challenges of staying connected, where network signals can waver and data prices shift unexpectedly.

Every call and data session becomes a small decision—will this SIM give me clearer reception or is the other one offering better rates today? It’s not unusual for someone to swap between SIMs in the middle of the day, depending on which provider is delivering more stable service or a bonus on data bundles at that moment.

This balancing act is especially visible for those who rely on their phones for both work and personal life. Some keep one SIM for business, making sure it’s always reachable, while the second one is used for streaming, social media, or connecting with family. The lines between work and leisure blur, but the need for reliability stays constant.

Travel across different regions adds another layer. Coverage can change dramatically from one town to the next, so a backup SIM can mean the difference between staying in touch and being cut off entirely. It’s not just about preference—it’s a calculated survival tactic in an environment where no single network offers a guarantee.

Globally, this kind of SIM juggling is familiar to audiences who might compare their experiences with other communication tools, like those discussed at https://pokerguru.lt/, reflecting a shared search for flexibility and control in how we connect.

Promises of better networks, the reality on the ground

While the search for flexibility is a global phenomenon, in Nigeria, the promise of better networks often clashes with the daily reality of inconsistent service.

Telecom operators regularly share news of new investments, upgrades, and ambitious rollouts. Announcements of advanced technologies and improvements—like the widely reported MTN Ericsson network upgrade—spark hope for faster data and reliable calls.

But for a large segment of users, these upgrades are more rumor than reality. In urban centers, some people notice a boost in speed or improved call clarity, but these benefits can vanish just a few neighborhoods away. For those in rural or peri-urban regions, the so-called leap to 4G or 5G may feel like it’s happening on another continent entirely.

Even with millions of active lines and a growing number of 5G connections, gaps in coverage remain stubborn. No matter how impressive the statistics or headlines, many Nigerians still face dropped calls, slow internet, and sudden outages—forcing a reliance on backup SIMs to bridge the gap.

For most, carrying two SIMs is not about habit but about necessity. The reality is simple: until every corner of the country experiences the consistency so often promised, the backup SIM will remain a quiet companion—ready for the moment when technology’s promise falls short.

Coverage, costs, and the evolving SIM economy

But the need for a backup SIM is about more than just reliability—money matters just as much. For Nigerians navigating daily costs, even small differences in call rates or data bundles can shape which SIM is used and when.

A single phone can become a mini cost-control center: one SIM for calls when bonuses apply, the other for data when a special offer pops up. People pay close attention to new deals, shifting between operators to stretch their naira further, especially as tariffs and promotions change with little notice.

The aftermath of the NIN–SIM policy showed just how responsive users can be. After a steep drop in active lines, numbers have started climbing again, showing that practical needs outweigh administrative hurdles. As Telecom subscriptions rise, it’s clear that owning two SIMs is a rational hedge—one that gives consumers leverage in a market where prices, packages, and even network access can shift overnight.

Brand loyalty fades in the face of these realities. For most, the few extra naira spent on a second SIM is well worth the flexibility and peace of mind it brings, especially with Nigeria’s telecom landscape still in flux.

a slow march toward single SIM dependence?

The telecom landscape is evolving, but the shift toward relying on a single SIM card is happening slowly, if at all. For every headline touting progress, countless users quietly weigh whether network improvements are enough to justify giving up their second line.

Recent achievements, like the milestone of Nigeria’s 5G connections December 2024, suggest a country inching closer to true digital connectivity. Still, for most subscribers, the promise of smoother, high-speed service feels patchy and uneven.

There’s a cautious optimism in the air, but it’s tempered by everyday experience. Calls still drop without warning, data speeds fluctuate, and outages linger in memory far longer than the excitement of a network upgrade announcement.

Some early adopters are tempted to simplify, letting go of their backup SIM as they find their preferred provider more reliable. Yet, that step requires a confidence most consumers don’t yet feel. The risk of losing access—even for a day—looms larger than the hassle of carrying two tiny cards.

For telecom operators, the stubborn dual SIM habit is both a practical puzzle and a signal. If the goal is real trust in a single network, the investment must go deeper than the infrastructure headlines, reaching every corner of Nigeria and every user experience. Until then, the double SIM remains a quiet insurance policy in millions of pockets.

Behind the upgrade announcements: What dual SIMs reveal about Nigeria’s digital divide

This quiet insurance policy, kept alive by millions, highlights a deeper digital divide that persists even as industry headlines celebrate progress. The everyday experience of Nigerian subscribers often stands in contrast to the bold claims of seamless advancement.

While stories about new infrastructure and Airtel network investments dominate the news, the true measure of progress comes down to whether people actually feel connected, treated fairly, and able to afford the services they need. As long as reliable coverage is inconsistent and costs fluctuate, holding onto two SIMs remains a practical response—an everyday workaround for a network that doesn’t always deliver on its promises.

In the end, the story told by the phones in people’s pockets is more complicated than any press release. It’s a reminder that real change happens not just with new towers or faster networks, but with the trust and confidence of every user.

World.title: Cashout delays are where trust breaks online
World.content:
When you play on an online gambling site, few moments matter more than when you ask to cash out your winnings. This is where your confidence in the site gets put to the test.

A smooth, prompt payout reassures you that things are fair. But when cashouts stall or the process feels unpredictable, doubts creep in—fast. You’re not the only one who feels this way; frustration over delays spreads through player communities and forums almost immediately.

People start questioning not just the speed, but the reliability, security, and even the fairness of the games themselves. In 2026, cashout speed isn’t just a customer service detail—it’s a make-or-break factor for every operator’s reputation.

Where delays start: a player’s tipping point

That first hint of a delay in getting your winnings isn’t just an inconvenience—it’s the point where hope quietly turns into doubt. One moment you’re excited to see the money appear in your account, and the next, you’re refreshing the page, wondering if something’s gone wrong.

Even a minor holdup can set off a string of questions. Why is it taking longer this time? Is there a problem with my account, or is the site itself having issues? It doesn’t take much for these small worries to snowball, especially when the platform’s explanations are vague or slow to come. The longer you wait without clear answers, the more suspicion creeps in and the less you want to believe that everything is normal.

This is the moment when normal withdrawal steps start feeling like roadblocks. Across forums and chat groups, you can see how quickly players move from patient to frustrated, comparing notes and sharing their own stories of waiting. When communication is unclear, it’s easy for rumors to spread—suddenly, one person’s delay becomes the cautionary tale for dozens more.

Platforms like LT BET come up again and again in these conversations. Real players talk openly about how their loyalty is tested when withdrawals become a guessing game. It’s not just about missing money; it’s a signal that maybe your trust in the site wasn’t as strong as you thought.

Delayed payouts: The ripple through communities and forums

When withdrawals drag on, players rarely keep it to themselves. Instead, they share their stories in group chats, forums, and public review threads—places where a single complaint can echo far and wide.

Someone posts about waiting days for their money, and suddenly others chime in with similar experiences. What started as a single delay turns into a pattern, and that pattern quickly changes how people talk about the site as a whole. These conversations move quickly, often gaining attention faster than any official statement can clarify or calm things down.

Every time a thread about withdrawal verification delays goes viral, it makes even loyal users second-guess their choices. It’s not just about one person’s cashout anymore; the whole community starts to wonder if their own funds are safe or if their next withdrawal will hit the same snags.

Research this year has shown that these moments of uncertainty do real damage. Once trust is shaken through just a few bad payout cycles, the ripple can linger in forum archives and player memories much longer than any technical fix or apology can repair.

Behind the scenes: why verification delays keep happening

Behind every delayed payout sits a quiet, complicated battle most players never see. Operators are under pressure to move money fast, but they’re also staring down a sharp rise in fraud that targets cashouts right when excitement peaks.

To protect their businesses and their players, many sites have added extra ID and anti-fraud checks—especially in regulated markets. But from the player’s point of view, this just feels like more waiting with little explanation. It’s a trade-off that rarely feels fair in the moment.

The numbers tell the story. Over the past two years, fraud rates in iGaming have surged by nearly 40% at both the signup and withdrawal stages, according to recent analysis. This spike has made every transaction subject to tighter scrutiny, turning what used to be routine into something unpredictable and tense.

Even when these checks genuinely catch threats, the process can add days to a withdrawal. Many players aren’t reassured by the reasoning—they just see their winnings locked behind a process that feels arbitrary. The Online-Casinos.com study on withdrawal speed highlights that quick, seamless payouts now top the list of what builds trust, but the reality behind the scenes remains messier than most realize.

Speed as a signal: how instant payouts are shifting the market

This focus on withdrawal speed isn’t just a trend—it’s quickly becoming the new baseline for what players expect from an online casino. Operators that have introduced instant or near-instant payouts are setting themselves apart, drawing attention from both seasoned gamblers and newcomers who see fast cashouts as a sign of a reliable site.

Industry data shows that when players find a platform with proven quick withdrawals, word spreads fast. Conversations in forums and review sites now revolve around which casinos actually deliver on their promise of speed, influencing reputation rankings and reshaping the standards across the industry. In places like Nigeria, where skepticism about slow payments is common, players are especially likely to share experiences and steer others toward sites known for efficiency.

For many, the label of “trustworthy” now hinges on this single factor. Operators who can consistently provide instant access to winnings, like those highlighted by the growing interest in the instant payment casino model, are raising the bar for the entire sector. The gap between what players want and what some platforms deliver is now more visible than ever, and the pressure to keep up is reshaping the market from the ground up.

When trust is lost: long-term consequences for platforms

As instant payout models redefine what players expect, the fallout for operators that fall behind is hard to ignore. When cashout delays stack up, frustration doesn’t just fade—it builds, leaving brands with a reputation that can be tough to shake.

Players who feel let down by slow or unpredictable withdrawals rarely keep it to themselves. Stories of delayed payouts echo through forums and social media, putting a spotlight on companies that mishandle these moments. Over time, a few negative experiences can snowball, turning a brand into a warning sign rather than a place to play.

The impact goes deeper than just lost business. Platforms that don’t address payout issues face scrutiny from regulators and risk being listed in reports like the Gambling Commission’s report on consumer trust, which noted that repeated withdrawal problems erode confidence across entire markets. Once trust is broken, former users set a higher bar for any comeback, referencing old complaints and reviews before even considering a return.

Ultimately, the speed and reliability of payouts shape whether players feel respected—or decide it’s time to move on. For operators, regaining trust means more than fixing a single issue. It’s a long climb back, built on every withdrawal that goes right from here on out.

Turning the tide: restoring faith in the payout process

So what actually helps rebuild trust once it’s been shaken? Clearer communication is a good place to start. When players know exactly what to expect, the uneasy wait feels less like a question mark and more like a process with an end in sight.

Platforms that keep users updated on withdrawal status and resolve issues quickly are already setting themselves apart. Visible progress bars, honest notifications about delays, and responsive support teams all signal that a site takes payouts seriously. These changes don’t just ease nerves in the moment—they build a new baseline for reliability.

It’s this consistency that matters most. Every smooth, timely cashout helps repair what delays have damaged, and every honest update adds a little more confidence. Ultimately, the path forward is simple but not easy: keep the promises made at the cashout screen, and trust will follow.

World.title: Dangote plans $10bn power investment across Nigeria, Africa
World.content:
By Okeagu Oluchi

President of Dangote Group, Aliko Dangote, has announced plans to invest more than $10 billion in Africa’s power sector over the next three to four years, describing electricity as critical to the continent’s economic transformation. Dangote disclosed this in an interview with Al Jazeera uploaded on Monday, saying the investment would support what he expects to be a major transformation across Africa.

“The next, three, four years, there will be a major transformation in Africa. And that’s why we’re looking at power, for example”, he said.

Explaining the plan, Dangote said the group could redirect funds from some proposed businesses, including steel, into electricity projects.

“We are going to invest in power. We want to, actually, there are one or two businesses that we might cancel, like steel, and we will put in the money. We want to invest over $10 billion alone in power,” he said.

He identified Africa’s electricity deficit as one of the continent’s major development challenges, noting that more than 600 million Africans still lack access to electricity. “It is something that we Africans should not really allow. Over 600 million of our people to remain in darkness,” Dangote said.

According to him, expanding access to reliable electricity would have implications beyond households, supporting industrial activity, investment and broader economic growth.

World.title: NSIA unveils  $300m Renewable Energy Fund
World.content:
By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief

The Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority, (NSIA) has launched the $300 million Nigeria Distributed Renewable Energy (DRE) Fund, a new investment vehicle designed to accelerate private-sector investment in renewable energy and expand electricity access to underserved communities and businesses across the country.

The Fund, which reached its commercial launch milestone on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, marks the transition from fund structuring to active capital deployment in Nigeria’s distributed renewable energy sector, according to a statement by the organisation yesterday.

The initiative is being implemented through a partnership involving the NSIA; Africa50; Sustainable Energy for All, SEforALL; and the World Bank, with the International Solar Alliance also supporting the broader continental vision.

Speaking on the launch, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of NSIA, Aminu Umar-Sadiq, described the milestone as a strategic signal to investors and development partners that Nigeria’s distributed renewable energy market was ready for investment at scale.

Umar-Sadiq was quoted as saying, “This is a major development milestone. It is a strategic signal to markets, investors, governments and development partners that Nigeria’s distributed renewable energy market is investable, credible and ready to operate at scale.”

According to him, the commercial launch would help move the sector from fund structuring into actual deployment of capital for renewable energy projects across the country.

Chief Executive Officer of Africa50, Alain Ebobissé, said the strength of the partnership behind the Fund was one of its major advantages, combining NSIA’s knowledge of the Nigerian market with Africa50’s pan-African investment and fund-management capabilities.

He said SEforALL brought energy-access expertise to the platform, while the World Bank provided global energy-sector leadership and catalytic capital.

Also speaking, SEforALL Chief Executive Officer and Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General for Sustainable Energy for All, Damilola Ogunbiyi, said the commercial launch represented an important step towards achieving Nigeria’s electricity-access ambitions and advancing Mission 300.

She said the creation of a dedicated financing mechanism for distributed renewable energy demonstrated how country-led initiatives could translate the continental electricity-access ambition into concrete investments and electricity connections.

Director General of the International Solar Alliance, Ashish Khanna, described the Fund as a landmark initiative within the Mission 300 platform, particularly because of its potential to demonstrate how innovative financing structures could mobilise private capital for distributed renewable energy.

Managing Director of Operations, World Bank Group, Anna Bjerde, said reliable and affordable electricity was critical to job creation and economic transformation across Africa.

World.title: Vehicle imports jump 42.5% to 103,375 in H1’26 — NPA
World.content:
By Godwin Oritse

The Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA) has recorded importation of 103,375 units of vehicles in the first half of 2026, H1’26, about 42.5 percent rise against 72,568 units handled during the same period in 2025, H1’25.

The figure was disclosed at the quarterly meeting of the Port Consultative Council (PCC) in Lagos, where the NPA presented its first-half operational performance.

The Managing Director of NPA, Dr Abubakar Dantsoho, represented by the Principal Manager, Statistics, Mrs Okenwa Igwebuike, attributed the sharp rise in vehicle traffic largely to transhipment activities at the PTML Terminal.

The development made vehicle handling one of the areas with significant growth in the authority’s half-year performance scorecard.

The authority said the comparison was aimed at tracking operational trends and measuring overall port performance during the period.

The vehicle import surge came against the backdrop of an overall positive performance across nearly every major indicator tracked by the Authority.

Vessel calls at Nigerian ports rose to 2,152 in H1’26, a 6.9 per cent increase, while gross registered earnings climbed to 96,693,108 from 79,981,595 recorded in the H1’25, representing a 20.9 per cent jump.

Total cargo throughput across the nation’s ports stood at 68,294,210 metric tons, up 12.2 per cent from 60,844,521 metric tons handled in the same period last year. Inward cargo alone accounted for 38,411,323 metric tons, against 36,338,068 metric tons in H1’25, an increase of 5.6 per cent.

Lekki Port emerged as the standout performer among the nation’s port locations, recording a 48.4 per cent increase in vessel calls and now handling nearly 40 per cent of total national cargo throughput, a growth the Authority attributed largely to operations at the Dangote Refinery, which accounted for 76 per cent of total cargo traffic recorded at the port during the review period.

Onne Port also posted strong growth, with a 26.6 per cent rise in vessel calls, supported largely by LNG exports and now accounting for 22.7 per cent of national cargo throughput.

Calabar and Rivers ports remained marginal contributors, jointly accounting for just over 4.0 per cent of cargo handled nationwide.

But all other port locations recorded a decline in vessel calls during the period.

Container traffic also trended upward, with total throughput reaching 815,346 TEUs, a 10.3 per cent increase over the 709,142 TEUs recorded in the first half of 2025.

Container imports made up the bulk of this volume at 546,755 TEUs, or 67 per cent of total container traffic, while exports stood at 203,980 TEUs, representing 25 per cent.

Transhipment traffic recorded the steepest growth of any container category, rising 169.5 per cent to 35,570 TEUs from 13,199 TEUs in the corresponding period last year, though it still accounts for just 4 per cent of overall container traffic.

Not all indicators trended positively. Ship turnaround time worsened, with vessels spending an average of 5.3 days at berth compared with a shorter turnaround recorded in the same period of 2025, a decline the report attributed a 6 per cent negative performance to.

Presenting the report, the NPA boss said the Authority’s benchmarking exercise against 2025 was designed to give the Port Consultative Council clear insight into operational performance indicators and developments in port activities from January to June 2026, in support of strategic decision-making.

The report identified the Dangote Refinery as a defining factor in the sector’s growth trajectory, noting that the facility now accounts for approximately 40 per cent of total annual port traffic.

World.title: Dangote Refinery IPO offers investment opportunity to Nigerians — FCMB
World.content:
Nigerians can invest in Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals FZE with a minimum subscription of N5,250 under an initial public offering launched Monday. The company is offering 4.1 billion ordinary shares at N525 each.

FCMB Group Chief Executive, LadiBalogun, said the offer gives Nigerians access to a world-scale business while demonstrating the growing reach of the country’s capital market.

“It presents an opportunity for every Nigerian to experience the benefits of investing in world-class and world-scale businesses that would otherwise be inaccessible,” Balogun said at the opening gong ceremony and ‘Facts Behind the Offer’ presentation at the Nigerian Exchange in Lagos.

The minimum subscription is 10 shares, allowing individual investors to participate with N5,250.

“This is an IPO for the people,” President of Dangote Industries, Aliko Dangote, said, adding, “We want Nigerians across various segments, including drivers, cooks, traders, employees and managers, to have an opportunity to own a stake in the refinery.”

According to Balogun Nigeria’s capital market was deepening as it attracted retail, high-net-worth, institutional and international investors through a widening range of channels.

He stated further: “Retail investors are buying shares on their mobile phones through fintechs.

“High-net-worth individuals and institutional investors such as pension funds are bringing depth to the market, while international investors are bringing scale.”

He said the breadth of participation demonstrated the market’s capacity to help credible Nigerian companies raise capital at scale. Balogun also described the refinery as largely insulated from the macroeconomic and currency risks associated with the Nigerian economy.

“The number of such companies on our Exchange is growing,” he said. “This indicates the potential and direction of the Nigerian economy.”

FCMB Group is participating in the transaction through three operating companies, including FCMB Capital Markets as a joint issuing house, CSL Stockbrokers as a stockbroker to the issue, and First City Monument Bank is a receiving bank and distribution agent.

Explaining the plan, Dangote said the group could redirect funds from some proposed businesses, including steel, into electricity projects.
