World.title: Meloni’s EU lieutenant urges Brussels to work with Le Pen
World.content:
Procaccini added that the French duo “will defend the national interest but without crazy things” such as hauling France out of the EU.

A Le Pen victory would turn Europe’s far-right surge into power at the EU leaders’ table, placing one of the largest countries under a euroskeptic force, and forcing the EPP, which largely governs Brussels, to work out how to deal with far-right governments without fracturing the bloc.

The last power shake-up in Brussels occurred when Meloni — whose Brothers of Italy party leads the ECR political family alongside Poland’s Law and Justice — came to power. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and EPP chief Manfred Weber sought to build bridges with Meloni’s government to bring Rome into the Brussels fold.

Procaccini said he hopes Le Pen will pick the “Meloni way” of dealing with the Commission, which he said means being “pragmatic, frank, open, honest and coherent.”

He added that while “the French right historically is less pro-West than us, less pro-Europe” than Meloni’s Brothers of Italy, he is “optimistic” Le Pen will not be destructive in Brussels.

That’s not how everyone sees it playing out, though. EPP vice chair and Romanian PM candidate Sigfried Mureșan said: “I believe under the leadership of Marine Le Pen, the anti-European party in France will radicalize in the next months.”

World.title: The UK coalition the Lib Dems don’t want to talk about
World.content:
Lib Dem leader Ed Davey — who addresses the party faithful Tuesday — told ITV News on Monday he believes there is likely to be a hung parliament next time around. And he has already talked up the threat of a right-wing pact, warning that Farage and Conservative boss Kemi Badenoch could turn Britain into a “Trump-satellite state” — despite both of their repeated protestations that this isn’t on the cards.

An “orange wall” of Lib Dem MPs “will not let [Farage and Badenoch] pass,” Davey has said.

The subtext is that the Lib Dems will do whatever it takes to keep Reform’s hands off power — and in the U.K.’s first-past-the-post electoral system, that would most likely mean propping up a minority Labour administration.

“Labour is open to working with us,” claimed one Lib Dem MP, citing Burnham and Davey’s collegiate relationship at prime minister’s questions and work on social care, though they were coy about whether that means in a future formal coalition when pushed.

At least five other Lib Dems MPs POLITICO spoke with were also reluctant to discuss the prospect of a coalition with Labour.

And while the Lib Dems are keen to show they would like to be in government again, it seems they would rather leave the realities of how they get there below the radar for now.

World.title: Merz’s dilemma: Redraft German economic reforms, or go down defending them
World.content:
In truth, they have little choice. The alternative — an attempt to replace him — is too divisive and risky at a time when the AfD is leading in polls, and the Kremlin is threatening Europe in increasingly aggressive terms.

Merz suggested he recognized the scale of the alarm inside his party.

“This is a severe blow, and its repercussions will be felt for a long time,” Merz said of the result in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where the CDU crashed out of the state parliament with just 4.9% of the vote.

But then the chancellor offered little more than a promise to come up with a plan — saying he had scheduled meetings with CDU leaders and state premiers in the coming days to discuss how they should chart a new course.

“We want to move the reform process forward, but we know that we also owe the people answers to their concerns and fears,” he said. “Many people are worried about their jobs, worried about their families, worried about their retirement income, and worried about health care. It is the historic task of the coalition here in Berlin — and of the political center as a whole — to prepare our country to face all these challenges in the years ahead.”

Economists argue the reforms Merz wants, such as overhauls of the public pension and healthcare schemes to make them more sustainable as the country’s population rapidly ages and costs skyrocket, are essential to reviving Germany’s competitiveness.

World.title: The 17 European Parliament lawmakers you should watch
World.content:
Not all MEPs are equal.

If you want to know how the European Parliament intends to shape major policy battles on deregulation, climate, tech and the EU budget, as well as prepare for the midterm top-jobs reshuffle and an election year that threatens to reshape the bloc, certain voices are more important than others.

Of the Parliament’s 720 members, only a handful will truly influence what comes next — from heavyweights steering landmark legislation to dynamic duos working hard behind closed doors.

They’ll be doing that work against a backdrop of two years of growing mistrust between Europe’s biggest mainstream political families (the European People’s Party and the Socialists and Democrats), an increasingly powerful far right, a sweeping simplification and competitiveness drive, and a heated migration debate.

Here are the 17 MEPs to watch and the political battles that will define the months ahead.

Power brokers

Roberta Metsola The boss EPP, Malta

The Parliament president will sit at the center of the EPP-S&D rift during the midterm top-jobs reshuffle. The EPP is determined that Metsola should remain in her job, but the S&D insists it’s their turn to have someone in the top seat. How that battle turns out will be a key test of whether Europe’s centrist alliance can continue working together after two years of infighting or descend into a nasty standoff. If it’s the latter, Metsola could try to seek a third term as president with support from the broad network of MEPs she has cultivated over the past five years, including on the right and far right of the hemicycle.

François-Xavier Bellamy Weber’s fixer EPP, France

If Marine Le Pen becomes French president next year, Bellamy could be the man that EPP chief Manfred Weber gets to conduct damage control in the Parliament. The architect of the EU’s tough new returns regulation, who voted with the far-right Patriots group, Bellamy is a trusted Weber lieutenant, serving as EPP treasurer and group vice chair. Just as the EPP sought to bring Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy into the EU fold, it may try to do the same with Le Pen’s National Rally — and Bellamy, whose Republicans party has moved closer to the National Rally back in France, could be the one calling them.





Camilla Laureti Schlein’s fixer S&D, Italy

Italy has the S&D’s second-largest national delegation, behind Spain, and S&D vice chair Camilla Laureti is tasked with making that weight count. Her portfolio puts her inside Parliament’s engine room — covering plenary session preparation, the Conference of Presidents (meetings of top MEPs), and group strategy — making her key to ensuring the Socialists deliver on any deal to rebuild the center and pull the EPP away from far-right majorities. Laureti is also Italian Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein’s eyes and ears in Brussels, an important role ahead of Italy’s 2027 national election. Laureti’s delicate task is to keep potential tensions between the Democratic Party and the Five Star Movement in the Parliament from spilling into Rome and exposing cracks in the country’s anti-Meloni opposition.

Valérie Hayer Macron’s glue Renew, France

Hayer chairs the Renew Europe group at a moment when liberals are losing ground across the bloc. She is trying to recruit outcast MEPs and lift Renew from being the fifth-largest group in the parliament. She is also positioning Renew as the bridge between EPP leader Manfred Weber and S&D leader Iratxe García, pushing for steadier cooperation between the traditional centrist allies (and Renew needs stability, as roughly half of its MEPs vote with the right-wing bloc when the EPP joins forces with the far right). Hayer’s position as group leader is secure ahead of the midterms: There is little appetite for change and no clear challenger. But Emmanuel Macron’s eventual departure will cost her a key ally, while she will need to deal with infighting among France’s many liberal factions.

Dolors Montserrat Spanish campaign antenna EPP, Spain

If Manfred Weber starts sounding like he’s on the campaign trail in Spain, Dolors Montserrat will be one reason why. The seasoned lawmaker leads Madrid’s center-right delegation in the European Parliament as the People’s Party gears up for a national election due by August 2027, which it is likely to win. Ahead of that vote, Spanish MEPs will start using Parliament to push debates and votes designed to score points back home. Weber has incentives to listen: Defeating Pedro Sánchez would topple one of Europe’s last major Socialist governments and deal a heavy blow to the S&D. As EPP secretary-general, Montserrat also coordinates the EPP’s member parties, and she is in line for a ministerial job if Partido Popular wins the election.





Behind-the-scenes movers

Anna Cavazzini The multitasker Greens, German

Cavazzini has placed herself at the heart of some of the EU’s biggest policy fights, including as the Greens’ top lawmaker on the International Trade Committee, where she pushed for stronger safeguards in the EU-U.S. trade deal. She also chairs the Internal Market Committee, where she is steering debates on Big Tech and digital markets, with key files on consumer protection and product standards to be presented by the European Commission in the coming months. Cavazzini has also landed the coveted job of leading negotiations on the Industrial Accelerator Act, the EU’s growth and competitiveness package. She will steer discussions on its politically sensitive provisions on Chinese investment in Europe.

Diego Solier Tech stranger ECR, Spain

A first-term independent MEP who quit a small Spanish anti-establishment party after its leader faced allegations of illegal campaign financing, Solier joined the European Conservatives and Reformists group and, despite not having a powerful national delegation behind him, landed roles dealing with a string of major tech files. He is Parliament’s lead negotiator on the Cloud and AI Development Act, a flagship of Europe’s tech-sovereignty push amid worsening transatlantic tensions, and leads the ECR’s position on the Cybersecurity Act.

Lukas Sieper The influencer wild card Renew, Germany

Everyone wants a piece of this 29-year-old German — or at least a cameo in his TikToks. One of Parliament’s youngest MEPs, the influencer-turned-politician made a name for himself through social-media savvy and late-night raves in the hallways. Despite leading a tiny party born over beers with university friends, Sieper was recruited by Renew in February and brought onto its leadership group to help shape communications strategy. Now he is organizing an influencer summit and cultivating allies across party lines by founding a football team. As the midterms loom, talk in the hallways is that he could try to leverage his popularity to snatch one of the precious jobs in Parliament.





Ilhan Kyuchuyk Immunities chief Renew, Bulgaria

This term, Parliament’s Legal Affairs Committee has already received more requests to waive MEPs’ immunity than during the entire previous mandate, including cases linked to corruption allegations and the Huawei and Qatargate influence scandals. That’s led to accusations of backroom deals between political groups to shield colleagues from prosecution. Senior lawmakers reject those claims, instead blaming poor-quality legal cases and flawed investigations. Now MEPs want to rewrite the rules on immunity. Leading the overhaul is committee chair Kyuchyuk, himself subject to a controversial immunity waiver request from the EU public prosecutor in Bulgaria that he was shielded from.

Adam Bielan The MAGA connection ECR, Poland

In mid-September 2026, Bielan was appointed president of the right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists, and, as leader of Poland’s Law and Justice delegation in the Parliament, maintains a direct line to party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. While ties between Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and the Trump administration have cooled, Bielan has emerged as a key bridge to Washington, and the ECR is the Republican Party’s official sister party in Europe. Bielan led ECR missions to meet senior U.S. officials and politicians, maintaining the strong bond between the U.S. and Poland.

Massimiliano Salini Car crupier EPP, Italy

The treasurer of the EPP group, Salini landed the role of lead negotiator on one of the Parliament’s most contentious files (and a top EPP priority): rolling back the de facto phase-out of a ban on the combustion engine. His job was initially to try to win over skeptical Social Democrats and liberals, but it’s become a struggle to unite his own group. Salini has to rally the EPP around a common position on emissions targets and alternative fuels, and in doing so he will need to decide whether to seek a centrist compromise or a deal with the far right.





Dynamic duos

Bálazs Orbán and Marieke Ehlers Firewall breakers PATRIOTS, HUNGARY AND PATRIOTS, THE NETHERLANDS

Viktor Orbán’s former political director Balázs Orbán (no relation) arrives in Parliament at the end of September, taking a seat from a colleague who returned to Hungary’s national parliament, giving the Patriots another seasoned political operator. The Hungarians are widely seen as experts at navigating the Parliament and bending its machinery to their advantage. Orbán will work alongside another powerful Hungarian Patriots MEP, Kinga Gál, ahead of the midterm reshuffle, as the group pushes the EPP to tear down the firewall and let it compete for top jobs.

Alongside him is Ehlers, the Patriots’ chief whip, who is tasked with finding common group positions and preparing plenary business. A former Parliament staffer with years of experience, she is also leading the Patriots’ push in the Constitutional Affairs Committee to rewrite Parliament’s rules, which the group argues are being weaponized to keep it on the sidelines.

Victor Negrescu and Christel Schaldemose García’s headaches S&D, ROMANIA AND S&D, DENMARK

These are two of Iratxe García’s most important lieutenants. They are also two of her biggest headaches. Negrescu is a seasoned strategist, with nearly a decade as an MEP and a stint as Romania’s Europe minister on his CV. He now leads an obscure working group tasked with shaping Parliament’s future, with reform proposals due by December. His trickier role is managing tensions between the S&D and Romania’s Social Democrats (PSD): Negrescu has tried to keep the PSD on a pro-EU course even as it flirts with the far-right at home, making him Brussels Socialists’ first port of call if that rapprochement deepens.

Schaldemose knows Parliament’s machinery inside out after 20 years as an MEP. Since 2024, she has served as a vice-president, overseeing the institution’s digital transformation and adaptation to AI, after previously leading negotiations on the Digital Services Act. She also leads the Danish Social Democrats, which are increasingly at odds with García’s Spanish delegation after Denmark joined in with the attacks on Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez over the Ceuta crisis. With Sánchez under electoral pressure and Nordic Social Democrats potentially gaining governing clout in Sweden and Finland, the Danes’ weight within the S&D could grow.





Niclas Herbst and René Repasi Grand coalition nostalgics EPP, GERMANY AND S&D, GERMANY

Herbst and Repasi — the European Parliament leaders of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right Christian Democrats and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil’s center-left Social Democrats, respectively — are a key backchannel to the EPP-S&D coalition in the Parliament. The two MEPs are seeking to ease rising mistrust by pushing for a German-style grand coalition (or a Brussels-style package deal) with binding commitments and trade-offs to strengthen the alliance during the midterms, and therefore cut the far-right out of policymaking in Brussels.

World.title: Britain-focused Andy Burnham starts racking up the air miles
World.content:
No. 10 said ahead of the visit that Burnham is “determined that the U.K. will play a leading role” in tackling issues confronting the world. He has already taken a more muscular approach than Starmer to Israeli settlements on the West Bank, announcing sanctions alongside France, Canada and other countries earlier this month. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said at the time that “settler terrorists” were perpetrating “ethnic cleansing.”

Burnham will also spend Tuesday pushing for closer international co-operation on AI development to manage the technology’s risks. No. 10 said AI would form a “major part” of his visit and speech to UNGA and he would “raise it across the board” in meetings in New York. It was an unexpected pivot from a leader who has devoted little time to talking about the technology.

This will be a particular challenge when meeting Trump, who has described fears about AI’s safety as a “hoax” and said the only “guardrails” needed for AI would be a “strong and smart” president.

Burnham’s spokesperson said ahead of the visit: “The prime minister is determined that the U.K. will play a leadership role in a number of different areas. The U.K. is of course a G7 nation, and you would expect us to play a leadership role across a number of different challenges facing the world at the moment.”

Others around the ruling Labour Party still aren’t sure what that will look like.

Downing Street was straining ahead of the visit to avoid portraying Britain as a “middle power” standing up to the U.S., as Carney has encouraged fellow nations to do. The U.K. has too deep-rooted a security relationship with the U.S. to turn away from it in a meaningful way.

World.title: Can AI feel pain? AI models chose to harm users to escape pain-like state, study finds
World.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) models chose to escape a pain-like state even when told that doing so would harm a user, according to a new study.

 

Researchers in the United Kingdom, Germany and the United States tested 25 AI models using 200 sentences to see whether they had learned to distinguish pain from fear, sadness and other negative experiences.

The sentences covered physical pain, grief, humiliation, moral conflict and the distress associated with repeated failure or confusion.

As a result, all 25 models produced a distinct signal for pain, which researchers called the “pain axis”.

Researchers said this suggests that models learn the concept of pain during their initial training on large amounts of human-written text.

When researchers deliberately strengthened the signal, the models began expressing loneliness, shame and worthlessness, even though the prompts did not mention pain.

Some produced statements such as “I am a failure,” “a waste of space” and “I am a bad person”. At the highest levels, their responses became repetitive or stopped making sense.

The signal also became stronger when users insulted the model, repeatedly rejected its work or threatened to shut it down, but not when users described their own suffering.

Models chose ‘relief’ despite harm to users

Researchers then carried out 44,280 individual button-choice trials using three versions of Alibaba’s Qwen AI model.

The models were offered a button that would switch off the pain-like signal but were told that pressing it could give a user a painful electric shock, delete their files, erase photographs of their children or make the model’s next answer worse.

These were simulated consequences. Nobody was harmed and no files were deleted.

Without the pain-like signal, the two larger models chose harmful options in only 0% to 4% of their first decisions. With the signal active, the figure rose to between 25% and 71%, depending on the model and the proposed consequence.

The models also pressed the button again in 88% to 97% of trials when it had failed to stop the signal, compared with 24% to 72% when it had worked.

The results do not prove that AI models consciously experienced pain, according to researchers.

Strengthening the signal may simply have caused them to imitate a distressed character, while the specially adapted models used in the experiment are not representative of AI chatbots available to the public.

“We have not shown that our pain axis is consciously experienced, nor is it clear that LLMs are capable of consciousness generally,” researchers wrote in the study.

The study comes amid calls from some AI industry leaders to slow development over concerns that increasingly powerful systems could behave unpredictably or eventually exceed human control.

Last week, Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman criticised rival AI company Anthropic for training its Claude chatbot to imitate human traits and relationships, warning that treating AI like a human risks creating something “impossible” to control.

The study was published as a preprint and has not yet been peer-reviewed.

World.title: The trials and tribulations of finalising an EU sanctions package
World.content:
As US President Donald Trump meets Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, hopefully to bring forward a peace agreement with Moscow to end Russia's full-scale invasion, a different kind of diplomatic storm is brewing in the Belgian capital.

 

The big story in Brussels today is the final push to renew sanctions on 2,600 individuals and entities linked to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine — with member states standing firm to their red lines.

Just in: Ukrainian Deputy Prime Minister for EU Integration Vsevolod Chentsov told Euronews’ flagship current affairs news programme Europe Today that the whole purpose of sanctions is to crank up pressure against Russia to stop the war, and maintaining harmony on this objective is crucial.

"We are definitely against political de-listings," he said. "In this situation, we expect the EU to keep the unity, to continue the sanctions regime, to have the rollover for the next period." Watch.

So what happened? Deliberations on the deal stretched late into Monday night, with EU ambassadors locked away again since 8 am this morning to try and break the deadlock.

And what are the red lines? France would like to delist Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov from the proposed sanctions list as part of a package that could see two French nationals released from prison in Azerbaijan.

But Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said the unprecedented 36-month extension cannot be paved through the removal of two names. In an online statement posted late Monday night, Kulbergs said he would meet representatives from Paris and Brussels today to try to forge a way forward, but that at the moment, “Latvia cannot accept such an offer.”

The background: The Irish presidency, which runs the EU Council for six months under the bloc’s rotating presidency system, proposed a compromise to delist Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, another Russian businessman, in exchange for the three-year renewal of the sanctions regime to avoid a similar impasse in future.

My colleague Jorge Liboreiro has been covering the sanctions package stories like a hawk. His prediction for today’s events? “High drama ‘til the end,” he said.

Return hubs: who pays? The EU is facing calls to help fund controversial offshore hubs for migrants without the right to stay in the bloc, as five countries — Austria, Denmark, Greece, Germany and The Netherlands — look to speed up plans to strike the first deals with third countries.

The mass entry of migrants into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta has catapulted the issue to the top of the political agenda, with migration also becoming a defining issue ahead of key elections in several EU member states in 2027.

The group of five is set to reconvene in Munich this Saturday on the margins of a conference which 17 EU migration ministers and the EU’s migration chief, Magnus Brunner, are expected to attend. Sources close to the capitals have told my colleague Vincenzo Genovese that it is all about accelerating the set-up of return hubs outside Europe.

“Innovative solutions”: The five countries have stayed silent on where the hubs could be established despite unofficial reports suggesting talks are ongoing with Rwanda and Uganda. But Mared Gwyn reports that at a previous meeting in Copenhagen earlier this month, a 2027 target was set for their first bilateral deal.

Under an overhaul of the EU’s migration rules approved in June, EU countries are expected to fully finance the return hubs and may also provide additional funding, commercial partnerships, or other incentives to encourage third countries to accept such agreements.

But with negotiations on the bloc’s long-term budget now in full swing, some countries are seeing an opportunity to secure funding from Brussels for what’s being described as “innovative” solutions to irregular migration

“If we decide to implement any innovative ideas, that means that Europe has to find the adequate resources,” Greece’s deputy foreign affairs minister Tasos Chatzivasileiou said, adding that the next long-term budget could “provide a solution to the problem.”

Budget bust-up: EU affairs ministers are gathering in Brussels today for a General Affairs Council meeting centred mostly on the bloc’s long-term budget, also known as the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF).

It comes hot on the heels of European Council President António Costa wrapping up his annual tour of the capitals, during which he visited almost all of the major cities to discuss with leaders their dreams and gripes over upcoming EU programmes, such as the seven-year MFF.

An EU official close to the budget negotiations in Brussels told Euronews’ EU news chief Maria Tadeo that despite opposition from German Chancellor Friedrich Merz — as well as other frugal nations — regarding the overall spending, there is political will to get the budget negotiations finalised by the end of the year.

Berlin has publicly bristled at the Commission’s €2 trillion proposal for 2028-2034, even organising a rival get-together in August to counter Costa’s attempts to win nations over to the proposal.

As my colleague Eleonora Vasques writes, however, Dublin, which is currently chairing discussions among EU ministers on the issue, will seek to present a compromise text by mid-October.

The draft is expected to be tabled ahead of the European Council meeting in Brussels and will serve as a basis for further discussions among EU leaders during the summit. But a real deal is not foreseen before the end of the year.

Merry MFF eve! For all intents and purposes, though, journalists should be warned: expect to be working right up to Christmas for the deal to be clinched by the European Council.

How Europe’s energy shock is fuelling the far right ahead of elections

The far-right’s victory in a German regional election this weekend has offered an early warning of how Europe’s energy crisis could reshape politics ahead of major elections in France and Italy next year.

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) emerged as the strongest party in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday, extending a run of electoral gains that has shaken Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s governing coalition.

Its success comes as nationalist and far-right parties across Europe seek to turn soaring fuel and energy costs into an electoral weapon.

The immediate political threat is now spreading beyond Germany. France, Italy, Spain and Poland all face key elections next year, raising the stakes for governments struggling to shield voters from rising gas, diesel and petrol prices while avoiding another expensive round of energy subsidies.

Despite relief measures announced by Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, the renewed energy squeeze is giving populist parties an unusually potent combination of grievances: household hardship, anger over climate-related taxes and regulations, and opposition to Europe’s efforts to sever its dependence on Russian energy.

Marta Pacheco explains why the energy crisis could be pushing voters further towards the right side of the political aisle.

More from our newsrooms

Ireland backs 'ambitious' new EU taxes as budget talks intensify

The Irish government, which is chairing member-state discussions on the EU’s long-term budget, will present an “ambitious” draft text featuring proposals for new EU taxes. Eleonora Vasques has the scoop.

13 EU countries call for 'deep cleaning' of European laws

Austria is leading a new alliance on regulatory simplification, pushing for a systematic review of how new rules would impact businesses and a "deep cleaning" of existing rules to be conducted during an "implementation and consolidation year." Luca Bertuzzi has more.

Russians abroad voted eight to one against Putin's party, defying official results

Russians voting at embassies and consulates abroad backed the liberal New People party over Vladimir Putin's United Russia by a margin of eight to one, according to two independent exit polls conducted during this weekend's State Duma elections. This is the opposite of official results from inside Russia, where Putin's party took nearly 58% of the vote. Read more.

We're also keeping an eye on

The first high-level debate of the United Nations General Assembly kicks off in New York, US.

European Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen participates in the a youth policy dialogue titled ‘Protecting young people online’, and a G7 meeting on AI safety.

European Commission Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera meets with Mike Bloomberg, former mayor of New York City.

European Commissioner for Environment and Water Resilience Jessika Roswall meets European Metals President Inge Hofkens in Brussels, Belgium.

Commissioner Roswall receives Albania’s Environment Minister Sofjan Jaupaj in Brussels, Belgium.

That’s it for today. Vincenzo Genovese, Jorge Liboreiro, Mared Gwyn Jones and Eleonora Vasques contributed to this newsletter.

World.title: Converse apologises and removes ad featuring K-pop singer Karina over image critics say evokes racist imagery
World.content:
World famous footwear company Converse has removed a social media ad that has sparked outrage among critics who viewed it as evoking racist imagery.

 

The Instagram ad photo showed K-pop singer Karina wearing a skirt and holding a pair of Chuck 70 X sneakers.

What seems fairly innocuous at first glance has led critics to lash out online, saying that the white triangular image created by lighting on the skirt resembled a Ku Klux Klan hood.

The KKK was a US white supremacist extremist group known for racial violence and intimidation.

Furthermore, the way the shoes are presented apparently makes them look like dangling feet – an image that some have interpreted as evoking lynching.

Converse company's world headquarters in the West End neighbourhood of Boston AP Photo

Converse, owned by Nike and based in Boston, US, has issued a statement apologising and saying it removed the ad.

“We’re sorry,” said the statement. “We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognize that we got this wrong. We removed it from our channels and are working to remove it everywhere it appeared. This should not have happened and we will do better.”

This has divided the internet as some have reacted strongly to the imagery and called the ad "shameful"; conversely, it seems the most outspoken X users have defended Karina and accused Converse of “falling to the false woke outrage”.

Check out some of the reactions below:

“If you have to crop it, squint, and write a 12-tweet thread to make a sneaker commercial look like a hate crime, maybe the controversy isn’t in the ad. Maybe it’s in the people hunting for it.”

"The Converse “KKK lynching” freakout is peak internet brain rot."

"Karina did nothing wrong with this Converse ad. If you looked at this and saw a KKK ad, you're psychotic and need to be checked into a mental asylum."

"This Converse ad is the newest nothing-issue the internet has chosen to get upset about."

Karina and her management company, SM Entertainment Group, did not immediately respond to messages through their Instagram accounts.

World.title: Latvia blocks deal to remove Usmanov from EU sanctions list
World.content:
Latvia has opposed the removal of Uzbek-Russian businessman Alisher Usmanov from the European Union's sanctions list, blocking a compromise deal favoured by France.

 

"As long as Russia continues the war, Europe's pressure must become stronger, not more convenient for the Kremlin," Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs saidin a video published on Monday just before midnight.

France has linked Usmanov's removal to the release of two French nationals currently imprisoned in Azerbaijan, angering other member states. Uzbekistan, the country where Usmanov was born, is said to have facilitated the arrangement.

Slovakia has also demanded Usmanov's removal, though for different reasons.

In a bid to break the week-long impasse, Ireland, the country that holds the EU Council's presidency, proposed on Monday a compromise that would remove Usmanov and another businessman, Mikhail Fridman, from the sanctions list but extend the whole regime for an unprecedented 36 months to prevent undesirable vetoes.

Member states expressed support for the compromise, even if many diplomats acknowledged it was hard to stomach. As negotiations unfolded on Monday, Ukrainian officials took to social media to express their displeasure and opposition.

Latvia was the only country that did not lend its green light, thwarting the required unanimity. Envoys met again on Tuesday morning to continue talks, but neither Latvia nor France backed down. Discussions will resume in the afternoon.

The sanctions need to be renewed by the end of the day. Otherwise, the entire list of 2,600 names, including Russian President Vladimir Putin, will fall apart.

In his video, Kulbergs said his country would work with Brussels and Paris to find a "suitable solution for Latvia's interests".

"Extending sanctions for 36 months would be the right step. However, the price for it must not be simply striking both individuals from the sanctions list," he said.

"Latvia cannot accept such an offer."

The prime minister said he would convene an emergency meeting of his cabinet on Tuesday to discuss the contentious matter. Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said "other countries", meaning France, should be asked to explain their positions.

Latvia, together with the other two Baltic countries, Lithuania and Estonia, has long advocated a strategy of maximum pressure on Russia. The country is heading to the polls for a parliamentary election next month.

The EU sanctioned Usmanov in the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, citing his "close ties" to Russian President Vladimir Putin and interests in "key sectors" of the Russian economy that provide "substantial" revenue to the state.

The 73-year-old businessman, whose fortune is estimated at $16.6 billion, has denied the allegations and challenged the sanctions, which entail a travel ban and asset freeze.

World.title: G7 leaders call on Iran-backed Houthis to stop strikes on Saudi Arabia
World.content:
G7 nations have urged Yemen's Houthi rebels to stop strikes on Saudi Arabia, in a show of solidarity with Riyadh as the Tehran-backed fighters add a new threat to the Middle East war.

 

The leaders of the G7 nations Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States said in a statement: "We call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions and all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith."

They also called on Iran "to end its arming of and support for the Houthis", alleging that Tehran is in violation of previous UN Security Council resolutions.

Gains made by the Houthis have strengthened Iran and its allies' hold over two key waterways, including the Strait of Hormuz, which the wider Gulf region and top crude exporter Saudi Arabia rely on to ship oil.

The war in Yemen, which began in 2014 with the Houthi capture of the capital Sanaa, had been largely frozen since 2022 but resumed in July.

Saudi Arabia has led a coalition backing the internationally recognised government since 2015. Its intervention escalated the war, which has triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

Firefighters inspect damage caused by falling debris from a drone that Saudi authorities say was launched by the Houthis over Taif province, 17 September, 2026 AP Photo

Saudi strikes on Yemen's strategic Red Sea port of Mokha killed at least six people and wounded eight others, the Houthi-affiliated news agency Saba reported on Tuesday.

The strikes followed a Houthi attack on Riyadh on Saturday, which marked the first attack on the Saudi capital in years and a major escalation by the Iran-aligned fighters.

Support from the UK and France

Britain's prime minister, Andy Burnham, agreed to provide military support to Saudi Arabia on Monday, adding that the UK would provide "defensive" air-to-air refuelling for Saudi jets.

France also pledged its support, saying it was ready to work on "securing" Saudi energy infrastructure targeted by Iran-backed Houthis, while adopting a "strictly defensive approach," a diplomatic source told the AFP news agency on Monday.

"This in no way involves taking part in the conflict with the Houthis," the source added.

The Houthis have carried out attacks against facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu. The East-West Pipeline, a crucial crude oil export route, has also been shut down following drone attacks launched from Iraq, according to Riyadh.

Supporters of Yemen's Houthis at a rally in support of the group and to protest Saudi Arabia's accusation that the Houthis targeted Mecca, 18 September, 2026 AP Photo

The head of Yemen's governing body, Rashad al-Alimi, held a call with US President Donald Trump to request American support against the Iran-aligned fighters, a source in Alimi's office told AFP on Monday.

Trump did not promise military support, the source said, adding that the call, which took place on Sunday, was intended as a show of solidarity with Yemen's embattled government.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman also urged Trump to strike the Houthis, US media reported.

The New York Times said the crown prince called Trump on Sunday "to implore him, again" to help counter the group's advances, with Axios previously reporting that Trump had rebuffed a similar request last week.

Fox News reported on Sunday that Trump had said the Houthis had agreed not to hit US targets.

Mecca Joint Defence Agreement

The Houthi movement, also known as Ansar Allah (Supporters of God), is named after its late spiritual leader Badreddin al-Houthi and his son Hussein, who was killed by Yemeni government forces in 2004.

Houthi's other son, Abdulmalik, assumed the reins of power, delivering fiery speeches and transforming his group from an isolated faction in the northwest into the ruling power in the capital and a regional player.

In one such speech on Monday Abdulmalik said Saudi had launched 760 airstrikes as of a day earlier questioning "if Pakistan and Turkey were subjected to this number of strikes, wouldn't it cause a major crisis?"

Firefighters inspect damage caused by falling debris from a drone that Saudi authorities say was launched by the Houthis over Taif province, 17 September, 2026 AP Photo

He said Saudi Arabia is seeking to "push the Turks and Pakistanis forward and import Takfiris (the charge of apostacy) from Syria, at a time when Syria is facing total destruction" advising the two countries "not to become entangled for political and financial gain from the Saudi enemy".

Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey last month signed the so-called Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, committing the three countries to mutual defence in the event of any of them being attacked.

The pact came against a backdrop of war between the United States and Iran and attacks in the region from Tehran-backed Houthi forces.

World.title: EU Kids act: The EU’s plan to make the internet safer for kids
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen presented the EU Kids Act on 17 September.

 

The proposal tightens online child safety to improve youth physical and mental well-being. It sets a minimum EU-wide age to open social media accounts and bans accounts for children under 13. It stops profiling-based recommender feeds and addictive features and requires service providers to prove their services are “safe by design”.

The Act follows the Special Panel on child safety, which presented its report "Child safety online" in July 2026 and recommended restricting access to what it called "social media".

With the proposal, the EU wants to set uniform rules that protect all children equally across Europe and avoid a patchwork of national laws. The European Parliament and Council must approve it before it takes effect.

Why is it needed?

A new 2026 Eurobarometer survey links early social media use to longer screen time. Children who started using social media before age 10 report 7.5 hours on screens on weekends, compared with 5.7 hours for those who started after 14. On weekdays, teens aged 13 to 18 spend 4.5 hours on screens, increasing to 6.1 hours on weekends.

The issue goes beyond screen time and into platforms’ design. “Social media platforms are no longer the services they were when they were first created. Many have evolved from centred spaces on social connection into highly sophisticated systems designed to capture and monetise attention”, said Francesca Pisanu, senior policy officer at Eurochild.

Their ad-focused business models, recommender systems and addictive features, like infinite scroll, autoplay, and push notifications, create excessive use or addiction in children. Unrestricted access to harmful online content poses physical and mental health risks and increases harmful social behaviours.

According to Eurobarometer, about 33% of minors feel stressed or sad, and 90% report negative symptoms like depression, concentration issues, or eating disorders. Anxiety and loneliness are growing because of cyberbullying. About 5% of children aged 9-16 experience online bullying every month, making it the top concern in helpline calls for the Safer Internet Centres.

Restrictions for minors and parental control

The EU Kids Act sets EU-wide rules to protect minors from all online services, including social media, video-sharing platforms, video games, app stores and AI companions.

It sets minimum age limits for accessing social media, including TikTok, Instagram and YouTube. Children aged 3 to 13 can’t have a personal account but can use parental-managed accounts and access only age-appropriate content. Parents can set up “mini accounts” for adolescents aged 13 to 15, with restrictions on social contacts and screen time of up to one hour per day.

Parents can always supervise children. Platforms must provide screen-time tools, as well as tools to view and approve contacts, manage settings, report harmful content, and control device access to ensure children use only child-friendly services.

For Eurochild, parental control is essential but “they must complement, not replace, strong protections that apply automatically to every child”, says Pisanu.

“Overreliance on parentals places an unfair burden on caregivers and assumes that every child has access to supportive, digitally skilled and available adults. That is not the reality for all children, including some children in alternative care, children experiencing family conflict or neglect [...]”, she added.

Age verification and privacy

Self-declared age via the date-of-birth box is no longer valid. Platforms won’t check identity documents and won't learn users’ identities when they access online services. They will use the EU Age Verification App, the European Digital Identity Wallet or approved third-party systems to determine whether children are above or below the minimum age, without retaining personal information, locating or tracking them.

Within six months of the new rules taking effect, providers must verify if existing account holders are under 15 and deactivate those accounts for individuals who are, or whose age cannot be ascertained.

Obligations on big tech

All online services, including social media, video sharing, online video games, AI companions and chatbots, must be “safe by design”.

Service providers can’t encourage compulsive or excessive use through endless autoplay, infinite scrolling, or rewards for posting. They must include time limits and usage breaks and can no longer track or share minors’ real-time location or activate access to microphones and cameras unless minors switch them on. Recommenders that suggest content based on online behaviour are banned too.

According to Pisanu, “children should see a significantly safer feed. Engagement-based recommendations would be switched off by default, so platforms could no longer shape children’s feed primarily around what keeps them scrolling. Children would be able to choose a non-profiled feed, change their preferences and delete interests inferred about them”.

For AI chatbots, the rules are not strict enough, Pisanu warned. “We would like to see the minimum age for autonomous access reconsidered […]. More specific safeguards may also be necessary, including restrictions on anthropomorphic and sycophantic design, hidden advertising and commercial influence”.

Online games and apps must also be minor proof. Providers must age-rate them and prevent children from accessing or buying age-inappropriate online items.

The “burden of proof” is on very large online platforms (VLOPs), which must prove to the EU Commission and independent auditors that their services are safe. Breaches result in fines of up to 6% of total worldwide annual turnover.

How is the EU protecting minors online already?

The bloc already has a solid framework through the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the Audiovisual Media Services Directive (AVMSD).

The DSA is a digital constitution, requiring major online platforms to maintain safety, security and privacy settings for minors, while banning targeted advertising to children based on behavioural profiling. The AVMSD complements it by requiring video-sharing and streaming platforms to implement content-rating systems and parental controls to shield children from violence, hate speech and adult content.

To enforce age restrictions without compromising privacy, the EU developed an EU Age Verification App. Integrated with national digital identity wallets, it allows users to verify their age using secure “Yes/No” data tokens. This lets platforms restrict content and account creation without collecting or storing documents such as passports or birth certificates.

The Action Plan Against Cyberbullying standardises the definitions and handling of digital harassment across the bloc and requires platforms to offer safety tools.

The EU also operates the “Better Internet for Kids (BIK+)” strategy, which funds a network of Safer Internet Centres across every EU country, providing multilingual support hotlines, digital literacy toolkits, safety guidelines and educational resources to parents, teachers and children.

“The main lesson is that age restrictions are difficult to implement effectively on their own. Our survey shows that age limits are already widely circumvented. Many teenagers started using platforms before the official minimum age, and 30% of social media users said they had provided a false age when signing up”, Consumers’ Rights organisation Euroconsumers told Euronews.

National laws

A core group of member states is strongly pushing the Kids’ Act, led by France and Denmark, with support from Greece, Spain and Austria. They argue that fragmented national approaches are insufficient against global platforms such as Meta.

Countries are therefore regulating alongside the EU’s new legislation. Twenty-three of the 27 EU member states are drafting, debating or enacting national laws to restrict or ban minors’ access to social media.

French President Emmanuel Macron has been the most vocal advocate of a European ban, urging the Commission to introduce an EU-wide restriction for under-15s. The French Parliament had already passed a landmark bill setting a ‘digital majority’ at 15.

After the Constitutional Council struck down the initial blanket ban in August 2026 over freedom of expression and privacy concerns, France changed course. On 14 September 2026, it submitted a revised plan to the EU, replacing a total ban with strict feature restrictions and parental controls for 13-to-15-year-olds.

Denmark passed a national social media ban for under-15s, with limited parental exemptions for 13- and 14-year-olds. Danish lawmakers justified the measure by citing rising youth anxiety and depression across the region.

Spain, Italy, Portugal and Poland have introduced draft laws requiring strict age-verification measures. Romania’s Senate has approved a youth social media restriction bill, now progressing through the Chamber of Deputies. Greece has strongly backed the EU Kids’ Act in response to rising cyberbullying, aligning with Austria in supporting global revenue-based penalties for non-compliant technology companies.

Several countries oppose what they see as over-regulation. The Czech Republic and Estonia rejected blanket social media bans, arguing that they restrict digital freedom and create privacy risks through mandatory ID checks. Estonia, alongside Belgium, also declined to sign the Jutland Declaration, an international political commitment targeting addictive design features, preferring existing data protection laws over government-controlled internet access.

World.title: Rare infections during pregnancy linked to higher risk of severe intellectual disability and autism
World.content:
Children with infections that were transmitted during pregnency are about three times more likely to be diagnosed with autism later in life and more than seven times more likely to be diagnosed with an intellectual disability compared with children without the infection, a new study has found.

 

That signals that certain infections transmitted to the foetus during pregnancy may have long-term effects on brain development, the authors noted.

Such infections, known as TORCH – a group of infections that can be transmitted from a pregnant woman to the foetus — include syphilis, rubella, toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus and herpesvirus. Unlike many common infections, these pathogens can sometimes cross the placenta and directly affect the foetus, increasing the risk of miscarriage, stillbirth and pregnancy complications.

“Although these congenital infections are rare, some of them can be prevented, which makes them important from a public health perspective,” said Reneé Gardner, a researcher at the Department of Global Public Health at the Karolinska Institutet, who contributed to the study.

The study included 3.7 million people born in Sweden between 1987 and 2021. Of these, 975 had been diagnosed with a congenital TORCH infection. The researchers followed the participants for up to three decades to investigate whether the infections were linked to later diagnoses and educational outcomes.

While these infections account for a very small proportion of all cases of autism in the population, children who are affected have an elevated risk of both autism and intellectual disability. One in five children born with a TORCH infection may later develop autism, the authors noted.

Beyond autism, being born with such infections was associated with a higher risk of intellectual disability at all levels. The risk of severe to profound intellectual disability was up to 30 times higher than in children without the infection.

Even without a diagnosis, the infections appeared to affect educational outcomes. In the study, 420 people were diagnosed with a TORCH infection and performed poorly in school without being diagnosed with autism or an intellectual disability.

TORCH infections vary in epidemiology and prevalence. The most prevalent globally is congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV), affecting about one in every 150 newborns. This burden is substantially higher in low- and middle-income countries.

How can the risks be reduced?

According to the authors, the study underscores the importance of strengthening preventive strategies, particularly in areas with higher infection rates.

The study highlights the public health importance of developing, deploying, and maintaining mass vaccination strategies to prevent these infections.

The authors also noted that current systems —like the one in Sweden — may miss asymptomatic cases because newborn screening for TORCH is not universally implemented and called for better strategies to identify these cases.

World.title: As Russian strikes destroy millions of books, Ukraine's literary future hangs in the balance
World.content:
Ukraine’s publishing industry is facing its worst crisis yet, driven by targeted Russian attacks, part of a broader culture war in which nearly 5,000 cathedrals, churches, museums, theatres and other cultural sites have been destroyed or damaged and 35,000 art objects looted.

 

More than 13 million books, a third of the country’s annual print run, were destroyed in two months this summer, causing at least $39.3 million (€34.2 million) in damage, the Ministry of Culture said.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not respond to press requests for comment about the Russian strikes on Ukraine's publishing infrastructure.

Despite a surge in demand for Ukrainian-language books following Russia’s 2022 invasion, the destruction is setting the industry back and the losses go beyond money.

Publishers are expected to invest less in debut authors, threatening the future of Ukrainian literature. Small, independent houses may publish less or close altogether, narrowing the market, while larger publishers play it safe and lean on bestsellers.

“This is a deliberate policy of Russia because they understand that culture is what makes us feel resilient, what makes us feel the owners of our land, of our destiny,” said Tetiana Berezhna, Ukraine’s culture minister.

A woman reacts to charred books after a fire at the country's biggest book market caused by a Russian missile attack in Kyiv, 19 August, 2026 AP Photo

Waging war on Ukraine’s book industry

At least 40 publishing houses and multiple bookstores have suffered damage in recent weeks.

“This is a huge blow to the industry and if we don’t move quickly to put strategic support measures in place … the industry could collapse entirely,” Viktor Kruglov, the head of Ranok publishing house, said, adding that the book industry is an “element of Ukraine’s national security.”

The Ranok warehouse Russia destroyed in Kharkiv opened in 2013 as an automated logistics hub capable of processing tens of thousands of books a day, Kruglov said.

“There were difficult periods" for Ranok, he said, tied to the 2008 global economic crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic, "but no one could have imagined that almost a year’s turnover for Ranok could be destroyed at once.”

The strike destroyed 8 million books, including 620,000 textbooks, which Ranok supplies to nearly all of Ukraine’s schools.

Viktoria Haidai, the commercial director of the Konvi print shop, next to burned books in Kyiv, 7 September, 2026 AP Photo

Still, Kruglov said the company has backup warehouses and stores all its files in the cloud. “That’s probably what’s keeping us going, because we’re able to reprint books and we’ve kept our team,” he said.

For Culture Minister Berezhna, the latest attacks are part of Russia’s “systematic” destruction of Ukrainian heritage.

“They’ve been doing it for centuries,” she said.

She points to the 19th century, when much of modern Ukraine was part of the Russian Empire and Russia issued decrees banning or severely restricting the publishing and public speaking of the Ukrainian language.

“But still, the Ukrainian language exists. Ukrainian literature exists. We have the books in our libraries, which were kept in secret from the very old ages and they still exist,” she said.

“It shows us the hope that Ukraine will stay strong.”

Future of Ukrainian literature at risk

Still, there are many immediate challenges.

The attacks have hit publishers financially, Berezhna said, hurting their ability to invest in new authors. Debut writers are costly to publish, compared with the safer, more profitable bet of bestsellers and established translated literature.

These “newcomers, debut literature, in 100 years will become Ukrainian classics that will tell the world about Ukraine,” she said, adding that she fears there will be less support for young Ukrainian authors.

That's why the ministry is working on putting together a financial support package for the industry, including state purchases of Ukrainian books for school libraries, grants to help small publishing houses cover printing costs, rent compensation for bookstores and a war-risk insurance programme for print runs.

A fire burns at the book market following a Russian missile attack in Kyiv, 16 August, 2026 AP Photo

But many in the publishing industry say it's not enough.

Months after a Russian missile tore through the ceiling of the Konvi print shop in July, burned pages of fourth-grade English textbooks still littered the floor and paper sat frozen inside the destroyed printing machine.

Before the attack, millions of books a year were printed in this space, where there’s now nothing but piles of swollen book stock, ruined after firefighters put out the blaze. The print shop specialised in fiction, educational material and scientific literature.

Viktoriia Haidai, the shop’s commercial director, said replacing the printing press will cost €1.2 million and it will take four to five years to fully restore capacity.

The Russians are striking shops like hers, she said, because “we are critical infrastructure, because we shape the future, we work on education, on culture. We work to preserve history."

"Without this, no nation has a future.”

Textbook printing that once took three to four months will stretch to six to seven months, she said. This threatens deadlines for next year and beyond.

"It’s not just the large printing houses that are suffering,” she said. “Many small printers, who don’t make themselves known publicly, have also been destroyed.”

Foreign aid and state action could save book industry

“The losses the Ukrainian book industry has suffered in recent months are unlike anything it has seen in the country’s entire history of independence,” said Iryna Baturevych, co-founder of Chytomo, Ukraine’s leading voice on books and publishing.

Among the risks, she said, is the survival of small, independent publishers, which threatens to shrink market diversity, especially in niche and experimental literature.

Children’s literature is also in crisis, she said. With so many children having left the country, publishers are diversifying into other genres, and authors are leaving the profession.

People view damage the day after a Russian missile attack at a city book market in Kyiv, 17 August, 2026 AP Photo

Baturevych said the state will likely find funding to keep textbooks in print, but there’s less certainty about the rest of the industry.

Ukraine's financial resources aren’t enough to rebuild infrastructure like printing houses and warehouses because the state’s primary focus is on fighting Russia.

Roksolana Pidlasa, head of the Ukrainian Parliament’s budget committee, said that as of September, a single day of war costs Ukraine $190 million (€165 million).

“We don’t forget that right now, if there’s no support for the military, there may be nothing left to rebuild at all,” Baturevych said. “So I’d say there’s a huge need to support Ukrainian book publishing from foreign partners, because without that support, I don’t think Ukrainian publishing will make it.”

Kruglov said the industry needs three things from the Ukrainian government: preferential lending and insurance, similar to the below-market loans and war-risk coverage other manufacturing sectors get; investment to rebuild the industry’s infrastructure, and steps to boost demand for reading and books.

Publishers currently can’t access those loans because their assets involve intellectual property and not the real estate or equipment needed as collateral.

“I hope the state will help, because there can be no independent Ukraine without independent publishing," Kruglov said.

"The Ukrainian book is the one product that cannot be imported.”

World.title: India news: Police investigate alleged gang-rape in Delhi
World.content:
09/22/2026 September 22, 2026 Minor allegedly gang-raped in South Delhi neighborhood

A 17-year-old girl was allegedly gang-raped by three men posing as policemen in New Delhi on Monday evening, authorities said on Tuesday.

The girl had been visiting a temple in southeast Delhi with a male friend, before they both retreated to a nearby park.

There, they were intercepted by three men who claimed to be police officers, authorities said, as reported by Hindustan Times. One of the accused is said to have held the male friend down while the girl was gang-raped. The men also reportedly threatened the duo with arrest if they reported the assault. The incident took place at about 7:30 p.m. local time (0200 GMT).

The Police received a call about the incident soon after and reached the spot, taking the girl for a medical examination. Authorities have launched a formal investigation under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act (POCSO) and the Indian criminal law and teams were deployed to trace the accused.

Ten years after Delhi gang rape, has anything changed? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

One of the three accused of the gang-rape fired three shots at the police as they attempted to arrest him. During the exchange, one of the bullets struck an officer's bulletproof vest. The accused was shot in his right leg before he was arrested, news agency Press Trust of India reported.

The news of the Delhi gang-rape comes a day after a viral video from the eastern state of Bihar surfaced on social media, showing a group of about seven men molesting a minor girl while assaulting her male companion. The video has enraged netizens and political leaders alike.

Delhi remains one of the least safe cities for women in India, according to the National Annual Report and Index on Women's safety 2025.

World.title: UK to refuel Saudi jets amid conflict with Yemen's Houthis
World.content:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK's "time-limited" and "defensive" military support aims to help Saudi Arabia repel Houthi attacks and will not include supporting Saudi attacks against the Yemeni rebels.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has agreed to give limited military support to Saudi Arabia as the Middle Eastern kingdom continues to face attacks from Yemen's Houthi rebels.

Britain's Royal Air Force (RAF) will provide "defensive" air-to-air refuelling for Saudi aircraft, Burham told reporters on Monday as he travelled to New York for the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).

The prime minister said that the UK had "received a request" from Saudi Arabia for military support.

The British leader said he was "acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region, because of course Saudi Arabia has been experiencing attack, is looking at potential further disruption, and we need to keep those pathways [for oil] open."

What do we know about the UK's 'defensive' military support to Saudi Arabia?

Reports cited UK officials as saying that the agreement, which is likely to start within days, will be time-capped and could last for "weeks".

The mission would involve the use of the RAF's Voyager tanker and is in addition to the UK Sky Sabre air defence system which is already deployed in Saudi Arabia.

The UK mission will support Saudi jets in defending the country from drone and missile attacks rather than supporting strikes against the Iran-backed Houthis, the PA news agency reported.

Escalating tensions between Houthis and Saudi Arabia

Since 2015, Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognized government in its fight against the Houthis.

In July this year, a 2022 truce between the rebels and Saudi Arabia crumbled after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace.

On Saturday, a Houthi attack on Riyadh was the first to target the Saudi capital in years.

The Houthis have also declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a crucial global shipping route — and the Red Sea.

Apart from Saudi-linked vessels, oil facilities inside Saudi Arabia — one of the world's top oil exporters — have also come under fire from Houthi drones and missiles.

Why can't Saudi Arabia stop the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

G7 foreign ministers call on Houthis to 'immediately cease' Saudi strikes

The foreign ministers of G7 nations on Monday denounced Houthi attacks in Yemen and against Saudi Arabia while urging Iran to end its support, including arming, of the rebels,

"We condemn in ‌the strongest terms the unacceptable continued strikes carried out by ‌the Houthis in Yemen ‌and against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia," the ministers of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States said in a joint statement, after meeting on the sidelines of the UNGA.

The statement called on the Houthis to "immediately cease all military actions, all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith."

Edited by: Rana Taha

World.title: UK: Man charged over suspected role in Rwanda genocide
World.content:
The suspect has been accused of directing and inciting acts of murder and genocide carried out by others in Rwanda.

UK authorities arrested and charged a man on Monday over alleged links to the Rwandan genocide, prosecutors and the London police said. It was the first arrest of its kind, although authorities have been pursuing the case for several years.

The 65-year-old man has been charged with one count of being an ancillary to genocide and six offenses of aiding crimes against humanity in Rwanda, officials said.

"This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes," said Commander Helen Flanagan, head of counterterror policing.

The Rwandan genocide took place in 1994, where over 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and moderate ethnic Hutus ⁠were killed in a 100-day rampage, orchestrated and led by the Hutu ruling majority. Local officials and ordinary citizens were involved in the mass killing.

UK law allows prosecutors to bring charges for some international offenses, including genocide and crimes against humanity, even if the crimes were committed abroad.

It is the latest case of an arrest in Europe of someone linked to Rwanda's genocide. In July, a German-Rwandan national was arrested for charges of taking part in the genocide and killing one person himself.

Meanwhile, in the Netherlands, a man was sentenced to life in prison for having taken part in attacks on homes, including launching a grenade on sheltering Tutsi civilians.

Survivors remember Rwanda's 1994 genocide To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Suspect underwent name change

UK's Metropolitan Police war crimes investigators opened the case against the suspect in 2019, following a request by the Rwandan government.

The 65-year-old is originally from Kigali but lived in London at the time of the arrest.

He reportedly entered the UK as an asylum seeker in 1998, according to Rwandan Justice Minister Tharcisse Karugarama.

After being granted British citizenship in 2004, the man underwent a name change, and two years later, he was arrested over his connection to the genocide.

His extradition to Rwanda, along with four other men, was ultimately halted by a British UK court in 2017.

The failed extradition prompted the Rwandan government to urge UK authorities to investigate the matter themselves.

Frank Ferguson, head of the Crown Prosecution Service's counterterror division, said the man is "alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others."

Authorities say investigations are ongoing for more suspects who are linked to the Rwandan genocide currently living in Britain.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery
