World.title: US-China rivalry is reshaping global trade — and Europe is caught in the middle.
World.content:
China's Xi Jinping is traveling to Washington this week. Regardless of what comes from his talks with US President Trump, the EU will likely remain stuck between erratic US trade policy and Beijing's export machine.

Last week, German and Chinese business leaders met in the German city of Düsseldorf for an economic dialogue. Although the panel focused on trade, and investment between China and Europe, ongoing US-China rivalry was the elephant in the room.

As Xi Jinping and Donald Trump sit down in the US capital Washington this week, there is some hope that talks will show progress on alleviating the ongoing trade war launched by the US president. The last time the two leaders met at a Beijing summit in May did not yield any tangible results.

"The assumption in Beijing, and that's the way they're operating, is that China and the US will hold each other in check for the foreseeable future," Mikko Huotari, director of the Berlin-based China think tank MERICS, told a policy briefing last week.

"Xi really doesn't need a breakthrough in Washington. He needs more time. And the same is true for Washington. So we have this strategic stalemate situation, which I think is the best description of what we see currently."

A deal could benefit Trump's Republican Party ahead of the important US midterm elections in November, but that outcome remains far from certain.

"We will discuss everything," Trump said about Xi's visit to the White House.

Cooperation on AI?

Beijing and Washington are competing on multiple levels and nowhere is this rivalry more consequential than with artificial intelligence (AI).

The US government prohibits the export of high-performance chips to China. Beijing, in turn, restricts the export of rare earth elements, which are indispensable for semiconductor production.

And amid concerns about the dangers of unregulated AI, there is some expectation that Xi and Trump will discuss AI guardrails during their talks. Xi has called for international cooperation on AI development, while Trump sees its regulation as a threat to the US' leadership in the field.

After meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York on Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that US and Chinese officials have already discussed creating a "notification mechanism" to share information about AI-related security incidents.

AI's expanding power alarms China's intelligence agency To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Europe's 'China shock'

From a European perspective, both China and the US are currently considered difficult partners.

The second "China shock … is already here" in Europe, said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in her 2026 State of the Union address last week.

The first "China shock" came 25 years ago, triggered by China's accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO), when inexpensive "Made in China" products began to flood the global markets.

The second one stems from Chinas technological progress in industries such as battery technology, green energy and mobility.

"It shows in our communities and in factories across our Union. It leads to deindustrialization in the industrial heartlands of Europe. This is unsustainable," von der Leyen said in her address.

The EU is aiming for a rapid transition to e-mobility and wants to drastically reduce CO2 emissions from road traffic. At the same time, Brussels is calling for additional tariffs on low-cost electric cars from China, as China enjoys competitive advantages with cheaper cars and high government subsidies.

China denies having an unfair advantage, and German automakers VW and BMW also oppose punitive tariffs due to potential revenue losses resulting from Chinese retaliatory measures.

What new alliances will reshape the world? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A Chinese participant at the Düsseldorf economic dialogue told DW anonymously that China's domestic consumption cannot absorb manufacturing.

"China's economy is weak. Companies are worried about their business and urgently need to tap into foreign markets," said the Chinese executive, who used to work in the European branch of a Chinese state-owned enterprise.

Trump pressuring EU over China, but also on trade, security

"Against the backdrop of the ongoing escalation of strategic rivalry between the US and China, the US is constantly urging its allies to tighten restrictions on China in the areas of technology, supply chains, and security," said Yang Xiepu, director of the Center for Sino-German Cooperation at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS).

Trade Reset: How Europe is replacing China and the US To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At the same time, Trump frequently threatens the EU with tariffs while injecting instability into the strategic NATO alliance. When the EU offered Canada "associate membership" last week, Trump floated the possibility of new punitive measures from the US.

While Carney expressed interest, Trump called the idea "ridiculous."

"If I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump said, without specifying what he considers about EU-Canada ties to be "hostile."

Copying Canada's 'middle' approach

Facing Trump administration's tariff upsets and caustic rhetoric, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is openly hedging his bets on the world stage.

"We know the old order is not coming back. We shouldn't mourn it," he declared at the 2026 World Economic Forum in Davos in January, with the US allies rattled by Trump threatening to annex Greenland from Denmark.

Carney said that great powers can "afford for now to go it alone" but middle powers need to work better together.

"When we only negotiate bilaterally with a hegemon, we negotiate from weakness. We accept what's offered. We compete with each other to be the most accommodating. This is not sovereignty," Carney told the forum.

"If we're not at the table, we're on the menu," he emphasized.

In early 2026, Carney visited China and agreed to a "new-era strategic partnership." Ottawa subsequently lowered import tariffs on Chinese electric cars from 100% to 6.1%. The quota stands at 49,000 vehicles per year.

Separately, China has launched a charm offensive toward US allies, "more specifically, the fragile allies," according to MERICS Director Mikko Huotari.

For example, Xi attended the BRICS summit in India in September despite the rocky relationship with New Delhi. He also attended the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Kyrgyzstan. In November, China will host the G-20 summit.

Carney has described this new form of diplomacy as "variable geometry" — different alliances for different issues based on common values and interests. In November, he will travel to Shenzhen for the APECE summit. He will also be at the table there — and hopefully not on the menu.

A new Cold War: Can the middle powers forge a path forward? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: US news outlets sue Trump over White House ban
World.content:
CNN, MS NOW, and Politico say the ban against them threatens press freedom and the right to independent journalism.

US news outlets CNN, MS NOW, and Politico plan to go to court against Donald Trump's administration, after he banned them from the White House, the three said in a statement on Monday.

"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," CNN, MS NOW and Politico said in their statement.

The announcement comes after Trump accused the media outlets of reporting "fiction" and "lied" in their coverage of his administration.

On Monday, Trump wrote on social media that his administration was not targeting "the Free Press" but was "instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer."

Trump's media ban is the latest escalation in his long-running feud with several US media outlets. In 2017, as he began his first presidential term, he blasted the press as "the enemy of the American people."

What did CNN, MS NOW, Politico say?

A day after Trump's announcement, the entry badges of reporters for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico had been disabled.

The news outlets accused the White House of revoking their journalists' credentials "without notice or process" because the administration "objected to our reporting."

"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference," they said in the statement.

The banned news outlets argued in their lawsuit that the constitution "does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting."

White House pool coverage suspended

CNN is one of five news organizations, including broadcasters ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC, that make up the White House television pool. The broadcasters share the costs of covering the president, take turns organizing coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.

On Monday, in response to CNN's exclusion from the White House television pool, the other major TV networks said they have suspended their coverage, which effectively eliminates the most important video source for White House events.

CNN had been scheduled to cover Trump's trip to New York for the United Nations General Assembly on Monday, but as a result of the ban, it was not able ‌to provide a pool feed.

Bryan Boughton, who runs the Fox News Washington bureau and the current TV pool chair, announced the suspension in an email Monday.

"This follows the White House's position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties," Boughton added. "There will be no replacement pool put in place," he added.

The lack of replacement reflected an effective boycott over the ban.

ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC addressed the situation in a statement, saying that "the public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting."

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

World.title: Nuclear power is back on Southeast Asia's energy agenda
World.content:
Rising electricity demand, shocks in energy security and climate commitments are reviving long-stalled plans for nuclear power across Southeast Asia. But proponents of nuclear energy still face major obstacles.

Southeast Asian governments are revisiting nuclear power as electricity consumption raises, exposing the region's dependence on fossil fuels.

The rise is largely driven by new factories, electric vehicles and the region's rush to host data centers against the backdrop of countries trying to reduce carbon emissions.

No Southeast Asian nation currently operates a commercial nuclear power plant, but several are placing their bets on nuclear energy and reviving plans that had been stalled for years.

On September 8, Vietnam's state-owned Petrovietnam and South Korea's KEPCO agreed to deepen cooperation on the planned Ninh Thuan 2 nuclear plan in Vietnamt. Six days later, Singapore's government said it was studying nuclear power and small modular reactors (SMRs)with an "open mind", though it stressed that it had not made a decision.

Vietnam wants to bring its two Ninh Thuan plants into operation by 2035 and pursue at least one SMR project.

Indonesia plans an initial 500 megawatts of nuclear capacity, with units targeted to begin operating in 2032, while the Philippines is working towards its first 1,200 MW of nuclear capacity from the same year.

Thailand's latest draft power plan proposes its first SMR in 2037, while Malaysia and Singapore remain at the study stage.

Can nuclear power cover AI's energy demands? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Energy shocks vs. the shadow of Fukushima

The renewed interest marks a sharp reversal from the caution that followed Japan's Fukushima nuclear disaster in 2011.

The accident stalled several Southeast Asian countries' plans to pursue nuclear energy, Alvin Chew, a senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS) at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, told DW.

But a string of geopolitical shocks in recent years has changed the energy debate.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) says Southeast Asia's electricity generation has risen by around 60% since 2015. Coal supplied most of that increase, pushing its share of regional generation from 37% to 47%.

The war in Ukraine and the current Middle East crisis have heightened energy-security concerns for developing countries, even as most Southeast Asian governments have committed to net-zero emissions by 2050 or 2060, Chew said.

The region's electricity demand is forecast to grow by an average of 5.3% a year between 2026 and 2030.

"Nuclear energy is deemed to be the viable solution to address both challenges of climate and energy security," Chew said.

Middle East conflict is firing up China's electric future To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Appeal of modular reactors

One reason governments are reconsidering nuclear power is that today's technology is starkly different from what was used 15 years ago in Fukushima.

SMRs have broadened the range of possible projects. Unlike conventional reactors, SMRs are designed as smaller units that can potentially be added in stages.

"In the past, deploying nuclear energy generally meant building very large conventional reactors, involving long construction periods, enormous upfront investments and requiring electricity grids capable of absorbing very large generating units," Jie-Sheng Tan-Soo, assistant professor and director at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy in Singapore, told DW.

"SMRs have changed the nuclear conversation in Southeast Asia because they potentially make nuclear compatible with smaller grids, smaller countries and more incremental investment," he added.

China has started implementing SMRs Image: Zhang Boqun/Xinhua/picture alliance

That does not mean SMRs will solve nuclear power's economics. Many designs remain at an early stage of deployment, meaning promises of cheaper construction through mass production have yet to be demonstrated on a broad commercial scale.

Another force pushing nuclear energy back onto the agenda is the rapid expansion of data centers, which require large quantities of reliable electricity, Julius Cesar Trajano, a research fellow with the Centre for Non-Traditional Security Studies at RSIS, told DW.

The IEA expects electricity consumption from Southeast Asian data centers to more than double by 2030.

More than 70% of existing regional data-center capacity is concentrated in Singapore and Johor in southern Malaysia.

"Countries are therefore approaching nuclear energy with greater emphasis on governance and regulatory capacity than during earlier attempts," said Trajano.

Building a nuclear safety net

The hardest problems, however, remain much the same. Nuclear plants, even SMRs, still require a lot of time and money, and newcomer countries must establish independent regulators, train specialist workforces and develop credible systems for radioactive waste and emergency response.

Geography adds another layer of difficulty. Parts of Southeast Asia are vulnerable to earthquakes, volcanoes and tsunamis, making site selection and emergency planning particularly sensitive.

Nuclear power also places unusually heavy demands on state institutions, Tan-Soo said. Governments need institutions that take a long time to establish and must remain reliable for decades.

"For countries developing nuclear power for the first time, building this ecosystem can take as much effort as building the plant itself," he added.

Does nuclear energy make financial sense? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Long road to wielding nuclear power

Public support is another matter. A Philippine government survey released last year found that more than 70% of respondents supported nuclear energy's potential role in providing electricity.

By contrast, the Indonesia Energy Transition Outlook 2026 reported that 78% of respondents placed nuclear as their least-preferred energy source.

"The biggest obstacle is the political will to proceed with adoption of nuclear energy, which, to a certain extent, is dependent on public perception," said Chew.

Southeast Asia's highly varied national capacities and electricity systems also make a common pathway unlikely, Trajano said.

Vietnam has revived plans for large conventional plants, Indonesia and Thailand are giving greater attention to SMRs, while Singapore is still building the expertise needed to determine whether nuclear power is suitable at all.

"There is clearly much more political momentum behind nuclear power in Southeast Asia today than there was a decade ago, and I think some countries could ultimately deploy it," Tan-Soo said.

"But moving from announcing a nuclear ambition to financing, licensing, constructing and safely operating a reactor is an enormous step."

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

World.title: Why gender-based violence persists in Southern Africa
World.content:
A series of killings in South Africa has renewed scrutiny of efforts to combat violence against women. Activists say laws alone are not enough without effective implementation.

On Thursday, police in South Africa found the partially naked body of Dineo M. The 38-year-old had been beaten and stabbed to death in Ekurhuleni, a municipality on the outskirts of Johannesburg, South Africa's largest city.

This is one of a series of killings of women in their 20s and 30s in Ekurhuleni over the past two months.

But for Dineo's sister, Carol, this is much more than another statistic in a country where gender-based violence (GBV) was declared a national disaster in 2025.

"We sit here today and we will never see her walk through the door. Her 2-year-old has no idea what is going on," Carol told DW. "How do you explain to her [...] your mother was brutally murdered, dumped behind shrubs, left unrecognizable? [...] That is why you don't have a mother today."

A community on edge

Authorities said it was not yet clear whether the killings were linked. However, they said they have identified similarities and have issued an alert for women in Ekurhuleni to take precautions.

Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said on Sunday that so far there was no conclusive evidence that the killings were carried out by a serial killer, "but nothing has yet been excluded while investigations continue."

For families and communities, the deaths have raised fresh questions about whether existing measures are enough to protect women.

South African Minister in the Presidency for Women, Youth and Persons with Disabilities Sindisiwe Chikunga said at a protest march in Johannesburg that violence against women often starts behind closed doors.

"Please, stop it. Stop raping women. Stop insulting women. Stop financially abusing women," she said, warning that verbal abuse can escalate. "They start with insults. They proceed to assault and then to murder. It cannot be."

Why laws fall short

For Naledi Masipa, campaigns manager at Gender Links, an NGO promoting gender justice across Southern Africa, the problem encompasses all of society.

"Having laws and policies does not automatically change what happens in communities and households," she told DW, adding that the entire support system must work, from reporting and policing to health services, psychosocial support and legal assistance.

If one part fails, she said, women continue to carry the burden. "The real test is whether a woman in an ordinary community feels safer."

Amnesty International South Africa said the response to the crimes must recognize the gendered nature of killings.

"Femicide itself is not recognized as a crime. It's just seen as another murder," said Tegan Snyman, a research assistant at the international non-governmental organization, pointing out that South Africa had declared gender-based violence and femicide a national crisis . She argued that more resources were necessary as well as a sense of urgency.

A regional challenge

The neighboring country of Botswana also struggles with high levels of gender-based violence.

Natasha Rampa, a permanent secretary in Botswana's Ministry of Youth and Gender Affairs, said that "at least 37% of women in Botswana have experienced violence in their lifetimes."

In June, Botswana and the United Nations launched a joint program focused on prevention, survivor-centered services and stronger institutions.

"Violence is unacceptable, and we must work together as a society to address this issue," Minister of Youth and Gender Affairs Lesego Chombo told parliament. He said that tackling gender-based violence (GBV) requires action beyond government.

Turning policy into protection

Zambia also faces persistent gender-based violence — despite laws and national programs aimed at tackling it.

Why are women still unsafe in South Africa? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Anne Mbewe-Anamela, the executive director of the Non-Governmental Coordinating Council, an umbrella organization in the country that champions gender equality, said the response must put survivors at the center.

"GBV is deeply rooted in power, inequality, and social expectations," she told DW. "We can have strong laws, but if communities still believe violence is a private matter or a normal part of marriage, then survivors remain silent and trapped."

For activists across the region, the challenge is, therefore, not simply creating more policies. It is making protection, support and justice work in practice. And for families like Dineo's, that difference is painfully personal. Carol knows her sister will never walk through the door again.

She wants Dineo's daughter to grow up understanding that what happened to her mother was not normal and that women deserve to be safe.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: India's road rage: When cars become weapons
World.content:
Road disputes are turning violent across India, raising questions about status and impunity behind the wheel for drivers of expensive cars.

A road altercation in Gurugram, a suburb of New Delhi, went viral last week after a 27-year-old female biker was allegedly chased and hit by a car.

The two sides gave differing accounts of the initial dispute, with the car driver telling Indian media that the group of bikers overtook his car and slowed down in front of it.

In turn, the motorcycle rider, Shivani Chauhan, said the car was following her and the argument started when she asked the people inside to keep a safe distance.

Chauhan's motorcycle-mounted camera shows the car hitting her from the side and them speeding away as she falls and rolls on the road.

"I could have suffered serious fractures or internal injuries and even died. Due to such people, the roads of Gurugram and Delhi feel unsafe," Chauhan was quoted as saying by Indian news outlets.

According to reports, the driver claims that he lost control of his vehicle and left the scene because he feared reprisals from the biker group. Police have since arrested the driver on charges including attempted murder and stalking.

Road rage escalates to violence, shootouts

The case was only the latest example of how quickly a dispute on India's increasingly crowded roads can turn violent.

In March in Hassan, in the southern Karnataka state, young men reportedly shouted at the driver of a Toyota Fortuner SUV to slow down.

Police said the driver turned the vehicle around and rammed the group, killing one man and seriously injuring three others.

In the northern city of Dehradun that month, an argument over giving way between two SUVs, a Toyota Fortuner and a Mahindra Scorpio, escalated into a chase and gunfire.

The altercation cost the life of one man, a retired Army brigadier Mukesh Joshi, who was not involved in the initial dispute.

"The occupants of the Scorpio waited outside the club till early morning and then chased the Fortuner. During the firing, the brigadier, who was out on a morning walk, was hit by a bullet in the chest," said senior superintendent of police Pramendra Dobhal.

Concerns over road safety prompted the administration of Daman, a small coastal town north of Mumbai, to take an unusual step. On September 9, officials gathered owners of Mahindra Thar and Toyota Fortuner SUVs and made them take a public road safety pledge.

District Collector Saurabh Mishra, the district's top administrator, warned that these kinds of larger vehicles should not be used to intimidate others or display power.

More cars, less space on Indian roads

India's roads are notoriously dangerous, with government figures showing 485 people were killed in crashes on an average day in 2024. The data also indicates that the number of vehicles is currently growing much faster than the expansion of the road network.

Notably, SUVs accounted for about 2.63 million vehicles, or 56% of India's car sales, in the 12 months leading up to March 2026, according to industry data. While more SUVs on the road does not necessarily mean more aggressive driving, the vehicles' size, height and presence can change the dynamics of a confrontation.

"For some drivers it is an expression of strength and domination," former police officer Yashovardhan Azad told DW.

"One drives with impunity to make an impression on smaller vehicles," said Azad.

He called for tougher policing using new technology, rigorous punishment and a nationwide programme to promote safer driving.

"Hitting a smaller vehicle intentionally is not rash driving. It is a measure of criminal intent," he said.

'SUV drivers have a beast in their hands'

Road safety expert Prince Singhal, founder of the Community Against Drunken Driving, sees both vehicles and drivers as parts of the problem.

"The issue of terror behind SUVs is not just a traffic challenge but also a behavioral issue," Singhal told DW.

"The SUV drivers have a beast in their hands and it's their mindset which decides the outcome."

How a start-up in India is turning old cars into EVs To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Singhal notes that SUVs are a practical choice for bad roads and long journeys, but also points to issues in their design.

"High bonnets and elevated bumper heights increased the risk of fatal head and chest injuries for pedestrians, children, and cyclists and all other road users compared to traditional lower cars," added Singhal.

With an SUV at hand, drivers often experience "a psychological sense of invincibility," which can lead to hostile behavior, road bullying and rule violations, he said.

Are drivers taking traffic too personally?

Psychiatrist Ravi Prakash, who studies traffic behavior at Veditha Mind Care Clinic in Bengaluru, agrees that the driver "feels both powerful and protected inside a large, sturdy vehicle."

He also warned that there are other mechanisms at play.

"There is a psychological phenomenon called 'personalization,' where people interpret an ordinary act by a stranger as something personally directed at them," he told DW.

Someone cutting across a lane may be in a hurry. But the other driver may see it as an attempt to assert superiority. A perceived insult can then threaten a person's identity and trigger a spike of anger.

"Usually, hitting the other person is not the goal initially," Prakash said.

The driver first tries to assert superiority through speeding, honking, gestures or shouting. When that fails, a desire to punish can emerge, what Prakash calls an "illusion of retributive justice."

'Anything that you tolerate becomes a culture'

Sociologist Dipankar Gupta says road rage happens "because traffic rules are not strictly enforced," with the problem in no way limited to SUV drivers.

"Even motorcyclists get into road rage," he told DW.

"It's like a child who is not disciplined and throws a tantrum," Gupta said of the wider breakdown in road discipline. When rules are routinely ignored and people do not want to face the consequences, he added, it becomes similar to "a punch up" in school.

Why India will shape the car of the future To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With cameras everywhere, however, such behavior has become harder to ignore.

"The anger is not new. What has changed is that everyone has a camera now, whether it is a dashcam, a helmet camera or a mobile phone," Deepanshu Gupta, cofounder of CrashFree India, a road safety nonprofit, told DW.

He warns that recording an incident is not the same as preventing it.

"Every driver knows that the odds of facing any real consequence are very low," he said.

"Anything that you tolerate becomes a culture. Aggressive driving is normalized here, but culture responds to enforcement," Deepanshu Gupta said.

He also noted that road rage is not a specifically defined offense in India, leaving police to choose between rash driving and far more serious charges such as attempted murder. "There is very little in between," he said.

In such conditions, responsibility rests on the drivers, particularly when a large vehicle is in a confrontation with a more vulnerable road user.

"The bigger the vehicle you bring onto the road, the greater your duty of care has to be," he said.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: Trump, a Mamdani: “Espero que sea un gran alcalde de Nueva York. Tiene potencial”
World.content:
Es difícil encontrar dos personas más en las antípodas que Donald Trump y Zohran Mamdani. Ya sea por su biografía, edades o ideas políticas, el presidente de Estados Unidos y el alcalde de Nueva York representan dos mundos totalmente distintos. Pese a tener tantas diferencias, los dos políticos han mostrado este lunes algunas de sus (pocas) coincidencias. Ambos han comparecido en el jardín de la Mansión Gracie, la residencia oficial de los alcaldes de Nueva York, en un tono amigable para mostrar más lo que les une que lo que les separa. “Espero que sea un gran alcalde. Tiene potencial para ello”, ha dicho Trump en un halago sorprendente hacia alguien que alguna vez ha calificado de “lunático de la izquierda radical”.

Mamdani no ha lanzado elogios a Trump. En lugar de su habitual sonrisa, ha comparecido con un semblante serio. Para uno de los líderes del sector izquierdista de los demócratas, mostrar cercanía con alguien como Trump supone un considerable riesgo político. La gobernadora del Estado, la también demócrata Kathy Hochul, defiende una postura distinta, de mayor confrontación y desde luego no se ven cuando el republicano viaja a Nueva York. Mamdani justifica la decisión, que puede no gustar a muchos de sus electores, con que si hay alguna vía de mejorar la vida de los neoyorquinos, él la va a intentar.

Esta es la tercera vez que ambos hombres se ven desde la llegada de Mamdani al poder. En estos nueve meses, la relación entre los dos ha cambiado mucho. El alcalde ha pasado de tildar de “fascista” al presidente a adoptar un tono institucional, sin forzar las muestras de simpatía, pero siempre con un tono de respeto. La primera vez que fue a verlo al Despacho Oval, los periodistas preguntaron a Mamdani si seguía considerando al presidente un fascista. El demócrata iba a contestar, pero Trump lo interrumpió. “Déjalo, dile que sí, y pasemos a otra cosa, perderás más tiempo tratando de explicárselo”, dijo.

Zohran Mamdani y Donald Trump, el lunes en Gracie Mansión de Nueva York. Julia Demaree Nikhinson (AP/LaPresse)

El alcalde ha hablado este lunes de lo importante que era para Trump visitar Mansión Gracie, un sitio que al republicano le trae muchos recuerdos, donde dice sentirse “como en casa”. Los dos han abordado un plan para construir 12.000 viviendas en Sunnyside Yard, en Queens, el distrito donde creció Trump, un proyecto que necesita una importante ayuda del Gobierno federal. Además, ha dicho Mamdani, Trump no es solo el líder del país, sino alguien que ha construido mucho. “Me comprometí en mi campaña a reunirme con cualquier persona que pudiera hacer algo por los neoyorquinos. En las anteriores reuniones que tuve con Trump fuimos capaces de liberar a un estudiante que había sido detenido por el ICE”, ha justificado la decisión de fotografiarse con el mandatario republicano.

El encuentro se produce en plena polémica por la decisión de Trump de retirar a la CNN, MS Now y Politico la acreditación para la Casa Blanca, un golpe sin precedentes contra la libertad de prensa consagrada en la Primera Enmienda. Mamdani ha aguantado con cara de circunstancias las preguntas al respecto de los periodistas sin entrar en el debate. Trump ha respondido, en su tono habitual: “Dijeron que me iban a boicotear, pero nunca me boicotean. La prensa tiene también una obligación. He ganado unas elecciones por mayoría, he hecho muchas cosas grandes, he parado ocho guerras y tenemos la mejor economía en la historia de nuestro país y siempre tengo prensa negativa”.

El Ayuntamiento ya había dicho al anunciar la reunión que esta se centraría en asuntos que afectan a “Nueva York y a los neoyorquinos”. Trataban con este aviso de rebajar las expectativas de aquellos que esperaran un enfrentamiento entre ambos a cuenta de la llegada del primer ministro israelí, Benjamin Netanyahu, a Nueva York esta semana para participar en la Asamblea General de la ONU.

Mamdani, muy crítico con la actuación del Gobierno israelí en Gaza, pidió en julio a la Administración de Trump que ejecutara la orden de detención que pesa contra Netanyahu, al que llamó “criminal de guerra y autor de un genocidio horrible”. Trump, aliado del primer ministro israelí, con el que inició este año la guerra de Irán, dejó claro en todo momento que no pensaba actuar contra Netanyahu, que podrá moverse con total libertad en Nueva York.

En los últimos días, Mamdani ha rebajado su retórica ante la previsión de que hubiera grandes manifestaciones contra el líder conservador israelí. “Mi enfoque en este momento es garantizar la seguridad de los neoyorquinos, asegurar que puedan desplazarse de un punto a otro y seguir expresando con honestidad mi visión del mundo”, aseguró el alcalde el jueves.

Este lunes será un día de contrastes para Mamdani. Tras verse con Trump tiene previsto cenar con el senador progresista y antiguo candidato a presidente Bernie Sanders, el hombre que le inspiró para entrar en política en 2016. Trump, por su parte, se reunirá con el presidente de Francia, Emmanuel Macron, que este año participará en la Asamblea General por última vez.

Antes de la reunión, Trump escribió que se dirigía a la Mansion Gracie, que es, según dijo, uno de sus sitios favoritos en el mundo. “Pasé mucho tiempo allí, con algunos grandes alcaldes, algunos en la media y otros muy malos. Será interesante ver cómo va la cosa hoy, invitado por el alcalde Mandani”, afirmó en un mensaje en Truth.

World.title: “Haría obligatoria la Educación Física hasta en Bachillerato”
World.content:
Antes de ser actor y humorista, David Amor estudió para ser profesor y llegó a la élite como balonmanista. Junto a Xabier Soutullo, graduado en Magisterio y también jugador, hablan de la importancia de integrar el deporte en la escuela y de cómo valores como la inclusión, la perseverancia o el trabajo conjunto construyen la educación del futuro

Antes de escuchar las carcajadas del público, el humorista David Amor (Salceda de Caselas, Pontevedra, 46 años) se rodeó de los gritos de ánimo desde las gradas como jugador de balonmano, deporte en el que alcanzó la gloria: fue internacional en las categorías júnior y juvenil, donde fue subcampeón del mundo en Moscú (1998) y de Europa en Suiza (1999). A nivel de clubes, jugó en División de Honor Plata (1999 y 2007) y en la Liga Asobal (2008). Todo ocurrió mientras estudiaba Ciencias de la Actividad Física y antes de que su vida tomara otro rumbo, el de la comunicación, el humor y la actuación. Hoy es conocido por una carrera que comenzó en la televisión gallega y que después le llevó a programas y series de ámbito nacional, en la que ha aplicado las enseñanzas que le dio el deporte durante años.

“Del deporte me llevo la satisfacción de la persistencia. A veces el resultado no es exactamente lo que tú querías, pero el camino es divertido”

De hecho, en su conversación con Xabier Soutullo (Vigo, 25 años), que también llegó al balonmano con siete años y que estudia para ser profesor, Amor rememora aquella etapa deportiva para hablar de algo que todavía mantiene: la perseverancia. Fue decisiva. Compañeros que parecían mejores terminaron por abandonar, mientras él se mantuvo firme. Esa misma forma de entender el esfuerzo, reconoce, la ha trasladado a su vida profesional. Soutullo además reflexiona sobre cómo en la pista se aprende a convivir, a trabajar con otros (aunque sean muy diferentes) y a perseguir un objetivo común.

“Me gustaría ser un profesor que atendiese a la inclusión del alumnado, crear un modelo del que todos formen parte”

A partir de sus similitudes, abordan la importancia de integrar el deporte en la escuela. “Yo haría obligatoria la asignatura de Educación Física hasta el Bachillerato, y la pondría todos los días”, reconoce Amor quien, a pesar de que estudió para ser docente de esta asignatura, nunca llegó a ejercer. Intrigado por la vocación que no siguió, le pregunta a Soutullo sus prioridades para cuando sea profesor. Su respuesta es lograr que en el aula los alumnos se complementen, que funcionen acompasados. En definitiva, escapar de la individualidad para trabajar como un equipo.

Pensemos la educación del futuro ‘Pensemos el mañana’, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja, busca fomentar el conocimiento, los valores de la educación, un aprendizaje sostenible y responsable y dar respuestas a los grandes desafíos de la educación del futuro. El proyecto pivota sobre seis ejes: 1 Aprendizaje y sentido vital 2 Bienestar y salud mental 3 Futuro y empleabilidad 4 Sostenibilidad y sentido colectivo 5 Tecnología y ética 6 Carácter y ciudadanía ¿Qué está ocurriendo en estos tiempos de cambios profundos y transversales? ¿Cuáles son los grandes retos para afrontar la transformación que viene? ¿Qué educación necesitamos? Diferentes personalidades de todos los ámbitos nos ayudarán a responder a estas y otras preguntas destinadas a impulsar cambios, dinamizar ideas y apoyar propuestas con impacto pedagógico y social. ‘Pensemos el mañana’ es un proyecto inspirador para las futuras generaciones llamadas a conquistar nuevas cotas del saber en un mundo complejo y cambiante.

World.title: El edificio de al lado se ha llenado de ‘pingüinos’ que emiten calor y ruido. ¿Qué podemos hacer?
World.content:
Los lectores envían sus preguntas al consultorio de vivienda de EL PAÍS en colaboración con Legálitas

Pregunta. El edificio de al lado se ha llenado este verano de equipos de aire acondicionado portátil o pingüinos. Son inquilinos de un edificio de un solo propietario. El ruido es infernal y el calor que emiten los tubos de salida es salvaje. Lo hemos notificado al propietario, que ha mandado aviso a sus inquilinos, pero nadie hace nada. La distancia entre edificios está entre 1,5-3 metros máximo en el patio. ¿Qué podemos hacer? Enebro

Respuesta. Al tratarse de fincas independientes, las relaciones de vecindad se rigen por las normas sobre contigüidad y prohibición de inmisiones del Código Civil, así como por las ordenanzas municipales en materia de contaminación acústica y térmica. Además, el propietario del inmueble colindante puede ser responsable de las molestias causadas por sus inquilinos.

El primer paso es obtener pruebas objetivas de las molestias mediante mediciones de ruido y temperatura, que acrediten el posible incumplimiento de la normativa. También conviene recopilar documentación que permita acreditar los daños sufridos, como informes médicos o psicológicos en caso de afectación a la salud o al descanso, facturas de gastos ocasionados o cualquier otro elemento que justifique una eventual reclamación por daños y perjuicios.

A continuación, debe remitirse al propietario un burofax con certificación de texto y acuse de recibo, requiriéndole para que cese la actividad molesta y retire o reubique los aparatos en un plazo razonable, advirtiéndole de la posibilidad de emprender acciones legales de cesación e indemnización de daños y perjuicios al amparo del artículo 1902 del Código Civil.

Además, de acuerdo con la Ley Orgánica 1/2025, antes de presentar una demanda civil es obligatorio intentar un Medio Adecuado de Solución de Controversias (MASC), como la mediación, la conciliación o una negociación formal. Por ello, resulta recomendable incluir esta propuesta en el propio burofax para cumplir con el requisito previo exigido por la ley.

Si el propietario no atiende el requerimiento ni participa en la negociación propuesta, podrá interponerse una demanda civil para solicitar el cese de las molestias y la correspondiente indemnización por los daños materiales y morales ocasionados.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: 10 experiencias en el Matarraña para sacarle todo el jugo a la comarca aragonesa en septiembre
World.content:
Pedalear por la vía verde de la Val de Zafán, caminar por el Solo Sculpture Trail, dormir en un antiguo molino de papel y más pistas en esta zona de la provincia de Teruel que es tierra de cañones y, sobre todo, de buitres

Wikipedia dice, todo el mundo repite —incluida la IA—, y será verdad mientras no se demuestre lo contrario, que el río mediterráneo mejor conservado del planeta es el Matarraña. Este afluente del Ebro, de casi 100 kilómetros de longitud, ha dado nombre a la comarca en la que Teruel se funde y confunde con Tarragona y Castellón, y ha labrado las rocas calizas de los Puertos de Beceite, donde nace, como si en vez de agua pura llevara carburo de silicio verde, abrasivo y cortante a más no poder. Aparte de fabulosos cañones y de pozas que piden a gritos bañarse hasta bien entrado el otoño, este rincón del noreste de la provincia de Teruel tiene muchas otras cosas que sorprenden al viajero.

La primera es que aquí no hablan como los demás turolenses, sino chapurriau, una variedad aragonesa del catalán cantarina y cadenciosa que, a los forasteros, salvo que sean de las provincias de al lado, les suena a valenciano. Matarraña —o Matarranya, como lo escriben también— es un no parar de sorpresas. Tomen nota de estas 10.

Más información 24 horas en Ayamonte, la ciudad de Huelva donde vivir uno de los mejores atardeceres de Europa

Penetrar en la comarca siguiendo a un tren loco

Por Matarraña pasó un tren hoy difícil de explicar, que iba de La Puebla de Híjar a Tortosa, del norte de Teruel al Bajo Ebro, y que pretendía llegar algún día hasta la orilla del mar. Un loco sueño ferroviario que duró 30 años (de 1941 a 1971) y que dejó este abrupto y solitario rincón del mapa aragonés lleno de puentes inútiles y de estaciones en mitad de ninguna parte.

Se esfumó el tren, pero su itinerario y su espíritu insensatos permanecen en la vía verde de la Val de Zafán. Una buena manera de hincarle el diente a la comarca es echarse a pedalear desde la que fue la estación de Valjunquera con las bicis y los guías de Senda. Salvo en un par de túneles, que no se ve nada, se va descubriendo un paisaje cada vez más ordenado de olivos y almendros y una luz cada vez más mediterránea. Hay una parada obligada en el alto viaducto que hay a 9,5 kilómetros del inicio, para saludar al río Matarraña. Al otro lado, en otra antigua estación, se halla el muy recomendable hotel La Parada del Compte.

Comer lo que comió Picasso

Pedaleando por una vía verde llana no es que se haga mucho ejercicio, pero hambre sí que se hace. Para calmarla, no hay mejor opción en toda la comarca que Fonda Alcalá. Ubicado en Calaceite, miembro de la Asociación Los Pueblos Más Bonitos de España, por esta casa de comidas algo más que centenaria —data de 1922— han pasado García Márquez, Álvaro Cunqueiro, Francesc Català Roca, Paco de Lucía, Serrat… No en este orden, lógicamente. El que no pasó, pero sí comió lo que aquí se hace, fue Picasso. Les perdius de Picasso, las perdices que le guisaron en esta casa y le llevaron enlatadas a Francia en 1967, y las judías blancas de Beceite con sardinas de cubo son dos platos legendarios, fundamentales. Pero el chef Ignacio Alcalá se inventa todos los días otros más excitantes y divertidos, que es lo que aprendió a hacer en las cocinas de Neichel y Can Roca.

Hacer senderismo en una galería de arte

He aquí sin duda lo más flipante de la comarca, naturaleza aparte: Solo Houses, una hermosa finca campestre de 200 hectáreas en el municipio de Cretas, donde llevan 13 años materializándose como naves alienígenas casas alucinantes de arquitectos de vanguardia que se pueden alquilar desde 850 euros por noche y donde pronto lo hará un hotel de habitaciones circulares exentas, con vistas al bosque diseñado por Smiljan Radić, Premio Pritzker 2026. Obviamente, alojarse aquí es solo para amantes de la arquitectura y gente con pasta.

Una mujer pasea entre esculturas del Solo Sculpture Trail, en la localidad de Cretas. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

El resto debe contentarse con ver los ovnis de lejos, paseando entre las vides de la bodega Venta D’Aubert y las esculturas del Solo Sculpture Trail, un circuito creado por los propietarios de todo esto, los galeristas Christian Bourdais y Eva Albarrán, para exponer al aire libre y vender obras que tampoco parecen de este mundo. Se tarda hora y media en ver las 20 esculturas y solo cuesta cinco euros. También se puede visitar la bodega y catar cinco de sus vinos por 25.

La bodega Venta D’Aubert. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

Asomarse a la vecina Tarragona por un desfiladero

Si pasear por un sendero de pago entre esculturas carísimas parece algo pijo y rebuscado, en el pueblo de al lado, en Arnes, podemos hacerlo en un lugar verdaderamente salvaje, el desfiladero de Els Estrets, y bañarnos en las aguas inmaculadas del río que lo atraviesa —un afluente del río Algás, que a su vez lo es del Matarraña—, sin pagar un euro. Al llegar al aparcamiento donde arranca la senda, descubriremos estupefactos Les Gronses, unas formidables moles anaranjadas donde pululan escaladores, cabras monteses y buitres leonados.

El desfiladero de Els Estrets, en la vecina Terra Alta de Tarragona. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

Y nada más echarnos a andar, un cartel que dice: “Parc Natural dels Ports”. Estamos en Cataluña, concretamente en la Terra Alta de Tarragona. Otro cartel advierte que el baño solo está permitido en el Toll Blau (el charco azul). Allí veremos dos o tres humanos y, más adelante, si es que se dejan ver, alguna nutria y la libélula Macromia splendens, en peligro de extinción. Mucho más fácil de observar, libando en las lavandas, es la mariposa Cleopatra. El desfiladero se recorre, yendo y volviendo por camino evidente, en un par de horas.

Dormir en un antiguo molino de papel

Vistas desde el hotel La Fábrica de Solfa, en Beceite. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

Beceite, además de un bonito pueblo, con muchas de sus casas colgadas sobre el encañonado río Matarraña, es el campo base ideal para explorar la comarca, porque está cerca de su paraje más deseado —el Parrizal, donde nace aquél— y porque hay un hotelito familiar que es un hotelazo. La Fábrica de Solfa, que así se llama, fue un molino de papel: con la fuerza del río se trituraba ropa vieja y se obtenía la pasta necesaria. Ahora es una fábrica de actividades: todas las que se cuentan en este reportaje y algunas más. De amorosos cuidados que prodigan Javier y Alberto Moragrega a los que llegan exhaustos después de hacerlas. Y de ricos platos: el recapte de fesols de Beceite, el ternasco de Aragón, las texturas de té de roca y todo lo que se sirve en el restaurante Marca al Agua. Tampoco se desayuna mal, viendo a las nutrias jugar en el río saltarín. Lo único malo es que aparecen al rayar el sol, así que hay que madrugar.

Darse un baño de multitudes y otro en un ‘fish spa’ natural

A solo tres kilómetros de Beceite se encuentra el Parrizal (o Parrissal), el desfiladero que nadie que visita esta comarca deja de admirar y recorrer, a tal punto que hay que reservar online para evitar mayores aglomeraciones de las que ya se forman sobre las tablas de dos palmos de ancho que hay instaladas en las paredes verticales del cañón, a buena altura sobre las aguas impolutas del recién nacido Matarraña. Avanzar nadando por el propio río, que sería lo deseable para librarse del sudor propio y de los atascos, está prohibido.

Pasarelas en la senda del Parrizal. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

Donde sí está permitido mojarse y remojarse es en La Pesquera, en las pozas que forma el río Ulldemó, afluente del Matarraña, a tres kilómetros también de Beceite. Comparadas con las de otros ríos de montaña, estas aguas de hipnótico color verde jade son hasta cálidas. Y mucho más relajantes: metes los pies y acuden docenas de diminutos barbos y madrillas a limpiar tus células muertas. Esto es ictioterapia y La Pesquera, un fish spa natural, sin kimonos ni musiquillas new age.

Remar con el último sol en el pantano de Pena

Kayak al atardecer en el pantano de Pena. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

A la misma distancia de Beceite que el Parrizal y La Pesquera, está el pantano de Pena, uno de los más antiguos de Teruel (de 1930) y el único de la cuenca del Matarraña. Si hubiera muchos pantanos, no sería el río mediterráneo mejor conservado del mundo. Ir allí a navegar en kayak al atardecer es una de las actividades que recomienda y organiza La Fábrica de Solfa. Desde el hotel se llega con una bici eléctrica en un cuarto de hora y, después de rodear el embalse en media más, se embarca y se rema hasta el centro para admirar cómo el penúltimo sol se duplica en la cabecera y el agua se vuelve de oro. Girando luego el kayak en redondo y apuntando con la proa hacia el noreste, se ve cómo los últimos rayos iluminan la Caixa, una cumbre que a los matarrañeses les parece que tiene forma de caja de caudales y por eso la llaman así. Si remando y girando se vuelca accidentalmente, o adrede para refrescarse, no pasa nada: aquí está permitido el baño.

Asistir al banquete de 500 aves carroñeras

José Ramón Moragrega entre buitres en el Observatorio de Aves Mas de Bunyol. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

En la sierra de Arca, donde está la Caixa, anidan multitud de buitres leonados. No es solo que allí hay cortados rocosos idóneos para ellos. Es que al pie de la montaña, en una masía de Valderrobres, vive José Ramón Moragrega, que lleva más de 30 años alimentándolos. Todos los días, Buitreman —así le llaman— sale a las 9.15 con una carretilla llena de pulmones de cerdo y la vuelca ante una muchedumbre expectante de estas enormes carroñeras. Hasta 500 de ellas se reúnen para compartir de muy malos modos este desayuno, formando una monumental tremolina de polvo, chillidos e iracundos aleteos. Todo puede verse y fotografiarse en el Observatorio de Aves Mas de Bunyol, una masía que es también un formidable hide, con grandes ventanales orientados a los cuatro vientos para no perderse nada, desde el momento en que Buitreman vuelca la carretilla y se aparta a toda velocidad de sus pequeños de picos afilados como cuchillos —por eso va con casco, porque más de una vez ha salido descalabrado—, hasta cuando aparecen los alimoches para disputarse las migajas de la tragantona.

Al despedirse de los visitantes, Moragrega les confía casi entre lágrimas su delicado estado de salud y que sus niños pueden quedarse pronto sin desayuno si alguna entidad pública o privada no asume la gestión del observatorio, que es también alojamiento rural. Es un negocio rentable, asegura.

Vuelta a las rocas huesudas del Masmut

Muchos buitres leonados que desayunan en Mas de Bunyol pasan el resto del día haciendo la digestión en las Rocas del Masmut, en Peñarroya de Tastavins, donde hay una importante colonia de ellos. El PR TE-157, uno de los Senderos Turísticos de Aragón, bien mantenido y señalizado, invita a rodear este manojo de peñas anaranjadas de más de 100 metros de altura, similares a los Mallos de Riglos, cuyo nombre se cree que viene de los masmuda, una tribu bereber que quizá estuviera asentada aquí cuando España era musulmana.

Es una ruta circular de poco más de tres horas, cuatro si el senderista se desvía a los tres kilómetros para subir al mirador del Masmut. Situado a 500 metros de las rocas y a similar altura, es un buen lugar para verlas como las ven los buitres, asomando como las falanges de un gigante muerto y enterrado bajo la costra caliza del Matarraña.

Un pícnic regenerativo para despedirse del Matarraña

La última sorpresa de esta ruta llena de ellas la puede dar Tel·lúric, una masía centenaria del municipio de Ráfels cuyos nuevos propietarios no es que respeten la tradición agrícola de los masos, de estas catedrales civiles del campo matarrañés, es que van un paso más allá. O un paso más acá, porque trabajan la tierra con tal cuidado que no solo no se agota, sino que se regenera. Los olivos, los almendros y las viñas que atiende Sorin Dragoman no son soldados invasores de ejércitos cuadriculados, sino pacíficos hermanos de los pinos, las carrascas, el tomillo, el romero, el té de roca y el poleo.

Con todo lo que aquí se produce (vinos, aceite y almendras con certificación ecológica y de agricultura regenerativa) dispuesto sobre un mantel a cuadros, y también con las carnes a la brasa que salen sin parar de la cocina, se organizan unos pícnics delante de la masía que son una manera estupenda de despedirse del Matarraña. El águila culebrera sobrevuela los cultivos de Tel·lúric sin sospechar que son cosa de humanos.

World.title: Government identifies 50 sites for accelerated housing programme
World.content:
Housing minister Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan has drawn up a list of 50 locations where the Dutch government wants to speed up housebuilding to meet the target of 100,000 new homes a year.

The plan includes 26 sites near railway stations that are already well served by transport links and utilities, making them relatively easy to develop.

The first five locations have already been identified in Maastricht, Haarlem, Leeuwarden, Deventer and Weert, with another five due to be announced later this year. All 10 developments are supposed to be finished by 2040.

The cabinet is investing €7 billion over the next eight years in affordable homes and wants to scrap planning rules and building requirements that slow down the process.

Affordable homes are supposed to account for two-thirds of all new projects, with at least 30% going on social housing.

Around €3 billion of the funding will take the form of subsidies, while investors who build houses for the mid-rental sector will receive a payment for each unit they construct from 2029.

The government is anxious to retain private investors who have been selling rental flats in response to the Affordable Rent Act, which has tightened the rules used to calculate rent levels, and lingering uncertainty over the “box 3” tax on income from assets.

Local and regional subsidies

Local councils will be encouraged to buy land for housing, with the national government providing financial support to share the risk. The municipalities and provinces will also be able to hire 200 equivalent full-time staff to work on issuing permits, while a team of experts will tour the country using their specialist knowledge to revive projects that have become stuck in the system.

Analysts noted that some of the regulations would have the effect of pumping more money into existing plans. “That means that some building projects probably won’t go ahead because they’re not profitable,” Stefan Groot, housing market economist for Rabobank, told NRC.

Boekholt-O’Sullivan said: “I will continue with what works and reform what doesn’t. It is clear what has to happen, money is avaiable and there are enough building projects.

“What matters now is moving from the drawing board to the foundations. The government can’t do it alone: we need builders, investors, local authorities and provinces to work with us.”

World.title: Heineken set to buy pub portfolio from debt-laden UK landlord
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Amsterdam-based brewing giant Heineken is poised to buy 300 pubs from Britain’s largest pub owner, Stonegate, in a €350 million deal.

Heineken is reported to have been holding talks over the summer with Stonegate, which is seeking to reduce its debts of £3 billion (€3.5 billion) by selling 1,000 of its 4,500 outlets.

Most of the debt is related to the British company’s decision to purchase Enterprise Inns in 2019, just before the coronavirus pandemic shut down the entire British pub sector for several months.

Pubs have also been struggling with the rapidly rising cost of beer, energy, wages and higher taxes on employers.

Heineken already owns around 2,350 pubs in Britain through its subsidiary Star Pubs & Bars.

World.title: Council of State: freeze “disproportionate” traffic fines
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Council of State has urged the cabinet to rethink its decision to raise traffic fines amid concerns that the penalties have increased out of proportion to other offences.

Justice minister David van Weel wants to raise fines across the board by 2.7% next year, in line with inflation.

If approved, the new fines would include €130 for parking without authorisation, €330 for running red lights and €450 for using a mobile phone at the wheel.

Speeding fines depend on the actual speed, ranging from €33 for going 4km/h over the limit to €424 for exceeding the limit by 30km/h. But fines are higher in built-up areas and 30km zones: driving 50km/h in a 30km/h limit will cost €351.

The Council of State, which issues non-binding advice on all government bills and decisions, queried if the raise was “necessary, fair and proportionate”, echoing criticism from other legal bodies in recent years.

They include the prosecution service (Openbare Ministerie), judges and the agency that collects the fines, the CJI, which said there was “imbalance” with fines for other offences such as common assault, which typically carries a penalty of €400.

Debt problems

Traffic fines have increased cumulatively by 220% in the last 30 years, while in 2024 127,000 families had problems with debt caused by outstanding traffic penalties.

The Council of State said freezing the fines rather than allowing them to rise with inflation was a “first obvious step” towards rebalancing the penalties.

It said the reason given by ministers – that the income from fines was needed to meet the justice ministry’s costs – was not a valid legal argument.

“The aim of these fines is to sanction behaviour that breaks the rules and improve road safety,” it said in a written advisory. “Raising the tariffs for traffic fines should relate to serving that purpose.”

World.title: Urgent help needed for children in emergency asylum shelters
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Children in emergency shelters are living in unsafe and dangerous conditions that violate international law, according to a two-year investigation by the Dutch Safety Board.

The organisation has been looking into the living situation for some 7,000 children who are currently living in crisis accommodations while awaiting the outcome of their asylum claims.

Children experience constant noise and a total lack of privacy in these shelters as well as a high risk of physical and sexual violence, the report found.

The safety board wants the immigration ministry to make sweeping reforms in the next six months.

“Emergency shelter is not normal. It was initially intended for a short period, but by now, children sometimes live in emergency shelters for years,” the organisation’s chairperson Chris van Dam said in a statement.

More than 60% of asylum seekers are now being housed in “emergency” shelters, like vacant offices, ships, event halls, and temporary container homes.

The safety board wants a structural solution to the shelter problems as well as improvements in emergency shelters, including setting a maximum length of stay and enforcing quality standards.

World.title: Maastricht and son of André Rieu at odds over Christmas decor
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Maastricht has limited how Pierre Rieu can decorate his hotel in the Limburg capital, telling the son of famous musician André Rieu that his current proposal is too extravagant.

Rieu had proposed to turn the historic city centre building into a life-sized Christmas gift, with string lights and an illuminated bow.

The 4-star Hotel Derlon dates from 1870 and was bought by Rieu in 2025.

He had done up the hotel in the same manner last year, but the city’s Planning and Monuments Commission found the decorations to be excessive, according to local news outlet L1.

The hotelier was told he needed to choose between the bow and the string lights to allow the building’s architecture to be visible.

Rieu told regional broadcaster 1Zuid he was irritated with the decision. “We’re talking about Christmas lights. I don’t think anyone is bothered by that,” he said.

World.title: More Dutch students studying abroad, Spain most popular choice
World.content:
More Dutch students are spending part of their degree abroad, but the proportion is still below pre-pandemic levels, according to latest official figures.

Some 24% of students who graduated from universities and vocational colleges in 2025 went abroad for part of their studies, with one in six (17%) staying for three months or longer.

Five years ago, during the most restricted phase of the coronavirus pandemic, just 16% of all students had spent time outside the Netherlands, the government statistics agency CBS said.

Spain was the most popular destination for students who took part in the Erasmus+ exchange programme between 2014 and 2024, accounting 16.9% of the total, followed by Germany (9.7%) and the UK (8.9%).

The last figure is noteworthy because Britain left the Erasmus+ scheme in 2020 as part of the Brexit agreement, though it is rejoining from next year.

Students who went abroad for their entire degree were most likely to go to Belgium, followed by the UK and the United States.

Online decline

One in seven students took part in online lessons or projects hosted by foreign colleges and universities, but here there was a declining trend, particularly among university students.

Just 10% of the latter group followed an online course, down from 14% in 2021, while for vocational students the proportion slipped from 19% to 18%.

More than one-third (36%) of recent graduates who spent time abroad also included an online element.

World.title: LGBT tolerance slumps in the Netherlands as debate turns vicious
World.content:
Less than a quarter of schoolboys in the Netherlands have a positive view of homosexuality, almost half the proportion of four years ago, according to a Europe-wide survey.

The HBSC (Health Behaviour in School-Aged Children) poll found that just 22% of boys aged 12 to 16 had a positive view of homosexuality, compared to 40% the last time the survey was carried out in 2021.

Gonneke Stevens, professor of Social and Behavioural Sciences at Utrecht University, said there was a “worrying turn in the trend” after decades of growing acceptance of same-sex relationships.

“In recent years sexual diversity has been increasingly questioned by leading figures in society, including politicians,” said Stevens, who led the Dutch research team in collaboration with the Trimbos mental health institute.

The COC, which campaigns for LGBGTI rights in the Netherlands, described the findings as a “frightening development.” Director Marie Ricardo said: “We badly need the young generation for a free country in which everyone can be themselves.”

The survey found girls were still more accepting of homosexuality than boys, but the proportion had fallen from 78% to just over half (51%) since 2021.

Manosphere

Stevens said there was a clear link between deepening intolerance and the rise of trends on social media such as the “manosphere”, which provides a platform for aggressive and discriminatory messages about women and gays.

“The fact is that in recent years young people have been exposed to these views and that in the same period they have taken a more negative view of homosexuality.”

Prime minister Rob Jetten, who is due to marry his male partner Nicolás Keenan next year, said the figures were “shocking”.

“The influence of social media as huge and the cabinet will look at how we can put pressure on the social media companies to take action if a lot of content is appearing online that has a bad influence on young people,” he told RTL Nieuws.

Hardline conservative organisations have also pushed back against efforts to teach children about tolerance by promoting spurious links between homosexuality and paedophilia.

In 2023 children’s writer Pim Lammers had to go into hiding after receiving death threats when his novel De Boer en de Dierenarts (“The farmer and the vet”), about a same-sex relationship, was targeted by the radical Catholic organisation Civitas Christiana after he was asked to write a poem for children’s book week.

The sex education institute Rutgers, which organises the annual “Week van de Lentekriebels” (Spring Fever Week), won a court case against Civitas Christiana banning it from making false statements or publishing its “black book”, listing people and organisations that it accuses of “sexualising” children. The judgment was upheld by the Court of Appeal in May.
