World.title: Hungary seeks US exemption from Russian energy sanctions during transition
World.content:
Hungary is lobbying Washington for temporary relief from new Russian energy sanctions as the country continues to buy Russian crude while attempting to diversify its oil and gas supplies. The move follows new US legislation giving President Donald Trump powers to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries purchasing Russian energy.

According to Bloomberg, Hungary is seeking to avoid penalties during the period in which the government says it is reducing the country’s dependence on Russian energy.

The issue was raised in Washington by Márton Hajdu, chairman of the Hungarian parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee and a politician from the governing Tisza party.

Following meetings with Republican and Democratic lawmakers on Capitol Hill, Hajdu said he had asked for support so that Hungary could receive an exemption during the transition away from Russian energy purchases.

The talks do not, at this stage, amount to an announced bilateral exemption agreement between the Hungarian and US governments. Rather, they represent political lobbying aimed at securing favourable treatment as the new American rules begin to take effect.

New Russian energy sanctions raise stakes for Hungary

US President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 into law on Friday, 18 September.

The legislation expands sanctions targeting Russia’s energy and defence sectors and its so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent restrictions. It also gives the US president authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from countries that continue to purchase Russian crude oil or natural gas.

The House of Representatives passed the legislation by 262 votes to 159 on 16 September after the Senate approved it in August, Reuters reported.

The measures are designed to increase economic pressure on Moscow by targeting not only Russian entities but also major foreign buyers of Russian oil and gas.

For Hungary, however, the timing is particularly sensitive. Budapest remains reliant on Russian supplies even as Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s government has pledged to change the energy policy pursued under former prime minister Viktor Orbán.

If you missed it: Péter Magyar would break away from Russian oil, but expects something in return from Brussels

Hungary says it is reducing Russian energy dependence

The Magyar government has repeatedly said that diversification cannot happen overnight without risking security of supply or increasing costs.

Economy and Energy Minister István Kapitány said last week that Hungary should be capable of meeting its gas needs without Russian imports by October 2027 if current plans proceed as expected.

He said Hungary has physical connections allowing gas to arrive from several directions, while the government is looking at alternatives including supplies from Romania’s Neptun Deep gas field and liquefied natural gas contracts.

On oil, the government is also examining how greater use of the Adriatic pipeline through Croatia could reduce reliance on the Druzhba pipeline, which has traditionally carried Russian crude to Hungary. Kapitány said talks had begun with Croatian partners over using the Adriatic route at full capacity.

The government’s position is therefore that Hungary should not face US penalties while it is actively restructuring its energy supply.

Washington decision could test Hungary-US relations

The request also comes at an important moment for relations between Budapest and Washington.

Bloomberg described the issue as an early test for bilateral ties following the change of government in Hungary earlier this year. The Magyar administration has signalled a different approach towards Russia while simultaneously trying to avoid disruption to the country’s energy market.

Whether Hungary ultimately receives an exemption from the Russian energy sanctions will depend on how Washington applies the new legislation.

The law provides the US administration with significant leverage over countries buying Russian energy, but the existence of tariff powers does not mean that the maximum penalties will automatically be imposed.

For Budapest, the immediate objective is therefore to convince US decision-makers that Hungary’s continued purchases should be treated as a temporary consequence of its existing infrastructure rather than a rejection of efforts to reduce dependence on Russian energy.

World.title: Hungary’s biggest restaurant awards 2026 announced – here are the Dining Guide winners
World.content:
On the evening of Monday 21 September, the Dining Guide announced this year’s outstanding achievements in Hungarian gastronomy at the Dining Guide Restaurant of the Year Gala. The evening’s biggest success was for Stand Restaurant, which, in addition to the Restaurant of the Year award, also won the Hungarian Restaurant Best of the Best title, thus rounding off the evening with two major accolades. Stand’s new management structure also played a part in the awarding of the Master Good Restaurant of the Year prize. In the absence of Szabina Szulló, the restaurant has been operating under a revised culinary leadership structure since October 2025, led by head chefs Tamás Széll and Benjamin Morris. The accolade recognises both the work of the current team and the achievements made under the new management structure.

A number of special professional awards were also presented at the gala: the Dining Guide – TORTER Promising Restaurant of the Year award went to Cova Budapest, whilst the Dining Guide – Innovative Kitchen of the Year award was presented to Alkimista Culinary Workshop. The Dining Guide – VLM Chef of the Year title was awarded to Márton Tatai, chef at Hoppá! Bistro, whilst Ádám Berecz, chef at Sulyom Tájétterem, was chosen as the Dining Guide – DEBIC Young Chef of the Year. The Dining Guide – Gosset Sommelier of the Year award went to Krisztián Juhász, sommelier at Borkonyha and Textúra, whilst the Dining Guide – KAVIÁRI Service Staff Member of the Year award was presented to Zsolt Király for his work at the Rumour by Jenő Rácz restaurant. The Dining Guide – Dallagiovanna Pizza of the Year award was won by Anyukám Mondta.

“The history of the Dining Guide began twenty-six years ago, and we presented the first Restaurant of the Year award to Fausto’s in 2005. It gives us particular pleasure that, more than two decades later, this iconic restaurant remains a defining force in Hungarian gastronomy. This also clearly demonstrates that, for us, truly great restaurant performance is not about a single successful year, but about the long-term, consistent delivery of quality. Over more than two decades, not only has Hungarian gastronomy changed enormously, but an audience has also emerged that chooses restaurants consciously, pays attention to quality and seeks well-founded recommendations. The Dining Guide’s rating system is based on the professional principles also applied by Michelin, but we combine this with our in-depth knowledge of the Hungarian hospitality sector, gained over several decades. This is important because we are not simply looking for the performance on a single evening, but also assessing a restaurant’s character, its development and its performance over the longer term. “This year, we visited nearly five hundred dining establishments to ensure that the 2026 guide provides a truly accurate picture of the current state of Hungarian gastronomy” – said Zoltán Herczeg, editor-in-chief of the Dining Guide and head of the professional jury.

The Dining Guide carries out the evaluation and ranking independently. Fausto Arrighi, the legendary former director of the Michelin Guide, also assists with the guide’s professional work in an advisory capacity, having been involved in the production of the publication for nine years now. The 2026 edition of the Dining Guide TOP100 Restaurant Guide features 180 restaurants alongside nearly 70 alternative dining venues.

If you missed it: Gordon Ramsay chooses Budapest for first Central European restaurant – opening date revealed

The finest of Hungarian gastronomy in one place

The Dining Guide TOP100 Restaurant Guide has been tracking and evaluating developments in the Hungarian hospitality sector for over two decades now. The ever-changing gastronomic scene takes shape year on year with new restaurants, changes of chefs and evolving concepts, and the guide reflects these changes to showcase the current cutting edge of Hungarian hospitality.

Stand Restaurant was named Restaurant of the Year 2026

Hungary’s finest dining establishment is Stand Restaurant, whose stable backbone is provided by co-owners including Ibolya Csahók, Zoltán Hamvas, Tamás Széll and Szabina Szulló, amongst others. In October 2025, Szabina Szulló took a break from intensive kitchen work for a while, but Benjamin Morris – who has been part of the team since 2020 – stepped up to the role of head chef and, together with Tamás Széll, the two of them now handle all the tasks that were previously carried out by the three of them. This is how they ensure the consistency that is the hallmark of the restaurant. Every single element of this top-class restaurant is characterised by a refined, strong ‘fine’ concept, which blends Hungarian cuisine with international trends in a unique way. Since its opening, Stand has represented a refined, elegant, contemporary Hungarian gastronomic movement based on local ingredients.

Jenő Rácz embarked on his international career at a young age: he worked in world-class kitchens in London, Copenhagen, Singapore and Shanghai. Upon his return, he opened Rumour by Jenő Rácz in May 2021, becoming the first to introduce the chef’s table concept to Hungary. Guests sit at a 21-seat counter surrounding the open kitchen, allowing them to watch the precise preparation and presentation of the dishes up close. The evening, with its gastronomic theatre atmosphere built around the chef’s personal presence, is complemented by playful elements and humorous touches, whilst the secret entrance door establishes a sense of exclusivity from the moment guests arrive. On the menu, Jenő Rácz’s Hungarian roots meet the global influences he has absorbed during his travels, carefully crafted and presented in an unconventional style.

Located in the heart of the Őrség region, Pajta opened its doors in 2012: the young couple, Ferenc Kvasznicza and Flóra Marjai, who left Budapest behind, realised their dream in an old barn, where gastronomy, nature and culture come together. The kitchen is led by the chef duo István Akács and Yazmin Salazar: Yazmin brings Latin American flavours to the plate, drawing on her Mexican roots, whilst István draws on his experience gained in leading European and Scandinavian restaurants – the fusion of the two forms the basis of Pajta’s distinctive, progressive international cuisine, built around strongly local ingredients. The farm-to-table philosophy is part of their daily routine: they often venture into the woods in search of wild mushrooms and fresh inspiration. The head chef at Pajta is Krisztián Paksa, who comes from the world of international haute cuisine, whilst Márton Király, a sommelier who previously spent many years as part of the Dining Guide’s team of writers, is in charge of the wines.

The 42 Restaurant & Bar in Esztergom has undergone a major transformation over the past year or two. In the summer of 2025, Kuzin Bistro took over the former ground-floor premises in the iconic building on Széchenyi Square, whilst the fine dining restaurant moved one floor up to a space featuring frescoes, which once served as the living room of a middle-class family. The owner, Sándor Varga, is the visionary behind and creator of the Alexander the Guest YouTube channel, which showcases the world’s leading fine-dining restaurants and boasts over half a million subscribers. Kevin Szabó has been at the helm of the kitchen since December 2025; his approach has been shaped by his background in competitive gastronomy – including his experience with the Hungarian Bocuse d’Or team – into technical precision and discipline. Kevin Szabó’s cuisine is rooted in Hungarian ingredients, whilst drawing freely on international gastronomy; the menu changes seasonally and includes a full vegetarian option. Every few weeks, the ‘Gastronomic Adventure’ evening, which draws a full house, brings the two establishments together, sometimes featuring a guest chef

SALT Budapest’s chef, Szilárd Tóth, continues to forge ahead as a pioneer of the farm-to-table restaurant style, which is still rarely seen in Hungary. The cuisine is shaped by the techniques of new Scandinavian gastronomy, but the dishes are rooted in the culinary heritage of Szilárd Tóth’s homeland, Szatmár and north-eastern Hungary. A book dedicated to this connection was published in 2026, in which memories of Szatmár appear on the plates in a dense, concentrated form. The restaurant’s interior is characterised by raw wooden surfaces, minimalist, pastel-coloured furnishings and shelves lined with jars from his own collection, filled with fermented or dried vegetables and fruit – all tangible evidence of the kitchen’s philosophy. The centrepiece of the dining area is the chef’s table, where Szilárd Tóth finishes preparing the dishes right before our eyes. SALT offers a fourteen-course tasting menu with wine and juice pairings; the restaurant, which seats around thirty people, welcomes guests from Wednesday to Saturday. The team is using home-grown produce in an increasing number of dishes; the vegetable garden is hosted by the SZIA Garden in Gödöllő.

Kornél Kaszás joined the Babel Budapest restaurant as executive chef in 2021. In 2022, they reopened with a completely new team and with the expert guidance of Swedish consultant chef Daniel Berlin. To this day, the spirit of the place is shaped by the joint efforts of Kornél Kaszás and his team, who continue to refine the restaurant’s mature Hungarian and regional identity through an ingredient-led approach. The restaurant is housed within the walls of a building originally constructed between 1913 and 1917 as a Piarist monastery; the historic setting and the minimalist, warm décor create a unique contrast. This fine-dining restaurant in the city centre offers friendly service and skilfully composed, intelligent and subtly elegant dishes that draw on the traditions of the Carpathian Basin whilst casting them in a modern, innovative mould. Good examples of this are their now-iconic casino eggs or their venison dish.

Tiago Sabarigo first made a name for himself in Hungary as the chef at Costes Downtown; then, in 2020, he and his wife, Éva Jenei, opened their own restaurant, Essência Restaurant Tiago & Éva, in the 5th district. Their Portuguese-Hungarian fusion cuisine has now established its own distinct identity and remains firmly at the forefront of the Hungarian culinary scene. Octopus and cod feature prominently on the restaurant’s menu as iconic ingredients that represent the meeting of Portuguese roots and Hungarian gastronomy. The tasting menu, which debuted in May 2026, begins with duck liver, apricots and fennel, followed by a dish featuring tomato essence, stracciatella and caviar; the ‘Palóc-style’ lamb loin with green beans and dill has become one of the most popular dishes. At Tiago Sabarigo and Éva Jenei’s restaurant, the contemporary, rustically elegant interior is dominated by Portuguese stylistic elements, whilst the open-plan kitchen at the back adds to the atmosphere.

The team at Sauska Padi, a new entry in the top 10, brings Hungarian home-cooking traditions, local ingredients and flavours designed to complement Tokaj wines to the plate; for them, the hallmarks of the wine region are just as important in the kitchen as they are in the glass. The kitchen at the Rátka estate’s restaurant is led by resident chef Máté Gerák, based on the concept of executive chef Attila Bicsár, who draws inspiration from, amongst other things, the forests and gardens of Zemplén and the region’s gastronomic heritage. The kitchen produces dishes that are worthy companions to Tokaj wines and sparkling wines, as they never lose sight of the fact that the restaurant is housed within the winery. The dishes are both familiar and innovative. They are based on different ingredients depending on the season: for example, game, mushrooms, various vegetables and fruits, poppy seeds, walnuts and aszú berries all feature on the menu.

Borkonyha, which has been operating on Sas Street in central Budapest since 2010, was the first top-tier Hungarian restaurant to win over the country’s culinary elite not through formal service, but through quality and a friendly atmosphere; it has maintained this reputation ever since. The concept is the brainchild of Ákos Sárközi, the executive chef, whilst the kitchen has been led for many years by Csaba Puskás, the head chef, with a stable team that has worked together for a long time. Pastry chef Anett Béres is responsible for the extraordinary desserts – at both Borkonyha and the neighbouring Textúra restaurant. Borkonyha combines modern international influences with a Transylvanian character: the menu regularly features pasta stuffed with Transylvanian ordá, tortellini filled with tripe and grilled hot peppers, or bulz, polenta balls with sheep’s milk cheese. The plates clearly bear the mark of artist Ákos Sárközi’s visually inspired use of form and colour, which lends a unique visual quality to the fine bistro-style dishes.

The highest standard of gastronomy in the South Transdanubia region is undoubtedly represented by Sauska 48 Villány in Villány, which has embodied the concept of ‘a restaurant at the heart of the winery’ since 2017. The head chef, the highly experienced Attila Bicsár, coined the term ‘uninhibited village gourmet’ here, for which the internationally renowned entrepreneur Krisztián Sauska, owner of the iconic Sauska wine estates, provides a fitting setting. Over the years, the restaurant has moved towards more complex tasting menus, whilst retaining its original Swabian-Hungarian identity. A favourite among guests is the duck liver terrine, served with apple compote, walnut cream and brioche. The elegant service allows time for wine presentations and conversation. The menu follows the availability of seasonal produce and the offerings of local producers, and the dishes are, of course, accompanied by Sauska wines from Tokaj and Villány. The wine list also features a section unique in Hungary,

‘A Glimpse into the Wider World: A Selection from the Sauska Family’s Cellar’, where guests can choose from the finest vintages – dating back as far as the 1960s, ‘70s and ‘80s – from the world’s most highly regarded wineries.

One of the flagships of Budapest’s fine dining scene, Arany Kaviár, celebrated its 35th anniversary in 2025. According to owners Attila Molnár and Szása Nyíri, the secret lies in their ability to always sense what guests might be craving at any given time. The memorable dining experience they provide stems from their attention to detail and their friendly, high-quality hospitality. The kitchen is led by executive chef Bence Molnár, who presents traditional Russian flavours with a contemporary twist, building on classic foundations whilst bringing a fresh perspective to the dishes. The caviar that gives the restaurant its name is a clear indication that guests at the Ostrom Street restaurant can sample the world’s finest caviar. The exceptional wine list is curated by sommelier Dávid Kincses, featuring rare wines from around the world as well as an outstanding selection of sparkling wines and champagnes.

Located on the ground floor of the Matild Palace Luxury Collection Hotel Budapest is the restaurant bearing the name of the legendary Austrian-American chef Wolfgang Puck, Spago Budapest by Wolfgang Puck, which opened its doors in 2021 as the brand’s first European outlet. The chef, who has been creating the menus for the Oscars for nearly three decades, is regarded as the pioneer of Californian cuisine, whilst his restaurants present classic dishes from various national cuisines through Wolfgang Puck’s unique interpretation. Since the restaurant opened, the kitchen has been led by István Szántó, executive chef, who has gradually expanded the international Spago concept with local flavours and a distinctive identity; indeed, a strong selection of sushi has also been added to the menu. Among the dishes that have become iconic are the goulash soup, created in István Szántó’s adaptation, tender game beef cheek and Somlói galuska ‘in a walnut shell’, as well as Wolfgang Puck’s signature dishes, including smoked salmon pizza, Wiener schnitzel, Scottish steamed salmon ‘Hong Kong’ style and Kaiserschmarrn.

World.title: Working in Hungary could become easier for non-EU professionals under new EU rules
World.content:
Working in Hungary could become considerably easier for some non-EU professionals under a new European Commission proposal designed to speed up the recognition of qualifications obtained outside the European Union. The planned rules could cut procedures that currently take more than a year to around four months.

The European Commission unveiled the measures on 15 September 2026 as part of its new Fair Labour Mobility package, a broader set of proposals aimed at making it easier for workers to move across the EU while reducing administrative burdens for employers.

According to the European Commission, recognition procedures for qualifications obtained outside the EU currently take an average of around 14 months. Under the proposed common standards, that could fall to approximately four months. The Commission says the changes could also cut employers’ administrative costs related to recruiting qualified workers from abroad by as much as half.

What could change for non-EU professionals working in Hungary?

At present, third-country nationals who want to work in a regulated profession in an EU member state generally have to have their professional qualifications recognised under the national rules of the country where they intend to work.

That means someone planning on working in Hungary may face a different procedure from a professional with the same qualification applying in Austria, Germany or another EU country.

The Commission now wants to introduce common EU standards for recognising qualifications obtained outside the bloc. The planned system would cover both EU citizens who obtained their qualifications in a non-EU country and third-country nationals who are already in the Single Market or are applying from abroad.

The objective is not to remove professional requirements, but to make the assessment process quicker and more predictable across member states.

For foreigners considering working in Hungary, this could therefore mean less uncertainty about how long recognition will take and what documents and procedures they will face.

If you missed it: Hungary has a record number of foreign workers – now businesses want the government to ease the rules

Seven professions could receive special treatment

The proposal goes particularly far for seven regulated professions for which EU-wide minimum training requirements already exist.

These are doctors, general care nurses, dentists, midwives, pharmacists, veterinary surgeons and architects.

Working in Hungary could become easier for non-EU professionals under new EU rules. Source: Depositphotos.com

Under the Commission’s plan, qualifications awarded by accredited institutions outside the EU could be recognised automatically if the institutions and programmes concerned have undergone the required European quality-assurance assessment.

The seven professions already benefit from an automatic recognition system for qualifying EU credentials under existing European rules. The new proposal could extend a comparable route to certain qualifications obtained outside the bloc.

This could be especially significant in professions where European countries are struggling to recruit sufficiently qualified staff.

Recognition would not automatically give the right to work in Hungary

There is, however, an important distinction for non-EU citizens.

Having a professional qualification recognised would not in itself grant someone the right to enter Hungary, live in the country or take up employment.

The European Commission explicitly states that EU member states would retain control over who is admitted to their territory and over the standards professionals must meet before they can practise a regulated profession.

In practice, a third-country national interested in working in Hungary could therefore still need the appropriate residence and employment authorisation even if recognition of their professional qualification becomes faster.

The proposal is consequently aimed at removing one major administrative obstacle rather than replacing national immigration rules.

When could the new rules take effect?

Nothing will change immediately. The measures presented by the Commission are legislative proposals and still need to be considered and adopted by the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union.

If approved, the changes would be introduced gradually. The Commission says simpler recognition of non-EU qualifications should become available within two years of the legislation being adopted. Other elements of the wider package, including digital qualifications and changes affecting regulated professions, are expected to follow within three years.

The wider package would also introduce digital tools for qualifications and social security documents, while strengthening EU-level cooperation against abuses involving mobile and third-country workers.

For non-EU professionals considering working in Hungary, the proposal is therefore worth following closely. It would not remove immigration requirements or guarantee that every foreign qualification is accepted, but it could make one of the most complicated parts of entering a regulated European profession substantially faster and more transparent.

World.title: Korean Film Festival returns to Budapest with 24 films and three visiting directors
World.content:
What happens when three generations set off from Gwangju to Budapest in an electric car? Can you save a family member who has turned into a zombie? And what secrets can surface from a family’s past after forty years? From 25 September to 2 October, the Korean Film Festival returns to Corvin Cinema with 24 feature films. From historical drama and road movies to occult action, this year’s programme brings a remarkably varied selection of stories to the big screen, while three Korean directors will also meet audiences in person at post-screening talks.

These days, Korean cinema is about much more than Parasite or Squid Game. What is perhaps less visible behind these international successes is just how diverse the country’s film scene really is. Organised by the Korean Cultural Center, the 19th Korean Film Festival sets out to showcase exactly that diversity, with this year’s programme built around four sections: Fresh, Faces, Focus and Extra.

It All Begins with a Child King

The festival opens on 25 September with Chang Hang-jun’s historical drama The King’s Warden. Set in 15th-century Joseon, the story follows the head of a poor mountain village who hopes his community might prosper by taking in an exiled nobleman. There is just one catch: the man entrusted to his care is no ordinary noble, but Yi Hong-wi, the young king who has been forced from the throne.

The historical drama was a major success in South Korea, attracting more than 16 million cinemagoers by April following its February release. It also won the Audience Award at the Udine Far East Film Festival and received several Baeksang Arts Awards.

Romance, Family Secrets and Demon Hunters

The Fresh section is perhaps the best place to see just how difficult it is to define contemporary Korean cinema by any single genre.

In Heartman: Rock and Love, a former musician’s first love unexpectedly reappears in his life. In The Ugly, human remains discovered after forty years set off an investigation into a family’s past, while Project Y follows two women who risk everything on a dangerous plan. At the other end of the spectrum is Holy Night: Demon Hunters, in which a trio with supernatural powers must save Seoul from a criminal organisation that worships the devil.

What Is It Like to Be a Child in Yoon Ga-eun’s World?

This year’s Faces section turns the spotlight on the films of Yoon Ga-eun. The director is particularly interested in childhood and adolescence, but not in an idealised version of them. In her films, friendships fall apart, families face crises, and young characters discover far too early what it means to feel like an outsider.

Four of her works will be screened at the festival, including The World of Love, which had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, as well as The World of Us and The House of Us.

If you missed it: K-pop in Hungary is no longer just a teenage trend: it is becoming a cultural movement – interview

From Gwangju to Budapest – by Electric Car

In this year’s Focus: On the Road selection, everyone is heading somewhere – although where they end up may not be where they originally intended to go.

The film with the most direct connection to Hungary is 3 Gen. Journey. A grandfather, a father and two children travel from Gwangju to Budapest by electric car over the course of 80 days. Elsewhere in the selection, a family heads to Gyeongju in search of revenge, two strangers set off into the unknown together, and another family embarks on one final trip, only to uncover a long-held secret along the way.

Festivalgoers will also have the chance to meet three Korean directors in person. Song Jinuk and Jang Kunjae will take part in CineTalk events on 26 September, followed by Lee Seonyeon on 27 September. The post-screening conversations will be held in Hungarian and Korean.

Five Films from Jeonju

The Extra section presents five films selected by the festival’s official partner, the Jeonju International Film Festival. The selection offers a glimpse into a less familiar side of Korean independent cinema, exploring relationships, financial insecurity, family ties and historical trauma.

Living Through the Same Season traces the memories of a relationship across four seasons, while Insomnia confronts a young married couple with a brutal moral dilemma after they lose all their savings in a housing rental scam. Two award-winning filmmakers will also be in Budapest in person: Jang Kunjae will meet audiences after the screening of Spring Snow, while Lee Seonyeon will discuss her debut feature, The Summer That Slipped Away.

One of the most distinctive films in the selection is the documentary Horoomon. The history of a now-popular Japanese dish is closely intertwined with the past of the Korean minority living in Japan. Beginning with something as everyday as food, the film opens up a much larger story about identity, exclusion and a century of historical memory.

Saving the Zombie for Last

The festival closes on 2 October with the comedy My Daughter is a Zombie. The premise sounds familiar enough: an outbreak begins and someone turns into a zombie. This time, however, that someone is a young girl – and her father refuses to give up on her.

He takes her to the countryside to stay with her grandmother, hides her from the outside world and attempts to teach her how to be human again. Adapted from a popular webtoon, the film playfully turns the conventions of the zombie genre on their head while telling, at its heart, a story about the relationship between a father and his daughter.

Audiences will once again be able to vote for their favourite film throughout the festival, with the Audience Award presented before the screening of the closing film.

Event: 19th Korean Film Festival

Dates: 25 September – 2 October 2026

Venue: Corvin Cinema (1082 Budapest, Corvin köz 1.)

Tickets: Available from 10 September online via Corvin Cinema and at the cinema box office

World.title: Self-driving cars in Hungary: How close is the country to truly driverless roads?
World.content:
Self-driving cars in Hungary no longer belong entirely to the distant future. Level 4 autonomous vehicles have already been demonstrated in real traffic in a Hungarian city, commercial robotaxis are operating in nearby Croatia, and Germany has put a driverless truck into regular service on public roads. Europe’s regulatory framework is also rapidly catching up. But how close is Hungary really to roads where vehicles can operate without a human driver?

The answer depends heavily on what counts as “self-driving”. Many systems already available in passenger cars can steer, accelerate, brake and even navigate complex roads, but still require continuous human supervision. Truly driverless technology represents a much bigger step.

Self-driving cars in Hungary: Level 2 is not Level 4

The distinction is important.

At Level 2, systems can control steering and speed simultaneously, but the driver remains responsible at all times. More advanced Level 3 systems can take responsibility for driving under certain conditions, although a human may still have to take over.

Source: depositphotos.com

Level 4 is fundamentally different: within a defined operating area or set of conditions, the automated driving system can perform the driving task without requiring a human to supervise it continuously.

The EU already has legislation covering the type approval of fully automated vehicles. The relevant EU regulation, updated again in 2026, includes fully automated vehicles designed to transport passengers or goods within predefined areas.

A further major step came in June, when the UNECE adopted the first global regulatory framework for fully autonomous driving systems. The rules establish common requirements for safety management, testing, validation and monitoring once vehicles are in service.

If you missed it: Leading Chinese commercial vehicle brand FOTON available in Hungary! – photos, video

Europe is moving beyond experimental prototypes

The most important change is that Level 4 technology is beginning to leave closed test tracks.

Germany provided a striking example in September. Swedish technology company Einride and supermarket chain Lidl placed a cab-less Level 4 electric truck into regular commercial operation on German public roads.

According to Lidl, the vehicle transports goods between a distribution centre and a nearby shop in Hesse up to three times a day. Germany’s Federal Motor Transport Authority approved the project, and no driver or safety operator is required inside the vehicle.

Robotaxis are progressing quickly as well. Waymo announced in August that it was preparing to bring its fully autonomous ride-hailing technology to Munich. The company says testing will begin with trained specialists behind the wheel before a planned commercial launch towards the end of 2027.

Bolt and Lucid, meanwhile, announced plans in September to deploy 25,000 Level 4 robotaxis across major European cities, with Bolt targeting an autonomous fleet of 100,000 vehicles by 2035, Reuters reported.

Driverless technology has already reached the region

Perhaps the most relevant development for Hungary is taking place much closer to home.

In Zagreb, passengers can already order autonomous rides through the Uber app. The service combines technology from China’s Pony.ai with Croatian autonomous-mobility company Verne.

Uber announced in August that Zagreb had become the first European city where customers could book an autonomous vehicle through its platform. A licensed operator is still sitting behind the wheel during the initial phase, but the companies intend to move towards fully driverless operation.

Even supervised systems are spreading geographically. Villanyautósok reported on Monday that Czechia had become the seventh European country to approve Tesla’s FSD Supervised system, following neighbouring Slovenia earlier in September.

However, Tesla’s current European system still requires human supervision and should not be confused with Level 4 driverless technology.

Hungary is already testing Level 4 vehicles in real traffic

Hungary itself is no longer limited to laboratory testing.

On 29 August, Level 4-equipped Zeekr 001 test vehicles from the ZalaZONE programme drove in real public traffic in central Zalaegerszeg.

According to ZalaZONE, the programme is intended to test advanced autonomous-driving technology outside the controlled environment of the proving ground and under genuine urban traffic conditions.

That does not mean ordinary Hungarians can already summon a driverless taxi. It does mean, however, that the technological infrastructure and testing environment needed for such systems already exist in the country.

What is likely to arrive first in Hungary?

The first genuinely driverless vehicles in Hungary may not be privately owned cars.

European developments suggest that robotaxis operating within restricted urban zones, autonomous airport or public-transport shuttles, and driverless logistics vehicles travelling along fixed routes are more likely to arrive first.

These applications are easier to control because the vehicles operate inside a clearly defined area and under predictable conditions. A car capable of driving anywhere in Hungary – through Budapest traffic, on rural roads, in snow and across national borders – poses a far greater technical and regulatory challenge.

So Hungary is not yet on the verge of replacing human drivers altogether. But the transition from experiments towards practical deployment has clearly begun.

With Level 4 vehicles already being tested on Hungarian public roads, robotaxis operating in neighbouring Croatia and fully driverless commercial vehicles entering service elsewhere in the EU, the question surrounding self-driving cars in Hungary is increasingly shifting from whether they will arrive to what form they will take when they do.

World.title: Boycotts and institutional warnings dominate Hungarian parliament session 🔄
World.content:
Monday’s session of the Hungarian parliament was dominated by President András Baka’s unusual pre-agenda address, boycotts by opposition parties and warnings over trust in some of the country’s key institutions. Prime Minister Péter Magyar later defended his government’s first months in office and pledged to review disputed state contracts and recover public assets where wrongdoing is established.

Opposition parties boycott Baka’s address

Political tensions were evident before President András Baka began speaking. MPs from opposition Fidesz and its Christian Democratic ally KDNP stayed away from the chamber, saying they did not recognise Baka as a legitimate president following the removal of his predecessor, Tamás Sulyok.

Our Homeland (Mi Hazánk) also boycotted the address, although for a different reason. Deputy group leader Előd Novák said the party was protesting a House Committee decision preventing MPs from responding to Baka’s speech or putting questions to the president.

The dispute comes amid Hungary’s transformed political landscape following the April general election, which ended 16 years of Fidesz-led government and brought Péter Magyar’s Tisza party to power with a two-thirds parliamentary majority.

Baka warns over trust in Hungary’s prosecution service

Baka focused his intervention on two major institutional questions: the election of Hungary’s next chief public prosecutor and recent amendments concerning the Constitutional Court.

The president said choosing a new chief prosecutor was not merely a personnel decision, but one affecting the future of the prosecution service and the rule of law.

He argued that every democratic state needed a prosecution service that was professionally credible, institutionally independent and trusted by citizens to act impartially.

Photo: MTI

“Today that trust does not exist. It must be restored,” Baka said.

He added that the prosecution service’s reputation had reached a low point, partly because the “perceived or actual political ties” of some officials had raised doubts about its independence. Baka also referred to a public perception that criminal justice had previously stopped “above a certain level”.

Don’t miss it – Hungary Weekly Briefing is out: Orbán’s new campaign, motorway deal and a possible break with Russian gas

Constitutional Court changes also draw criticism

Baka also expressed reservations about recent amendments to the Constitutional Court Act, despite signing the legislation.

He stressed that the Constitutional Court should command broad confidence among the public, the legal profession and political actors, and argued that the nomination of judges should include safeguards allowing professional and civil-society perspectives to be considered alongside political ones.

Baka also questioned provisions setting out how the Constitutional Court elects its president from among its members. He said the institution’s autonomy would have been better served by leaving the matter to the court’s own internal rules.

Magyar says Hungary is a ‘functioning country’

Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s subsequent speech combined a broader message about national solidarity with a defence of his government’s record since taking office.

Magyar described Hungary as a “functioning country” and said the country would not again allow itself to be “misled, abandoned or betrayed”. He highlighted the government’s first 133 days, citing measures on family benefits, household energy costs and public spending, while also rejecting warnings previously voiced by political opponents about the consequences of a Tisza government.

One of Magyar’s strongest arguments concerned EU funding. His government reached an agreement with the European Commission in May to unlock EUR 16.4 billion in previously frozen recovery and cohesion funds. Hungary subsequently said it had fulfilled the conditions required to access EUR 10 billion from the EU recovery facility.

Magyar promises reviews of disputed contracts

The prime minister also expanded on one of his government’s central political themes: recovering public assets and scrutinising deals concluded under previous governments.

Magyar said it should become a “national minimum” that assets belonging to Hungarians must be returned to them. He called for all disputed contracts to be reviewed and said the state should enforce the public interest wherever legal violations are established.

Addressing Fidesz and KDNP MPs, Magyar accused circles linked to the former governing parties of having taken public assets worth tens of trillions of forints. This was a political allegation made by the prime minister; establishing criminal wrongdoing in individual cases is a matter for the relevant authorities and courts.

He also argued that savings from what his government regarded as wasteful or disproportionate contracts should instead be channelled towards families and restoring order to the public finances.

Media Council appointments move forward

Away from the main speeches, parliament’s culture committee also backed media lawyer Gábor Polyák to head Hungary’s Media Council, alongside six candidates for membership.

Polyák told the committee that his vision was one of “peace in the media”, with a public sphere in which different opinions have a genuine opportunity to be heard.

Monday’s session therefore brought several of Hungary’s post-election institutional debates together in one place: the future of the prosecution service, the Constitutional Court, media regulation and the review of contracts inherited from the previous government. Decisions taken in these areas are likely to remain central to political debate as the new administration moves beyond its first months in office.

As we wrote earlier, Hungary scraps EUR 73 billion motorway deal linked to Orbán-era allies, launches criminal complaints

UPDATE: 🔄Péter Magyar: We do not consider Zoltán Szathmáry’s election as Chief Public Prosecutor a foregone conclusion

“We do not consider the election of Zoltán Szathmáry, nominated by the Head of State, as Chief Public Prosecutor to be a foregone conclusion on the part of the Tisza faction,” PM Magyar stated on Monday during a press conference held in Parliament.

Magyar said that they respect the Head of State’s right to make the nomination. He stated that the Tisza faction had not yet reached a final decision on the matter, “but based on the preliminary information available to us and the information we have received, I can say at this stage that we do not consider it certain that Mr Zoltán Szatmári, the prosecutor nominated by the President of the Republic, will be able to secure either a two-thirds majority or a simple majority of support from the Tisza parliamentary group.”

Péter Magyar promised:

“The final decision will be announced after the parliamentary group meeting and ‘following an examination of further information’. But if you ask me now, we do not see any chance of the Tisza parliamentary group electing the nominee”

— he said.

President András Baka announced on Monday that he was nominating Zoltán Szathmáry for the post of Prosecutor General.

World.title: As Tech Giants Harvest Data, Montenegro Struggles to Track Them
World.content:
Mirko Radunovic from Podgorica planned to organise and monitor his gym training sessions by registering on a mobile fitness app.

Knowing the app's purpose, he did not find it off when it asked him to enter information about his age, health and exercise habits.

“I entered information about my age, health, nutrition and life habits, to create an appropriate training plan. After some time, I started receiving s for fitness equipment and supplements,” Radunovic told BIRN.

“When the app suggested that I add progress photos, I stopped using it. I removed it from my phone – but didn't ask for my data to be removed," he added.

World.title: Albania to Adopt EU Disability Access Standards – But Will They Be Enforced?
World.content:
Katerina Jaupaj understood from an early age that she could not take a step without thinking about the consequences. She was 18 months old and had only just started walking when she broke her leg for the first time.

Jaupaj was diagnosed with osteogenesis imperfecta, better known as brittle bone disease, a rare genetic disorder that affects the production of collagen and renders bones fragile. Those with the condition face a high risk of fractures, even from impacts or movements that would be considered ordinary for others.

The fear of injury followed Jaupaj throughout her childhood. While at school, she began using a wheelchair, but this only proved another source of anxiety.

World.title: ‘Our War is Being Judged’: In Kosovo, Outrage at Hague Verdict Simmers
World.content:
Thaci, Krasniqi, Veseli, and Selimi were sentenced to 25, 25, 18, and 13 years in prison respectively. They were found guilty of the war crimes of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder, committed from April 1998 to June 20, 1999, in Kosovo and two locations in Albania. They were found not guilty of crimes against humanity.

On Monday, the parliamentary group of the Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK – the party widely seen as originating from the KLA, which has been led by both Thaci and Veseli in the past – announced it was initiating an attempt to change the law underpinning the court.

The PDK proposed that the trial proceedings to continue through to the conclusion of the appeals phase. However, if the case is sent for retrial, it should not start over in The Hague but instead in Kosovo.

In the case of a potential retrial, “new jurisdiction applies, and once the conditions are met, the case will be transferred to Kosovo for proceedings,” PDK leader Bedri Hamza told media on Monday.

He argued that the protests cannot be ignored, saying that “the parliament of Kosovo cannot act as if this matter does not affect the Republic of Kosovo”.

It’s not yet clear how much support the PDK proposal will get. But anger about the verdict is also shared by the ruling party, Vetevendosje. Prime Minister Albin Kurti, the leader of Vetevendosje, wrote on X on Monday that the court’s findings “were based on factual inaccuracies, historical misunderstandings, and legal errors. We expect these to be fully corrected on appeal.”

The Specialist Chambers were established under a law adopted in 2015 by the Kosovo Assembly, under pressure from Pristina’s Western allies. The court is part of Kosovo’s judicial system but located in The Netherlands and staffed by internationals as part of efforts to prevent witness-tampering during trials. Thaci was one of the politicians who supported the court’s establishment, saying it would prove the KLA’s war was just.

Kosovo’s former ombudsperson, Hilmi Jashari, told BIRN on Friday that a change of regulations on appointing and overseeing the judges at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers would be beneficial for a fair trial. But Jashari cautioned that demands to fully repeal the law on the court would not be a good way forward.

“I have heard recently that the only solution is to repeal the law [governing the Specialist Chambers]; then one hears suggestions that the president should pardon the convicted individuals, but practically speaking, embarking on such an undertaking is impossible from a legal and juridical standpoint,” Jashari told BIRN and Internews Kosova’s Kallxo Pernime TV programme on Friday.

Edward P. Joseph, a lecturer at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies in Washington DC, told Kallxo Pernime that the anger towards the court in Kosovo is understandable – particularly as the verdict comes soon after Bosnian Serb wartime general Ratko Mladic, who was convicted of genocide, was buried with military honours in Belgrade.

“Consequently, this decision appears to Serbs in Belgrade as a form of vindication or absolution, while casting a shadow over the realities of the 1990s in Kosovo. That is why I find it very concerning,” Joseph said, claiming that Serbia and its supporters in Russia and China would exploit the verdict to spread their own narratives.

Serbia’s Interior Minister Ivica Dacic has welcomed the guilty verdict in exactly this way, saying it represents a “clear, though long-overdue, confirmation of what Serbia and the Serbian people have been saying loudly for more than a quarter of a century – that the so-called KLA was a criminal and terrorist organisation”.

Meanwhile on Monday evening in Pristina, protesters gathered again in the main square, determined that their message will be heard.

World.title: UN Chief Condemns Mladic Glorification in Meeting with Bosnian Leader
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Monday condemned the ongoing glorification of the late convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic during a meeting in New York with Denis Becirovic, chair of Bosnia’s three-member state presidency.

The encounter took place at the UN’s New York headquarters to discuss international law, regional stability and Bosnia’s current challenges. Guterres targeted recent revisionist actions and the denial of genocide in Bosnia, describing them as direct violations of international legal and civilisational norms.

According to the statement released afterwards, the conversation focused on implementation of the UN General Assembly’s Srebrenica Genocide Resolution, adopted in 2024, and the need to combat historical revisionism in the region.

“The UN maintains an unyielding stance against historical revisionism and the glorification of war criminals, which continues to jeopardise reconciliation efforts,” Guterres stated. “International law and civilisational standards must be respected to maintain regional stability.”

Becirovic invited Guterres to visit Sarajevo and the Srebrenica Memorial Centre in the future. He emphasised the importance of establishing permanent international outreach educational programmes on the 1995 genocide to prevent future historical revisionism and protect the historical truth established by international courts.

Mladic’s funeral in Belgrade on September 7 was attended by ministers and high officials both from Serbia and Bosnia’s Serb-led entity, Republika Srpska and was organised with military honours.

EU officials have condemned the government of Serbia – an EU membership candidate state – over the glorification of Mladic, saying it was incompatible with the bloc’s values.

World.title: Across Croatia, Protesters Demand Tougher Response to Violence Against Women
World.content:
Women’s organisations staged symbolic public protests in 17 towns and cities across Croatia on Monday, titled “While the Minister Sheds Light, Women Remain in the Dark” – a slogan pouring scorn on a comment made by Family and Social Policy Minister Alen Ruzic after a woman’s murder.

The groups’ demands include moving violence against women from the realm of misdemeanours into the criminal justice sphere.

“We demand a specific law against all forms of gender-based violence,” the organisations and initiatives said ahead of the National Day Against Violence Against Women, observed on September 22.

They also called for a unified, mandatory and standardized assessment of the risk of recurring violence and femicide, as well as mandatory specialized training for everyone involved in risk assessment and decisions concerning the protection of women.

World.title: Serbia ‘Still Ignoring’ UN Court Monitor over Vojislav Seselj Case
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp



Vojislav Seselj. Photo: EPA/KOCA SULEJMANOVIC.

Monitor Dagmara Albrecht told the UN’s International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals in her latest report that she has not received any new information from the Serbian authorities about the status of the contempt-of-court case against Serbian Radical Party leader Vojislav Seselj and four of his party members.

The International Residual Mechanism transferred the contempt-of-court case against Seselj and his followers to Serbia in 2024, saying that conditions were adequate for it to be processed there, and appointed Albrecht to monitor progress.

But since then, Serbia has been ignoring questions about the status of the case, according to Albrecht. In her latest report, she said that since her previous report in May, she had “received no response to my numerous inquiries addressed to the Ministry of Justice of Serbia”.

In the May report, she also said that although the Ministry of Justice had promised to provide her with information, her emails went unanswered.

Her latest report suggests the case may not have moved forward. “Based on information previously received, the Seselj et al. case is still awaiting a preliminary opinion of the Ministry of Justice,” she added.

The case against Seselj and his followers – Miljan Damjanovic, Miroljub Ignjatovic, Ljiljana Mihajlovic, and Ognjen Mihajlovic – relates to his 15-year trial in The Hague for wartime crimes.

The indictment charges them with having “knowingly and wilfully interfered with the administration of justice; disclosed information in violation of court orders, including orders for the protection of witnesses; and failed to comply, without just excuse, with court orders to cease and desist from the publication of confidential information”.

Seselj already has a conviction for inciting crimes with his wartime speeches. The UN war crimes tribunal sentenced him to ten years in prison in April 2018. He did not serve any jail time, however, because of the time he had spent in custody prior to the verdict.

The Serbian Radical Party leader has been charged with contempt of court several times by the Hague-based tribunal. In 2011, he was convicted of revealing information about witnesses in a book he authored.

In 2012, Seselj and Radical Party colleagues Vjerica Radeta and Petar Jojic were also charged with pressurising witnesses in his trial using threats, blackmail and bribes to change their statements or not testify. This case is still ongoing in The Hague after the tribunal declined to transfer these proceedings to Serbia.

World.title: Romania Probes Far-Right Former Presidential Candidate Georgescu for Fraud
World.content:
Calin Georgescu at the Municipal Court in Bucharest, December 2025. Photo: EPA/ROBERT GHEMENT.

Romanian police on Monday detained far-right politician Calin Georgescu and anti-fraud investigators searched his home and other locations as part of an investigation in which he faces charges of defrauding a Romanian businessman of more than 1 million euros, according to judicial authorities.

“We carried out five residential searches … in a case in which three people acted with the aim of obtaining undue financial benefits,” said Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism, DIICOT.

Prosecutors allege that from September 2021, a group allegedly led by Georgescu convinced the businessman that he could obtain a loan of 6 million euros in exchange for providing a guarantee. The victim then allegedly transferred some 1 million euros.

Subsequently, the suspects allegedly told him that the loan could be increased to 15 million euro, but an additional guarantee was required, after which the businessman allegedly transferred another 100,000 euros. The promised loan never materialised.

Georgescu has not issued any statement on this issue but he has previously claimed he was being investigated by the authorities because of his political activities.

His political ally, George Simion, who heads the far-right Alliance for the Unity of Romanians, AUR, condemned the move. “Any of us could be next. Stop the abuses! Romania is a dictatorship!” he wrote on Facebook.

Hundreds of Georgescu’s supporters gathered outside DIICOT headquarters, where he and other people were to arrive for questioning. Authorities have installed protective barriers and deployed gendarmerie units in the area.

This would be the third criminal case against Georgescu. He is already under investigation for endorsing fascist ideas in interviews, online posts and public appearances and also faces trial for complicity to undermine the constitutional order, spreading false information and founding an anti-Semitic organisation.

He denies all the charges.

After he unexpectedly won the first round of the Romanian presidential elections in November 2024, the Constitutional Court ordered a rerun of the vote, citing alleged manipulation of public opinion by a “foreign state”, likely referring to Russia.

Georgescu was banned from participating in the re-run in May 2025, which was ultimately won by centrist Nicusor Dan.

World.title: New Law for Foreign Workers in Croatia Faces Criticism
World.content:
September the 22nd, 2026 – A new law facing foreign workers in Croatia as of 2027 is already causing a stir and facing criticism from migration experts.

You go to another country, get a job, learn around thirty basic phrases of its language and that is, according to the law, enough to be considered “integrated.” Most would argue that this statement is so ridiculous that it’s difficult to quantify. Poslovni reports that the aforementioned notion is all that will be required of foreign workers in Croatia as of 2027. They will have to prove knowledge of the Croatian language at level A1.1 in order to extend their residence and work permit. Apparently, that’s “integration”.

Is basic knowledge of a few dozen words really the same as integration into society? According to Ivan Balabanić, senior research associate at the Institute for Migration Research, the answer is very clearly “no.” The data that his institute collects shows that Croatia is only beginning to scratch the surface of a problem that, as the number of foreign workers grows, will become ever more complex. Balabanić views the obligation to pass A1.1 Croatian simultaneously as an integration measure and as an administrative condition, but emphasises that its meaning should primarily be integrative.

“Knowledge of the language of the country in which a person lives and works is one of the first preconditions for beginning to feel part of society. Nevertheless, such a low level of language knowledge by itself does not resolve questions of the legal security of foreign workers nor their finding their way in Croatian administration. Integration does not begin with a language course, but at the moment when a foreign worker knows their rights and can actually exercise them,” Balabanić highlighted.

croatia’s responsibility as a state

Precisely for that reason, while the worker hasn’t mastered Croatian, information about residence, work, the healthcare system and the protection of rights must be available to them in a language they understand, and that, Balabanić emphasises, in one place, and not scattered across a series of different institutions. Alongside economic integration, which in Croatia today mainly comes down to the relationship between the worker and the employer, the social dimension is equally important, and that, according to his words, cannot be one-way. Foreign workers need to get to know the norms and values of the society they are coming into, but the domestic population must also accept that Croatia is becoming culturally more diverse.

How weak that readiness is at this moment is shown by a study by the Institute for Migration Research from November 2025, conducted on a sample of 1,000 respondents: only 2.4 percent of citizens would accept a foreign worker as a friend, 5.7 percent as a neighbour, and as a family member only a negligible number of respondents. “That’s why I would say that Croatia is still in an early phase of the integration of foreign workers. Language is an important first step, but without legal security, available information, social contacts and the readiness of the domestic population to accept new fellow citizens we cannot speak of a serious integration policy,” Balabanić said. When it comes to the financing of integration, Balabanić clearly emphasises that the largest part of the cost should be borne by the state.

“The logic is simple: foreign workers come to Croatia primarily because of the needs of the domestic labour market and the shortage of labour in certain sectors. If the state creates a system that encourages the arrival of foreign workers, then it must also take on the largest part of the responsibility for their integration,” he is clear.

That, he emphasises, does not mean that the responsibility must be exclusively state. Local self-government has an important role because integration takes place in concrete communities – the needs of workers in Istria are not the same as the needs of those in Lika or Zagreb. Employers bear their share of responsibility within the work environment, but Balabanić warns that it would be wrong to shift the entire burden onto them, since they already bear significant costs of employing foreign workers. The least burden, he believes, should be shifted onto the workers themselves, although they too have the obligation to actively participate in integration by learning the language and respecting the law.

the so-called information vacuum

Precisely there Balabanić sees the real danger that integration becomes something that the state formally requires of the foreign worker, while at the same time not providing them with the tools to fulfil that requirement.

“It wouldn’t be logical for Croatia to actively attract foreign workers because its economy needs them, and then declare their integration exclusively their personal problem,” he said. When it comes to the biggest obstacles in the everyday life of foreign workers, Balabanić avoids singling out only one. The language barrier, inadequate accommodation, violation of labour rights, difficult access to healthcare and social isolation, he says, are intertwined – but the common denominator of most of these problems is the chronic lack of available and reliable information.

Croatia, he admits, is gradually responding regulatorily to the new situation; amendments to laws and regulations are being adopted, but the open question remains how many of them the administration manages to implement in practice. Tightened criteria for employers, for example, were supposed to regulate the market, but at the same time increased the administrative burden, so some workers waited months for the extension of their permit. A particular problem is the healthcare system – according to another study by the Institute from November 2025, conducted on 429 foreign workers from Asia and Africa in Zagreb and Zagreb County, only 28.7 percent of respondents have a chosen general practitioner, which seriously complicates regular health care.

Language remains an obstacle even when workers themselves try to find information, because the official websites of institutions are very often available exclusively in Croatian. Because of that many find themselves in what Balabanić calls an information vacuum, in which the main, sometimes the only, source of information becomes the employer or the employment agency. “A series of entirely practical questions, from whether the employer can keep the passport, whether they have the right to unemployment benefit, whom to turn to if their rights are violated – for a large number of workers remain without a reliable answer. Croatia today does not primarily lack regulations. It lacks a system that will enable the foreign worker to actually exercise the rights they have,” Balabanić highlighted.

financial burden

Particularly vulnerable, he warns, are workers in whom several unfavourable circumstances overlap – those who went into debt in order to reach Croatia at all through long chains of intermediaries, and therefore more readily accept poor working conditions, as well as those employed by an employer on whom they depend for salary, accommodation and information about their own rights. The education of children is for now not among the most pronounced problems, since a large part of labour migrants still live in Croatia without family, but with the growth in the number of those who stay long-term and bring families, that topic, Balabanić estimates, will become increasingly important.

World.title: Croatia in Top 20 Countries With Highest Quality of Life – But It Doesn’t Mean What You Think
World.content:
September the 22nd, 2026 – Croatia has entered into the top 20 countries with the highest quality of life, but it certainly doesn’t mean what you think it means…

The new ranking by World Population Review brings quite a surprise, and that’s that Croatia has placed 20th among countries with the highest quality of life. However, what’s odd to note is that behind this attractive ranking lies a methodology that is important to explain. Poslovni reports that Croatia has surprisingly found itself among the 20 best-placed countries in the world according to the quality of life ranking published by World Population Review. With an index of 181.7 points Croatia occupies 20th place, immediately behind Slovenia, which is 19th with 182.4 points.

the ranking leaves you scratching your head…

Particularly interesting is the fact that according to this ranking numerous developed countries remain behind Croatia. Lithuania is 21st, the United Kingdom 22nd, Czechia 23rd, Belgium 26th, Canada 27th, Ireland 28th, France 29th, Portugal 31st, while Italy is only in 40th place.

At the very top is Luxembourg with 218.2 points. It is followed by the Netherlands (216.5), Denmark (215.1), and a major surprise is Oman, which with the same result as Denmark occupies fourth place. They are followed by Switzerland, Finland, Norway, Iceland, Austria and Germany. Australia is 11th, New Zealand 12th, Sweden 13th, the USA 14th, and among the top 20 are also Estonia, Qatar, Japan, Spain, Slovenia and Croatia.

this ranking isn’t what you might think it is

Nevertheless, it is necessary to emphasise that this is not an official international ranking of the “standard of living” in the classical economic sense. World Population Review for this ranking uses Numbeo’s Quality of Life Index, which attempts to encompass everyday quality of life through eight areas: purchasing power, safety, healthcare, cost of living, the ratio of property prices to income, time spent in traffic, pollution and climate conditions. It is precisely the last items that help explain why Croatia stands so high. For example, Numbeo’s data for Croatia show high scores for safety and very favourable climate conditions as well as a relatively low level of pollution.

World.title: Croatia Among EU Countries With Lowest Share of Insured Climate Losses
World.content:
September the 22nd, 2026 – Croatia is exceptionally vulnerable to climate events, yet it is remains among the EU countries with the lowest share of insured climate losses.

Even before the catastrophic fire in Omiš, Croatia already had a 75 percent larger burned area in 2026 than in the comparable period back in 2025. Poslovni reports that the European Commission estimates that today. only around 25 percent of catastrophic losses across Europe are covered by private insurance, which is why national budgets too often become the “insurer of last resort.”

the number of fires in croatia increased

The number of fires in Croatia rose by 7.62 percent, while the burned area rose by 75.06 percent compared to the same period last year. That difference says more about climate risk than any single image of a burning hill; an individual event today simply carries greater damage than a few years ago. Recent fires near Omiš, on Pelješac and Brač further confirmed this. The Omiš fire affected more than 1,000 hectares and led to the evacuation of around a thousand people. By mid-September, around 668,000 hectares had burned in fires across the European Union, almost twice the twenty-year average for the same part of the year, although less than the record 2025. The figures from across Europe warn that this season was not an exception but a continuation of a trend that Croatian companies, banks and insurers still need to take more seriously. Behind the scenes of burning hills lies the statistics about money, about premiums, damages and about who ultimately pays the bill when one decides to gamble with climate risk.

“Climate risk is increasingly becoming everyday life and the question is whether we have an idea of how much it can cost us. Companies that today assess their exposure only through last year’s damage are building a false sense of security,” believes Jasminka Horvat Martinović, President of the Management Board of Marsh Croatia, warning that this is a major trap of the moment in which a large part of the Croatian business sector finds itself.

A Reuters analysis, based on data from the European Environment Agency, shows the scale of the problem at the level of the entire Union: climate disasters and extreme weather conditions cost the European Union around €822 billion in the period from 1980 to 2024, and as much as a quarter of that amount occurred in the last four years. According to the latest EEA data, less than 20 percent of total losses in that period were covered by private insurance. For Croatia the gap is even larger: less than three percent of total economic losses linked to weather and climate extremes were insured.

unsurprisingly, croatia isn’t doing anywhere near enough

Croatia is thus among the European countries with the lowest share of insured climate losses. The floods in Spain in 2024 imply reconstruction costs of around 0.7 percent of GDP in the period 2024–2026, which is approximately €11 billion, while the German floods of 2021 cost the state treasury around €30 billion because insurance covered only a smaller part of the damage.

“The problem is no longer in the cost that disasters bring but in the fact that they are becoming regular. As long as they are treated as one-off budget burdens, the system does not adapt. The result is that an ever larger part of the bill ends up with taxpayers,” emphasises Horvat Martinović.

Some countries have already gone a step further than considering new models. Portugal in April, after major floods at the beginning of 2026, announced a fund for natural disasters and earthquakes and a system of compulsory insurance of housing and business infrastructure, with a public assistance mechanism for lower-income households. In Greece, from 1 June 2025, insurance against forest fire, flood and earthquake has been compulsory for companies with annual turnover greater than €500,000, with coverage of at least 70 percent of the value of the assets covered.

In the meantime a new step has also been taken at the level of the European Union. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on 16 September announced the establishment of the Climate Insurance Alliance with the aim of reducing the large gap in insurance against climate disasters. The Commission estimates that today only around 25 percent of catastrophic losses in Europe are covered by private insurance, which is why national budgets too often become the “insurer of last resort.” The new initiative should include insurers, investors, risk modelling experts, public institutions and policyholders and encourage solutions such as group and parametric insurance.

croatia’s fire risk is enormous

That European statistic primarily reflects floods and storms, but the same pattern of underinsurance also applies to fires, and the Croatian 2026 season shows this on its own local example.

According to data from the State Firefighting Operational Centre 193 of the Croatian Firefighting Association, in the period from 1 January to 10 August 2026, 29,358 firefighting interventions were recorded in Croatia, of which 8,832 were fires. Of that, 5,575 open-space fires and 3,897 vegetation fires were recorded, and 9,646 hectares were burned. Compared to the same period in 2025, the number of open-space fires rose by 12.99 percent, the number of vegetation fires by 23.40 percent, and the burned area by 75.06 percent. What makes that statistic particularly relevant for the business community is the relationship between the two figures. On the day of that cut-off the total number of fires rose by 7.62 percent, and the burned area by 75 percent. The risk, therefore, does not grow so much by frequency as by consequence. An individual event today carries a significantly greater loss than a few years ago. The Omiš fire shows this precisely; it was not the largest by area – the Split one from 2017 was four to five times larger. In addition, fires are no longer exclusively a coastal story. The risk, in other words, is moving from a seasonal to a permanent category.

The Croatian business sector mostly reacts to risk after it materialises, instead of structuring it in advance. “A strategic approach is important, and that means recognising the risk before it becomes damage,” emphasises Horvat Martinović, adding that companies should carry out in-depth analysis of exposure to climate risks, scenario models and adapted insurance solutions, from parametric covers, where the payout is activated automatically on the basis of pre-defined parameters such as the amount of precipitation or wind speed, to solutions for critical infrastructure and renewable energy sources. For example, in the energy sector, better mapping and prevention can reduce risk by 20 to 30 percent.

In the meantime newer data from the Croatian insurance market are also available. In the first seven months of 2026 the total collected premium rose by 6.9 percent to €1.3 billion, while the non-life insurance premium rose by 7.3 percent. Insurance against fire and elemental damage accounted for 9.5 percent of the non-life insurance premium. At the same time the amount of settled claims in non-life insurance rose by 15.9 percent, and 9.7 percent of that amount related to fires and elemental damage.

croatian companies need to ask themselves some serious questions

The growth in the number of policies on the Croatian market looks like a sign of maturity. But if a large part of property still remains uninsured or underinsured, that growth only means that the bills tomorrow will be larger than today. What distinguishes companies that survive a major loss is a pre-set risk management strategy, not the policy itself.

Croatian companies, Horvat Martinović believes, need to ask themselves the practical question of whether their risk assessment has been made on the basis of what happened last year, or on the basis of what is already now visible as coming. Climate risk is entering insurance prices, property values and public budgets ever more strongly; waiting for the next major event to show where the system is vulnerable, concludes Horvat Martinović, is becoming an ever more expensive strategy.
