It is interesting to ask who Geronti Kikodze was and why his opinion on this issue should appear in a school history textbook. Geronti Kikodze was not a historian at all. He was a literary scholar and therefore could not claim professional expertise in history,” Giorgi Astamadze says.

The historian recalled Kikodze’s ties to the Bolshevik authorities and the senior positions he held in the Soviet occupation administration. Giorgi Astamadze argues that “the openly collaborationist views of such a person on the national question have no basis, either in terms of his competence or from a moral standpoint.”

“The current Georgian regime’s publicly stated position that ties with Russia supposedly saved us has now been officially incorporated into a school textbook. And they have done so through the words of the writer Geronti Kikodze, presenting his opinion as a scholar’s view,” the historian says.

Interestingly, the previous Georgian history textbook included an assessment of the Treaty of Georgievsk by Ivane Javakhishvili, a classic of Georgian historical scholarship. He sharply criticised the treaty.

“The 1783 treaty brought nothing to Georgia. But the harm was enormous. Instead of improving Georgia’s political position, it made it dramatically worse. Much has been said about this treaty and the protection offered by the Russian state. In reality, however, the assistance Russia provided to Georgia was very limited,” Ivane Javakhishvili wrote.

Are the years 1918–1921 — the period when Georgia gained independence — missing from the textbook?

After the first part of the textbook was published, social media users actively discussed the absence of events from 1918–1921 — Georgia’s declaration of independence, the establishment of the First Democratic Republic, its political leaders and the subsequent Soviet occupation of Georgia in 1921.

Previous history textbooks treated this period as a separate and important topic.

Does this mean that 1918–1921 has been removed from the curriculum?

“It is not known yet. Historians consider this unlikely. Most likely, this material will appear in the next parts of the textbook. The introduction to the first part says that the textbook will consist of four parts.

In principle, the other parts should cover the First Republic, the Soviet occupation, the Soviet totalitarian system, the Russian-Georgian wars, including the August 2008 war. We are waiting. I hope the authors will write these sections in a way that dispels doubts and preserves the textbook’s factual character,” Giorgi Arkania says.

Does the textbook create the impression of a party narrative?

The authors of the new textbook are Jaba Samushia, Giorgi Kalandia and Aleksandre Boshishvili. Samushia also serves as a reviewer.

Jaba Samushia and Aleksandre Boshishvili are affiliated with the academic community of Tbilisi State University. Samushia has served as the university’s rector since 2022.

Giorgi Kalandia heads a state cultural institution. Since 2019, he has served as general director of the Art Palace of Georgia.

Because of these connections, some historians consider the authors affiliated with the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Additional questions concern the selection process: the state chose the authors, but it is unclear exactly how it did so.

“I hope that political considerations did not lead to certain issues being deliberately left unaddressed. However, after reading the textbook, one definitely gets the impression that some issues have been overlooked. For example, the coup I mentioned earlier.

The word ‘coup’ still creates a certain degree of political discomfort, and perhaps that is why the textbook does not give this period enough attention. The same applies to the proclamation.

Perhaps the authors considered it inconvenient to emphasise the word ‘occupation’ and remind students about the repressions,” historian Giorgi Arkania says.

Historian Giorgi Astamadze puts it more directly. He says the interpretations do not surprise him because historians close to Georgian Dream wrote the textbook. “I was completely certain that this was how it would turn out,” he says.

“We cannot allow new generations to remain unaware of what Russia has done to Georgia for more than two centuries: occupation, deception, humiliation, the abolition of the monarchy and the Church’s autocephaly, and the constant struggle against the Georgian Orthodox Church. These are facts that every young person in the country should know,” politician Pikria Chikhradze says.

On 14 September, she held a special briefing dedicated to the history textbooks. She said directly that “the authors linked to Georgian Dream used the opportunity to bring party narratives into school textbooks”.

Can schools refuse to use the new textbook?

For around two decades, Georgia had an entire textbook evaluation system. Different groups of authors and publishers produced textbooks, which the ministry then evaluated. Schools could have several approved textbooks for the same subject and grade and choose between them.

In 2026, the government began gradually replacing this system with a single state textbook model. Under the new system, the Education Ministry takes responsibility for producing textbooks.

Education Minister Givi Mikanadze said that the main principle would now be: “one grade — one subject — one standard textbook”.

Once the reform is complete, this principle should apply to both state and private schools. The ministry plans to complete the process by 2028.

But schools have no choice when it comes to the Georgian history textbook for the 10th grade discussed in this article. They must teach from this new book.

The replacement of school textbooks is part of a large-scale reform announced by the education minister. He spoke about the reform as early as October 2025.

The minister said the changes were necessary to ensure that school textbooks focused on “national values” and aimed to “raise citizens with a state-oriented mindset and national values”.

He also warned that the design of textbook covers would change, with “patriotic themes” appearing on them.

Protest against new Georgian history textbooks

World.title: Why can Russia conscript students from Abkhazia?
World.content:
Russia conscripts Abkhaz students

A schoolteacher, lawyer and blogger from Abkhazia, Said Beya, has looked into the issue of Abkhaz students studying in Russia being conscripted into the Russian army.

Said Beya: “Recently, there has been active public discussion of reports that the Abkhaz Foreign Ministry is trying to reach an agreement with Russia so that our students with dual citizenship are not required to register for military service in Russia.

Many people are asking: ‘How is this even possible? We are already registered for military service at home!’

Let’s look at the legal side of the issue and see where exactly the mistake was made.



What is the legal basis?

The status of people holding both passports is governed by the Agreement between Russia and the Republic of Abkhazia on resolving issues of dual citizenship. The document was signed by the Abkhaz and Russian sides in Sukhumi on 19 September 2022. Following a lengthy ratification process, the agreement fully entered into force on 25 April 2025.

The main source of the problem lies in Article 5 of the agreement. It states:

‘Persons holding citizenship of both parties shall perform compulsory military service in the party in whose territory they permanently reside at the time of conscription.’

The agreement protects those who have already completed military service in Abkhazia, meaning they cannot be conscripted in Russia. But if a young man has not yet served in the Abkhaz armed forces and travels to Russia to study, he becomes vulnerable to conscription.”

Why does Russia have the right to do this?

For the Russian authorities, anyone holding a Russian passport while in the country is regarded exclusively as a Russian citizen. An Abkhaz passport carries no weight with Russian military recruitment offices.

Under Russia’s law on military service, any Russian citizen who moves to a new place for more than three months is required to register with the local military authorities.

Students who come to Russia to study obtain temporary registration in halls of residence or rented accommodation, usually for several years. The Russian side interprets this unequivocally: if a young man lives and studies in Russia, then under Article 5 of the agreement, Russia is his current place of residence. This means the military recruitment office is entitled to require him to report for registration and conscript him for military service, unless he is eligible for a student deferment.

Why did the Abkhaz side fail to address this issue when signing the agreement in 2022?

This is now the main question facing the Abkhaz diplomats and officials who drafted and signed the document in 2022.

There appears to be a significant legal omission:

A crucial exemption is missing. Article 5 of the agreement does not contain wording along the lines of: “…with the exception of citizens temporarily staying in the territory of the other Party for the purpose of receiving an education.”

Had such a provision been included, Russian military recruitment offices would have had no grounds to make such demands of Abkhaz students.

In 2022, our authorities signed a framework agreement without taking some of the legal nuances into account.

Years later, after large numbers of students were told to register for military service in Russia, the Abkhaz Foreign Ministry has been forced to hold urgent meetings with the president and seek to renegotiate the issue with Moscow.

While these negotiations continue, the requirements imposed by Russian military recruitment offices on students temporarily registered in Russia unfortunately remain lawful.

For now, the only way for these students to avoid conscription is to make sure they obtain an official student defermentin Russia in time.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s 2027 budget: how will fall in oil revenues be offset?
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s 2027 budget

The Azerbaijani government forecasts lower state budget revenues from the oil and gas sector in 2027, while tax revenues are expected to rise. Preliminary figures point to moderate growth in government spending and a greater role for non-oil revenues in financing the budget.

These changes will also affect working people. From next year, the income tax rate on salaries in the private non-oil sector will increase. As a result, higher tax payments on wages will partly drive the growth in budget revenues.

According to a statement published by the Finance Ministry on 16 September, these figures are only preliminary. The figures may change before the government submits the draft budget to parliament.

How will budget revenues and spending change in 2027?

In 2027, state budget revenues are forecast at 39.234 billion manats, while spending will reach 42.4 billion manats (around $25 billion). Compared with the approved figures for 2026, revenues will rise by 1.6% and spending by 1.7%. The difference between revenues and spending — the budget deficit — is expected to reach 3.166 billion manats (around $1.86 billion).

This comparison uses the planned figures for 2026 and 2027. If actual budget execution in 2026 differs from the approved figures, the growth rate in 2027 compared with the actual results will also differ.

Higher spending in monetary terms does not automatically mean that the state will provide more services. Price rises must also be taken into account. If maintaining schools, buying medicines or repairing roads becomes more expensive, some of the additional funding will go towards maintaining the existing level of services.

A 1.7% increase in the overall budget also does not mean that funding for all sectors will rise at the same rate. The government may increase spending in one area while cutting it in another. For citizens, therefore, the overall size of the budget matters less than which services receive the funding.

Why are oil revenues falling?

Budget revenues from the oil and gas sector are forecast at 15.48 billion manats (around $9.1 billion). This is 955 million manats (around $562 million) less than the amount planned for the current year. Of this reduction, 935 million manats (around $550 million) comes from a cut in transfers from the State Oil Fund. Next year, the government plans to transfer 11.9 billion manats (around $7 billion).

The main change, therefore, is a reduction in the amount the State Oil Fund transfers to the state budget. This should not be interpreted as an equivalent fall in the country’s oil sales revenues. The fund’s revenues and the amount it transfers to the state budget are separate indicators.

The budget will nevertheless continue to receive significant support from the State Oil Fund. The planned transfer will account for 30.3% of budget revenues, meaning roughly one in every three manats will come from the fund.

Where will the additional funds come from?

Revenues collected by the State Tax Service are forecast at 18.43 billion manats (around $10.85 billion). This is 1.52 billion manats (around $894 million), or 9%, more than the amount planned for the current year. Customs revenues will increase by just 3 million manats and are expected to reach 6.865 billion manats (around $4.04 billion).

Personal income tax revenues are expected to rise by 690 million manats (around $406 million) to 3.07 billion manats (around $1.8 billion). This is around 29% more than the amount planned for the current year.

Corporate income tax revenues are planned at 6.983 billion manats (around $4.01 billion). The government therefore expects higher tax revenues from both personal incomes and corporate profits.

The increase in tax revenues cannot be explained solely by stronger economic activity. Revenues can rise not only because of higher wages, employment and corporate profits, but also because of changes in tax rates and more effective tax collection. More detailed calculations are needed to determine how much each factor contributes.

However, the additional revenues will not be enough to cover all spending. According to preliminary calculations, the government plans to finance 2.751 billion manats (around $1.62 billion) of the 3.166 billion-manat budget deficit through borrowing. It plans to cover the remaining amount with funds left in the Treasury account and proceeds from privatisation.

Overall, the government plans to cover around 87% of the deficit through borrowing. Borrowing allows the government to finance current spending, but it also creates obligations for future budgets to pay interest and repay the debt. Assessing budget sustainability therefore requires looking at borrowing terms and how the government plans to use the funds it raises.

What will change for salaried workers?

According to an official explanation from the State Tax Service, in 2026 the tax rate on the first 2,500 manats (around $1,470) of monthly taxable income for employees in the private non-oil and gas sector is 3%. In 2027, it will rise to 5%, and to 7% from 2028.

For example, if monthly taxable income after allowances is 1,000 manats (around $588), income tax will rise from 30 to 50 manats (around $17.65 to $29.40). With the tax base unchanged, this means an additional 20 manats (around $11.80) a month, or 240 manats (around $142) a year.

This calculation covers income tax only. The final amount a worker receives after tax also depends on other mandatory deductions and the tax allowances that apply to them. The changes do not affect workers in all sectors.

If an employer does not increase the gross salary and other deductions remain unchanged, the higher tax will reduce the worker’s take-home pay. To keep take-home pay at the same level, an employer may need to increase its labour costs.

Will higher social payments offset the higher tax burden?

Vugar Bayramov, a member of the Milli Majlis Economic Policy Committee, views the expected increase in the share of non-oil revenues to more than 60% positively. He considers this important for budget sustainability. According to him, structural reforms and greater transparency in public procurement could allow the government to allocate additional funds to social needs.

Economist Natig Jafarli said on 8 September, before the publication of the preliminary budget figures, that he expected pensions and salaries for public-sector employees to rise by 8–10%. He stressed that higher social payments sometimes only offset rising prices. This is the economist’s expectation.

Even if such increases take place, it cannot be said that they will offset the additional tax burden on private-sector employees. Higher salaries, pensions and benefits affect different groups of the population.

The preliminary figures point to the following trend: as transfers from the State Oil Fund decline, the government plans to increase tax revenues. What this will mean for citizens will depend on which services receive the additional funding, as well as on how their incomes and everyday expenses change.

World.title: Azerbaijan security service terrorism case spans five countries – what  is known so far?
World.content:
Azerbaijan security service operation in five countries

Azerbaijan says money collected for religious ceremonies was transferred to terrorist organisations using cryptocurrency. In a statement issued on 18 September, the State Security Service (SSS) said the alleged financing scheme and preparations to assassinate public and religious figures were being investigated as part of the same criminal case.

However, the statement published by the media does not specify the amount of money involved, the organisations alleged to have received it, or the five countries where the operations were carried out.

Information available from open sources does not allow the scale of the case to be independently verified. Available reports largely repeat the account provided by the agency conducting the investigation.

Charges brought

The SSS named the defendants as Vugar Abdullayev, Jalal Hajiyev, Javid Aliyev, Nijat Ahmadov, Nazim Aliyev, Ilkin Hasanzade, Aykhan Huseynov, Elshan Asgarov, Fakhraddin Imanov, Nail Rasulov and Elgun Ismayilov. Although the statement says 10 people were detained, it lists 11 defendants. The reason for the discrepancy is not explained.

They have been charged under Criminal Code articles relating to financing terrorism, forming a criminal organisation, preparing an assassination attempt against a state or public figure, and other offences. According to the SSS, a court ordered the defendants to be remanded in custody.

Link between two strands of case

In the SSS account, Jalal Hajiyev’s name appears both in connection with the alleged assassination plot and the financing scheme. The agency says Vugar Abdullayev and other defendants gathered information about the movements and security arrangements of the alleged targets. Hajiyev, meanwhile, is alleged to have used his contacts abroad to arrange money transfers to people involved in armed conflicts, as well as to terrorist organisations.

Although the two strands are being investigated as part of the same case, the SSS does not specify how they are linked financially. Were the funds allegedly transferred abroad used to finance preparations for the assassination attempts in Azerbaijan? Although some of the same individuals feature in both strands of the case, no evidence has been presented to establish a link between the movement of funds and the planning of the alleged attacks.

How was money traced?

According to the SSS, the funds were collected through fake s posted on social media, purportedly seeking donations for religious ceremonies. The agency says investigators obtained evidence showing where the money came from and how it was transferred.

To independently assess these claims, key evidence would include an archive of the s, payment details, transaction dates and information about the recipients. It is also unclear whether those who transferred the money knew its alleged true purpose or were themselves deceived – a distinction that could imply different degrees of responsibility.

The reference to cryptocurrency alone does not explain how the alleged financing scheme worked. The SSS does not say which digital assets were used, who controlled the addresses involved in the transactions, or how investigators established links between the recipients and terrorist organisations.

A 2023 report by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) describes the risks of social media fundraising and the use of virtual assets for terrorist financing. It also highlights the difficulty of proving that funds were intended for terrorist purposes and stresses the importance of protecting legitimate charitable activity.

International experience suggests that the mechanism described by the SSS is possible in principle. However, the allegations against specific individuals would need to be supported by evidence in the criminal case. So far, that evidence has not been made public.

World.title: Azerbaijan's ADEX 2026 exhibition records 45 foreign delegations from 33 countries
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 22. A total of 45 foreign delegations from 33 countries have registered to date for participation in the ADEX 2026 exhibition to be held in Azerbaijan.

This was reflected in a report published on the exhibition’s official website.

According to the information, countries to be represented with delegates include the U.S., Belarus, Bahrain, United Arab Emirates, Great Britain, South Korea, Czech Republic, Afghanistan, Georgia, Jordan, Iraq, Israel, Italy, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Latvia, Malaysia, Morocco, Montenegro, Nigeria, Uzbekistan, Pakistan, Russia, Serbia, Saudi Arabia, Slovakia, Sudan, Northern Cyprus, Türkiye, Turkmenistan, Ukraine, Uganda, and Vietnam.

In addition, 14 countries—the U.S., Azerbaijan, Belarus, Great Britain, the Czech Republic, China, Israel, Italy, Pakistan, Romania, Russia, Slovakia, Turkey, and Uzbekistan—will be represented by national pavilions at the exhibitions.

In total, more than 270 companies from 29 countries have confirmed their participation in the "ADEX" and Securex Caspian exhibitions. Alongside Azerbaijan, companies from the U.S., Germany, Belarus, Belgium, the United Arab Emirates, Bulgaria, the UK, Brazil, South Korea, the Czech Republic, China, France, Spain, Italy, Lithuania, Hungary, Uzbekistan, Pakistan, Poland, Romania, Russia, Serbia, Singapore, Slovakia, Turkey, Ukraine, and other countries will participate with stands at the exhibitions.

From 30 September to 2 October 2026, ADEX 2026 – the 6th Azerbaijan International Defence Exhibition – will take place at the Baku Expo Center. Modern military technologies and equipment, as well as the capabilities of Azerbaijan's defense industry complex, will be showcased at the exhibition, which is one of the major military-technological platforms in the Caucasus region.

The 15th International Exhibition for Internal Security, Safety, and Rescue Equipment—"Securex Caspian"—will also be held at the Baku Expo Center during the same period.

Leading U.S. companies such as Northrop Grumman, SIG SAUER, Lockheed Martin, Vantor and Ondas will be represented at the exhibition for the first time. Rheinmetall and Rohde & Schwarz from Germany, as well as BAE Systems and other companies from the UK, will also make their debut. Türkiye, meanwhile, will be the most widely represented country at the exhibition.

Among the exhibition’s traditional international participants are Roketsan, Aselsan, Baykar, Turkish Aerospace Industries (TAI) and Havelsan from Türkiye; Leonardo from Italy; CSG from the Czech Republic; EDGE Group from the United Arab Emirates; and INDRA from Spain.

Türkiye’s Roketsan is the General Sponsor of ADEX, while the U.S. company Northrop Grumman is the Country Partner Sponsor.

One of the key new features of ADEX 2026 is that, for the first time, Pavilion 4 of the Baku Expo Center will be allocated to Azerbaijan’s national exhibition.

World.title: Russia highlights strategic partnership with Turkmenistan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 22. Russia highlights efforts to further deepen its strategic partnership with Turkmenistan in birthday greetings to President Berdimuhamedov.

This was reflected in a letter sent by Russian President Vladimir Putin to the President of Turkmenistan, Serdar Berdimuhamedov, on the occasion of his birthday, according to a press release published by the press service of the Turkmen government today.

Putin noted that under Berdimuhamedov’s leadership, Turkmenistan continues to advance its socio-economic development and strengthen its position on the international stage.

The Russian president said Moscow highly values Berdimuhamedov’s efforts to further deepen the strategic partnership between the two countries.

“We will continue joint work on current issues of the bilateral and international agenda for the benefit of the friendly peoples of Russia and Turkmenistan, in the interests of ensuring stability and security in Central Asia and the Caspian region,” Putin said.

The letter also expressed Putin’s wishes for President Berdimuhamedov’s good health, happiness, well-being and further success in his state activities.

For reference, Russia and Turkmenistan maintain a strategic partnership covering trade, energy, transport, diplomacy and humanitarian ties. Russia remains one of Turkmenistan’s key trading partners, with bilateral trade exceeding $1.6 billion annually, according to Turkmen government data. In 2025, bilateral trade continued to expand, with trade turnover rising 21.4% in the first quarter, while the two sides worked on an intergovernmental action plan for 2025-2027. Cooperation also extends to the fuel and energy sector, industry, agriculture, banking and finance, and digital technologies.

Energy remains an important component of the relationship, although Russia is no longer the main destination for Turkmenistan’s natural gas exports. The two countries have also been developing transport cooperation, including routes linking Turkmenistan with Russia and other markets through the Caspian Sea. Discussions have included the Volga-Caspian Canal with an outlet to the port of Turkmenbashi and the eastern bypass of the Caspian Sea within the International North-South Transport Corridor. At the political level, Moscow and Ashgabat cooperate through the UN, CIS, the Caspian littoral states and the Central Asia-Russia format. In September 2026, Turkmenistan said preparations were underway for the 14th meeting of the bilateral intergovernmental commission, with the agenda covering trade, energy, transport, finance, industry and other areas.

World.title: Kazakhstan Temir Zholy to transport 163,000 tons of steel pipes from China
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 22. Kazakhstan’s KedenTransService, a subsidiary of Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ), plans to transport 163,000 tons of steel pipes from China in September-October 2026 as part of a multimodal logistics project, the company said.

The project involves organizing multimodal transportation of steel pipes from China by rail and road.

“The shipments are carried out by rail and road transport along two routes: imports to Kazakhstan and transit shipments to Turkmenistan. In September-October this year, the planned transportation volume will amount to 163,000 tons of steel pipes,” the company said.

The company noted that organizing the shipments requires strict compliance with special loading and securing procedures, as well as close coordination between rail and road transport.

In January-August 2026, the volume of freight transported across KTZ’s network reached 212.7 million tons. Domestic transportation amounted to 112.4 million tons, while exports increased by 6.8% to 61.5 million tons.

Earlier in September, KTZ Express, another subsidiary of KTZ, expanded the geography of international transportation by adding new Asian routes to Kazakhstan’s transport and logistics system. The company organized its first multimodal container shipment of chemical products from Japan’s Port of Kobe to Almaty.

The route, spanning approximately 6,000 kilometers, combines sea and rail transportation. From the Port of Kobe, the containers are transported by sea for about 1,620 kilometers to Lianyungang, China, where, following customs clearance, the cargo is transferred to rail and travels another approximately 4,400 kilometers to Almaty.

At the China-Kazakhstan border, the containers are transferred to rolling stock operating on Kazakhstan’s rail gauge at the Altynkol crossing, after which the shipment continues to its final destination in Almaty.

World.title: China reaffirms commitment to stronger ties with Turkmenistan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 22. China reaffirms its commitment to strengthening traditional friendship and mutually beneficial cooperation with Turkmenistan in birthday greetings to President Berdimuhamedov.

This was reflected in a letter sent by Chinese President Xi Jinping to President of Turkmenistan Serdar Berdimuhamedov on the occasion of his birthday, according to a press release published by the press service of the Turkmen government today.

Xi recalled his recent meeting with Berdimuhamedov in Beijing, held during the Turkmen president’s visit to China to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Summit in Tianjin and celebrations marking the 80th anniversary of the victory of the Chinese people in the Second World War.

The Chinese president said the two leaders exchanged views on further strengthening traditional friendship and mutually beneficial cooperation between China and Turkmenistan across various fields.

“I attach great importance to the development of China-Turkmenistan relations and am ready to make joint efforts to promote the building of a ‘China-Turkmenistan Community of Shared Future’ for the benefit of the peoples of both countries,” Xi said.

The letter also included Xi Jinping’s wishes for President Berdimuhamedov’s good health and success in his work.

For reference, China-Turkmenistan economic relations are centered on energy cooperation, with natural gas serving as a key pillar of the bilateral strategic partnership. China became the main market for Turkmen gas following the launch of the Turkmenistan-China gas pipeline in 2009. The pipeline system currently comprises three operating lines, A, B and C, with combined capacity of around 40 billion cubic meters (bcm) per year. Turkmenistan has supplied China with more than 460 bcm of natural gas since the start of exports, according to Turkmen government data. China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) has been a key partner in the development of Turkmenistan’s gas resources and related infrastructure.

The latest major step in the partnership came on April 17, 2026, when Turkmenistan and China launched the fourth phase of development of the Galkynysh gas field in Mary region. Under the project, CNPC is constructing facilities to process 10 bcm of commercial gas annually, along with production wells and associated infrastructure. The project covers the full production chain, including gas gathering, treatment and processing facilities and pipelines. The fourth phase is expected to strengthen Turkmenistan’s production and export capacity, while further deepening CNPC’s role in the country’s gas sector. The launch followed the signing of the project agreement on April 16 during Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang’s visit to Turkmenistan.

World.title: Equinor and GCMD strike five-year partnership on maritime decarbonisation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 22. Equinor and the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) have agreed a five-year partnership to accelerate the deployment of alternative marine fuels and other technologies aimed at cutting emissions from shipping, GCMD said.

The partnership will combine GCMD's experience in conducting real-world maritime trials with Equinor's position as a vessel charterer, energy provider and developer of lower-carbon solutions.

The organisations will focus on addressing technical and operational barriers to the wider adoption of alternative fuels, including biofuels, ammonia and methanol, while also examining technologies that can reduce emissions from the existing shipping fleet.

GCMD's work on alternative fuels centres on operational safety and monitoring, reporting and verification of emissions. Its trials are designed to generate operational data on the safe bunkering and handling of new fuels, while its assurance work seeks to improve confidence in fuel quantity, quality and greenhouse gas emissions reductions.

Equinor brings experience from chartering vessels powered by LNG, LPG and methanol, as well as testing biofuels and supplying methanol to the maritime sector. The Norwegian energy company is also involved in trials of ammonia as a marine fuel, including work on the safety, regulatory and bunkering infrastructure needed for its wider use.

"The partnership brings together GCMD's capabilities in conducting real-world maritime pilots with Equinor's experience as a charterer, energy provider and developer of low-carbon solutions," the organisation said.

The companies will also explore technologies beyond alternative fuels, including energy-efficiency solutions and onboard carbon capture and storage (OCCS).

GCMD has conducted trials to quantify the real-world fuel savings from technologies such as wind-assisted propulsion and has worked on financing mechanisms intended to facilitate their wider adoption. Its Project CAPTURED demonstrated an end-to-end system for capturing and liquefying CO₂ onboard ships, generating evidence that contributed to the recognition of captured CO₂ under the EU Emissions Trading System.

Equinor's experience in carbon capture and storage extends to the Northern Lights project in Norway, developed jointly with Shell and TotalEnergies. The project transports liquefied CO₂ by ship to an onshore terminal before sending it through pipelines for permanent storage beneath the North Sea.

Northern Lights started storing its first CO₂ in 2025 and has an initial annual storage capacity of 1.5mn tonnes. Its second phase is planned to increase capacity to at least 5mn tonnes a year, according to Equinor.

"Together, the organisations will leverage their complementary expertise to help address technical and operational gaps in scaling alternative marine fuels and supporting the development and uptake of other maritime decarbonisation solutions," GCMD said.

Equinor has been developing lower-emission marine-fuel options as part of its broader maritime strategy. The company has experience with LNG, LPG, biofuels, methanol and ammonia, while its maritime activities also include the development of solutions for reducing emissions from vessels used in its offshore operations.

The company has also supported the conversion of the offshore supply vessel Viking Energy to operate on ammonia. Equinor has described the project as a demonstration of ammonia's potential as a marine fuel and part of efforts to develop practical solutions for lower-emission shipping.

The partnership comes as shipping companies and fuel suppliers face the challenge of moving from pilot projects to commercially scalable alternatives to conventional marine fuels. That transition requires not only sufficient supplies of low-carbon fuels but also compatible vessels, bunkering infrastructure, safety standards and reliable systems for measuring emissions reductions.

Through the five-year collaboration, GCMD and Equinor will seek to combine their operational experience and pilot projects to help close those gaps and support the broader adoption of maritime decarbonisation technologies.

World.title: Former soldiers to face call-up obligations of ten years
World.content:
New recruits entering the Australian Defence Force (ADF) will be required to remain "on the books" for ten years after leaving the military.

The ADF has doubled the "commitment period" required of all personnel from five years to ten, in an effort to grow the pool of people it can call upon in a crisis.

The requirement to remain in Australia's reserve forces has been in place for anyone entering the ADF since 2016.

The longer time frame will automatically apply to recruits from October 1, while existing personnel will be able to opt-in to ten years.

The commitment only requires members to stay at "service category two" — essentially an unpaid contingency reserve, with no service, training or other obligations other than a duty to respond if called up.

Defence has been looking for ways to lift the number of reserve personnel for some time and a 2024 review of reserves recommended making this change after warning the number who could be called upon was too low.

It estimated that the change would double the ADF's "contingent reserve" — people who are out of active service but could be called upon in a crisis — to close to 20,000 within five years.

Defence Minister Richard Marles has welcomed ADF recruitment figures, which are on the rise. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

There is also a sense within Defence that some former personnel feel the five year window is too short and they want the option to easily return to service for longer — even if they have been inactive for years.

Asked about the change, Defence Minister Richard Marles pointed to recent ADF recruitment figures as a positive sign for the military.

"We manage recruitment very carefully," he said.

"We are seeing recruitment rates which we haven't seen for a very long period of time, so we are actually investing in our people, making the critical decisions."

Last week, the ADF announced its permanent headcount had reached more than 64,000 — a 25-year high.

The $173,000 cost of recruitment

The 2024 Strategic Review of the Australian Defence Force Reserves pointed out the enormous cost of training full-time military personnel.

It estimated the average cost of training a soldier in their first 12 months is $173,000, and suggested it "rises exponentially" as they build experience and new technical skills.

The review argued it makes economic sense for the ADF to try and maintain connection with a highly trained potential workforce in the years after they leave service.

Recent figures suggest most former ADF personnel leaving service actually opt to initially join the reserves at a higher "service category", meaning they maintain training and some active service.

TikTok and online games delivering military recruits Targeted advertising on social media and in online games has helped deliver a boost to Australian Defence Force recruitment, offsetting a perennial problem of declining service rates.

But it pointed out that there are thousands of former ADF members leaving service each year and joining the contingency reserve that it has almost no visibility of, and could be using better.

The ADF has also been on a years-long campaign to lift its recruitment levels, missing its permanent recruitment target in 2024-25 by 23 per cent.

Jennifer Parker, a former naval officer and adjunct professor at the University of Western Australia, said she does not think the increased service obligations will hinder recruitment.

"I don't think that an obligation for inactive reserves really will factor into the minds of young people joining Defence when you weigh up the pros and cons and the incentives," she said.

"So I don't think it will impact recruitment at all."

Jennifer Parker has called for substantial change to how the ADF Reserve is built. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Ms Parker argues doubling the service commitment makes sense as it grows the pool of people that the ADF can call upon in a time of conflict or crisis.

But she points out those people will not necessarily have the current skill sets or knowledge to be as useful as they could be.

"Depending on what their category is and what their skill set was when they served, those skill sets require currency and training to be able to be used," she said.

"So it's more a pool of people, as opposed to people with specific current skill sets. And there is a certain benefit in that.

"But I do think they are perhaps tinkering around the edges a little bit. A more detailed strategic review of the reserves is required to understand what the functions are that we require from the reserve force."

Growing the reserve

As of March 2024, the total number of people in the ADF Reserve was 41,717 — including 9,406 people in the unpaid service category two.

The only time the ADF's reserves have been formally called out was in January 2020 to respond to the Black Summer bushfires.

The 2024 reserve review noted that outside of periods of conscription, Australia's level of reserves has remained fairly steady for decades, even as the broader population has grown.

And it argued that the reserve has "no coherent design" and a role that is "not clearly defined".

While the army takes a large number of recruits directly into its reserve, both the air force and Navy Reserve is made up almost entirely of former full-time personnel.

Morrison announces ADF reservists' deployment Scott Morrison announces the deployment of 3,000 ADF reservists and government resources to help with firefighting and recovery operations along with emergency accommodation and the leasing of a further four firefighting aircraft.

The review set a modest target for the ADF of recruiting another 1,000 reserve personnel by 2030 and recommended some administrative changes.

Jennifer Parker argues there is a case for more substantial change — to build an ADF Reserve that is more capable, and more ready to serve if called upon.

"There needs to be a fundamental review that looks at what we want the reserves to do practically," she said.

"You would change the structure of the reserves. You would start recruiting more navy and air force reservists off the street, you'd start upskilling them, and you would have (training) requirements."

While those changes wouldn't affect the current pool of inactive reserves, she said until there was a more structural change, defence is "playing around the edges".

World.title: RBA governor's final speech before board meeting cements rate rise bets
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

All four major banks and the bulk of money market traders believe the Reserve Bank will raise interest rates next week and governor Michele Bullock did nothing to dissuade them in her last public appearance before the meeting.

Speaking at a Committee for Economic Development of Australia (CEDA) event in Sydney, Ms Bullock said Australia's jobs market was probably still a bit too tight and putting upwards pressure on wages, business costs and inflation more generally.

"Between 4.5 and 5 [per cent unemployment] will probably take enough heat out of the labour market that eases pressure on inflation," she said.

The latest August unemployment data will be released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday and is the last major piece of economic data before the RBA Monetary Policy Board meeting on September 28-29.

Echoing comments she made at a federal parliamentary hearing on Friday, Ms Bullock said it was critical that imported inflation from the global energy price shock was not allowed to translate into rounds of domestic price increases.

"We need to be very careful to ensure that policy is set in a way that minimises the second round and indirect effects which might perpetuate ongoing inflation," she said.

" I think monetary policy really just needs to continue to focus on making sure that we limit indirect effects and we try to keep inflation expectations anchored. "

Major banks hike fixed mortgage rates

After Friday's testimony the three major banks that had been forecasting the Reserve Bank would stay on hold in September changed their forecasts to predict a rate hike at the meeting next week.

Interest rates back at 'sensible level' If you are struggling with current interest rates, the Reserve Bank's leaders delivered the sobering message that they are only just getting back to a "more sensible level".

The economics team at NAB was already anticipating a September move, while CBA and Westpac now expect the RBA to lift rates once more in September, with the risk of a second move in November.

ANZ's economics team has added a September rate rise while maintaining their forecast of a November hike as well, which would take the cash rate to 4.85 per cent, the highest level since late 2008.

Futures pricing on Bloomberg suggests a 90 per cent chance rates will rise next week, with about a 50/50 chance of a follow up hike in November.

The bank and market predictions are already having a real effect on interest rates, with fixed mortgage pricing rising dramatically in recent days.

Today the Commonwealth Bank lifted its two-year fixed home loan rate by 0.48 of a percentage point to 6.82 per cent, and other fixed rates by between 0.15-0.3 of a percentage point.

Comparison website Canstar said that follows similar moves of up to 0.2 of a percentage point by the other three major banks last week.

The lowest one or two-year fixed home loan rates offered by the big four of 6.49 per cent are now noticeably above their lowest variable rates of between 5.99 to 6.25 per cent, indicating an expectation that rates will increase.

AI 'great white hope' or massive financial bubble?

Ms Bullock's wideranging economic discussion also touched upon the issue of artificial intelligence.

She noted that, over the longer-term, as people and businesses found the best uses and workflows for the technology, it would add to productivity, putting downward pressure on inflation.

"AI is the great white hope to improve productivity," Ms Bullock said.

"When I talk to colleagues around the world about this, I think everyone thinks that."

Australia's migration fix ignores productivity problem Reducing population growth does little to address the deeper problem: An economy struggling with weak productivity.

However, that potential longer-term benefit is coming with a short-term headache, as AI providers scramble to build data centres and other enabling infrastructure.

"But I think everyone also agrees that there are very few signs yet that AI is actually influencing the supply side of the economy," Ms Bullock said.

"There's lots of evidence that it's influencing the demand side of the economy.

"So we've got this sort of awkward sequencing event at the moment where, in Australia at least, we are in a situation of excess demand and the AI boom is adding to that demand ahead of any potential supply impacts that it might have going forward."

Ms Bullock also acknowledged the risk that investment enthusiasm and the valuation of companies was running ahead of their realistic earnings potential.

"All central banks are a little bit worried about that," she said.

"You know, it might not be a bubble, but it might be.

"And if it unwinds in a disorderly manner, then that could have implications for the financial system and also for the real economies."

She said it was an area the RBA was keeping an eye on, with its twice yearly Financial Stability Review out next week.

"Some people think it's a bubble, some people don't. I don't have a particular view one way or the other, but it's a risk that I think we're watching," Ms Bullock said.

World.title: Film studios shun women but men make them less money, report shows
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Barbie was an undeniable hit, raking in $US1.45 billion ($2.03 billion) at the worldwide box office.

Avatar: The Way of Water grossed more than $US2.3 billion ($2.85 billion) globally and is the third highest-grossing film in history.

These films have something in common.

Women played a role in co-writing the films and, in the case of Barbie, directing.

A new analysis, Women in Directing and Screenwriting: The Capital Allocation Puzzle in Commercial Film, has found movies with a female screenwriter returned higher median profits than male-only productions.

The Frontiers in Communication study covered 30 years of film, including theatrical and non-theatrical releases.

"Films with a woman screenwriter but no woman director had 34 per cent higher median profits than films with only men in those roles, despite similar budgets," said Anja Huwiler, the study's author and a researcher at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz.

"Yet 39 of the 44 films in the top 1 per cent of production budgets were male-only productions, and none involved a woman director."

Greta Gerwig directed Barbie and co-wrote the screenplay, while Lindsey Beer wrote the draft script. (Supplied: Caroline McCredie)

Films written but not directed by women with budgets comparable to male-only productions generated the highest median profit.

Movies written but not directed by women also generated a higher return on investment.

Films in which women had both screenwriting and directing roles achieved a similar return on investment to male-only films when operating on half the budget.

Avatar: The Way of Water was directed by James Cameron, who wrote the screenplay with Rick Jaffa and Amanda Silver. (Supplied: 20th Century Studios)

While films written by women made more money, movies with higher budgets were male-dominated.

"The extreme uncertainty of film financing can make familiar people and established ways of working feel safer, especially when decision-makers are risk- or loss-averse," said Ms Huwiler.

"This can reinforce the status quo even when the financial evidence points elsewhere."

The report also found that the share of films crediting at least one woman as a director or screenwriter was growing at a sluggish pace.

After the #MeToo movement in 2017, women's participation rose, but the study found no lasting acceleration in the rate of growth.

Men hold privileged position 'not earned'

Senior lecturer in screenwriting at the University of Melbourne Radha O'Meara said the findings of the report were in line with what she sees in the Australian screen industry, despite the international focus.

"Gender discrimination in the Australian screen industry is often couched in the language of financial risk, and this report confirms that men screenwriters and directors are actually the greater financial risk," Dr O'Meara told ABC News.

"Sexism is alive and well in the Australian screen industry, sometimes blatant, often veiled or subtle."

Radha O'Meara says creative women should be given more chances. (Supplied: Radha O'Meara)

Dr O'Meara said the data shows that men hold a privileged position in the screen industry that they have not earned.

"The films they write and direct are less commercially successful than those created by women.

"Men are allowed to fail in their creative pursuits — write or direct a film that flops — and are given another chance to prove themselves.

"Women who create a project that flops are condemned and ostracised.

"This is a clear double standard."

Dr O'Meara said government screen agencies could do much more to pursue fairness and stamp out discrimination but are often too closely aligned with the industry to push back on faulty logic.

"Government screen agencies seem quick to celebrate a minor improvement rather than work to address the glacial pace of change.

"This data shows that, even in purely commercial terms, creative women should be sought out and given more chances to create stories and develop careers in the screen industry."

World.title: NRL grand final loses headline act for pre-match entertainment
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The NRL says it is prepared to have no pre-match entertainment at its grand final this year after talks broke down with Australian artist Tones And I.

Instead the league is offering to increase funding to grassroots competitions with the money set aside for a pre-game performance.

Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'Landys told the ABC the money spent on pre-match entertainment could be put to better use.

"I'd prefer to see 20,000 underprivileged kids who can't afford to play rugby league play rugby league, rather than spend a million dollars on 11 minutes of a musical performance," he said.

The move would be a stunning break from tradition — the grand final has regularly featured pre-match entertainment, including international pop-star Teddy Swims last year.

Teddy Swims performed at last year's NRL grand final. (Supplied: NRL)

Billy Idol and Tina Turner are among other acts to have taken the stage for the event.

V'Landys said the total cost of such performances ran close to $1 million and that the plan for grassroots funding was one he had been mulling for sometime.

V'Landys was unconcerned as to whether the event could be underwhelming without pre-match entertainment.

"Our game sells itself," he said.

"People come to watch rugby league — they don't come to watch a pop concert."

V'Landys did not provide details on the record of why or how the negotiations with Tones and I broke down.

The Sydney Morning Herald reported that the issue centred the NRL's insistence that Tones and I perform the song Dance Monkey, which she had refused to do.

"You spend money to get outcomes and I think it's a better outcome to get kids that can't afford to play with their mates, gear etc, to play rugby league," V'Landys said.

"I'm a fan of Tones and I. She is a great performer, no doubt about that, and she's got some great songs, but as I said, we both decided to go to a different direction.

"We consider a lot of artists over a period of time, but as I said, I've been toying with this idea for a couple of years now, about giving the money to kids to play rugby league rather than a musical act."

Peter V’landys (right) says the league has decided it would prefer to spend its money elsewhere. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

The grand final hosting rights are bid for by state governments across the country. New South Wales holds the rights now, but it is not clear if the minister for sport or the premier were consulted over the matter.

Neither office has replied to requests for comment.

NSWRL chief executive David Trodden said he had "a short conversation" with V'Landys about the prospect of funds being directed towards grassroots footy.

"I applaud his decision to use the funds to support grassroots rugby league, and particularly those children who may have financial constraints on their ability to participate in such a wonderful community sport," Trodden said.

"Rugby league has a unique ability to provide community support to those who need it the most."

World.title: Witness tells how he helped in alleged cold case murder
World.content:
A man who assisted in the alleged murder of a Warrnambool man more than two decades ago has told a jury he was told to keep quiet about the crime, otherwise he would be killed next.

Warning: This article includes violent descriptions of an alleged murder that some readers may find distressing.

Steven Frederick Johnson, 74, has pleaded not guilty to one charge of murder in relation to the disappearance of 38-year-old Christopher Jarvis on June 13, 2006, from his Wangoom home near Warrnambool.

Mr Jarvis's burnt-out car was found at the regional city's popular coastal lookout, Thunder Point, later that day.

His body has never been found.

It is the Crown's case that Mr Johnson orchestrated a violent attack on his tenant, Mr Jarvis, over $2,210 in rent arrears, before disposing of his body and setting his car alight.

The court has heard the two men were engaged in a civil dispute, with a VCAT hearing scheduled for the day after Mr Jarvis disappeared.

The defence argues that Mr Johnson was seeking to resolve the rental dispute by lawful means and he had no involvement in Mr Jarvis's disappearance.

The trial is being heard in the Victorian Supreme Court, sitting at Warrnambool. (ABC News: Jean Bell)

In the Supreme Court sitting at Warrnambool today, a man, who cannot be named for legal reasons, gave evidence about how Mr Johnson would refer to his neighbour, Mr Jarvis, as the "prick next door [that's] got to go", and that his tenant owed him money for rent and a car.

The court heard the man agreed to help Mr Johnson get Mr Jarvis out of the rental property.

"I assumed Steve was going to go out there and rough him up … to scare him into paying," he told the court.

The court heard the men met up near Mr Jarvis's home early in the morning and approached him from behind as he closed a gate, while his Ford station wagon idled in the driveway.

The man told the court he watched the accused hit Mr Jarvis over the head with a pistol before he grabbed the man by the shoulder and threw him to the ground.

"I seen [sic] fear in Mr Jarvis's eyes," he said.

Shallow grave

The unnamed man said Mr Jarvis called out for help, and Mr Johnson then put his hand over Mr Jarvis's mouth.

"He was thrashing around on the ground," the man told the court.

The man said he held Mr Jarvis's legs to the ground, and Mr Johnson fired an empty pistol near his ear, causing blood to flow from his head.

The court heard that the two men put the injured man in the back of his own car, before Mr Johnson drove out to Framlingham Forest.

The court heard the men dug a shallow grave in the bushland.

The unnamed man said Mr Johnson stripped Mr Jarvis naked, putting his bloody clothes back into the car before he used a baseball bat already in the vehicle to strike Mr Jarvis on the head with force, killing him.

"Mr Jarvis was making slight groaning noises, then everything went dead quiet," the man told the court.

The court heard Mr Jarvis's body was then pushed into the grave.

Christopher Jarvis's Ford station wagon was found burnt-out at Thunder Point. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

The court heard the men then drove separately to Thunder Point, with Mr Johnson driving Mr Jarvis's car and the unnamed man driving his own black Holden Commodore ute.

The unnamed man said Mr Johnson drove Mr Jarvis's vehicle into the sand dunes, doused it with petrol and set it alight.

The court heard Mr Johnson got in the black ute's passenger seat, with the unnamed man behind the wheel.

"He looked me in the eye … and said to me, 'You say anything about this and you're f*****g next,'" the man told the court.

"I took that as a death threat."

The court heard the unnamed man then drove away from Thunder Point at great speed, dropping Mr Johnson off at his Wangoom home, before returning to his own home.

Accused was 'greedy', court hears

Yesterday, the unnamed man told the jury that he met Mr Johnson around 1992 through the accused's business running a rubbish tip.

Crown prosecutor Mark Gibson KC asked the man about what he observed about how Mr Johnson was with money.

"You want me to be truthful?" the man asked.

Mr Gibson replied he did.

"He was a greedy c**t," the man told the court.

Earlier, the court heard Mr Jarvis's 36-year-old daughter Bree Jarvis had not had contact with her father since he disappeared shortly before her 16th birthday.

The court also heard from Mr Jarvis's nephew, Simon McLaren, who told the jury that he went alone to Thunder Point the day after his uncle went missing.

"[I found] his car burnt out … surrounded by shrub, no police tape or barriers or cordon," he told the court.

The court heard Mr McLaren took his uncle's baseball bat, bandana and mobile phone from the car, before handing them to police about a year later.

Retired Warrnambool teacher Michael Kibblewhite also gave evidence about how he saw a large cloud of smoke at Thunder Point on the morning of the alleged crime, and a black ute travelling at speed away from the lookout.

The trial continues.

World.title: War of words over Greens' proposal to co-locate data centres and pools
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A war of words has erupted over a suggestion from the ACT Greens that co-locating data centres with Canberra's public pools should be considered.

The idea is included in a motion set to be debated in the ACT Legislative Assembly this week by Greens MLA Laura Nuttall.

The motion includes several elements, but one point, calling on the ACT government to "consider co-locating data centres with public pools to use cooling water as a heating source", has drawn significant criticism from Chief Minister Andrew Barr.

ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr says data centres belong only in industrial areas, away from pools in residential districts. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"The primary and best location for data centres is exactly where they have been planned and built in the ACT for decades, and that is in industrial zones," Mr Barr said.

" Co-locating data centres [with public pools] would effectively be eating into community space and amenity. "

Ms Nuttall said she was "disappointed" but "not surprised" by Mr Barr's reaction.

"Mr Barr has not taken our motion in the best faith possible," she said.

"We are just asking the government to consider it, we are not actually asking them to commit to doing it."

Facebook post a 'wilful misrepresentation'

Greens MLA Laura Nuttall's private members bill calls for new data centres to implement best-practice water and energy consumption. (ABC News: Tobias Hunt)

Ms Nuttall also raised concern about a Facebook post made by Mr Barr, which showed an image of a pool next to a large data centre.

"I felt it was a wilful misrepresentation of what the ACT Greens are actually asking the government to do," she said.

"We are not talking about a massive data centre like the one that we suspect Mr Barr has AI-generated on his Facebook page.

"We are talking about things like in the UK, where as far back as 2023, they have had data centres the size of washing machines powering public pool."

Chief Minister Andrew Barr posted this AI-generated image of a data centre next to an outdoor pool on Facebook when announcing the government was against the proposal. (Facebook)

Ms Nuttall described the post as "a bit cringe" and said it was a "blatant attempt to divert community attention away from what actually matters".

Mr Barr defended his post.

"What? The Greens are going to now start suggesting that Facebook posts are inappropriate?" he said.

" What did they think? No one was going to respond to any element of what they have brought forward? "

Ms Nuttall said the pool suggestion was only a "small part" of the wider motion, which also called for a moratorium on new data centres in Canberra until a new framework was in place.

"We want to make sure that the ACT government enshrines best practice in how data centres use energy and water," she said.

" I think it's a total misdirection for the government to be zeroing in on one point about pools. "

The ACT government estimates there are already 15 data centres in Canberra. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Mr Barr said the government would also not be supporting a call for a moratorium.

"I am not in the business of turning down investment in new data centres that support important elements for our university sector, for the Australian government, for things like climate and weather modelling," he said.

Parties 'have always had points of difference'

The debate comes a week after the Greens ended their long-standing confidence and supply agreement with Labor.

But Mr Barr said it was not unusual for the Greens and Labor to disagree, and said MLAs could expect "greater scrutiny on the fine detail of private members' motions".

"We have always had points of difference," he said.

" We have had disagreements over dozens of policy issues over the last 40 years, we will no doubt have disagreements over the next 40. "

Opposition leader Mark Parton said while he thought a discussion about data centres was "really important" to be had, he said the Canberra Liberals were also not supportive of the pool suggestion and the moratorium.

The ACT government estimates there are already 15 data centres in Canberra, and expects a new framework on data centres to be released next year.

World.title: Monster pothole on SA road a deathtrap, motorcyclist says
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The South Australian government has admitted that the quality of a stretch of road near Mannum is "not acceptable" despite repeated attempts by its contractors to patch it.

The result of weekend works on Ridley Road, between Mannum and Cambrai, sparked concern among locals, including Mannum resident Paul Smith, who has been documenting the condition of the road on social media.

The motorcyclist said was "outraged" by the state of the road, particularly by a large pothole that was repaired at least four times over the past week.

A section of Ridley Road photographed prior to road works. (Supplied: Jubba Photography/Paul Smith)

"What I saw was beyond belief," Mr Smith said.

"If someone hits it on a bike, they're going to die.

"I don't think the politicians and the pencil pushers understand that we don't get a second chance on a motorbike."

Mr Smith said the pothole was so large that could pose a hazard to other smaller vehicles.

Paul Smith says the patching on the weekend did not restore his confidence in the safety of the road. (Supplied: Jubba Photography/Paul Smith)

Will the planned repairs be enough?

In a statement, a spokesperson for SA's Department of Infrastructure and Transport said the potholes were caused by heavy rain over winter.

It said that contractors it engaged earlier this year had conducted temporary patching along Ridley Road but more permanent work had been scheduled for next month.

The Department of Infrastructure and Transport says more repairs are planned. (Supplied: SA Department of Infrastructure and Transport)

"We acknowledge that this road has deteriorated to a point that is not acceptable to the Department or the community," the statement said.

Mid Murray Council chief executive officer Andrew Johnson said the council had received multiple community complaints about Ridley Road.

He said the council was in discussions with the state government about the quality of local roads and had questions about their future as conversations about a Greater Adelaide Freight Bypass continue.

"The proposal to get the freight off of the freeway is to send it through that road," Dr Johnson said.

"Unfortunately it's just not up to it in its current condition, and that's beyond the potholes — it needs to be widened, it needs to be made safer, it needs to be strengthened."

Andrew Johnson says the council is engaging with the state government about the road network. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

Safety above rules

Safety concerns about South Australian roads are not new.

Motorists in the Yorke Peninsula and South East have been calling for an urgent fix to a multi-billion dollar maintenance backlog since 2023.

Earlier this year, the ABC also reported several sections of major highways in the state, including parts of the Sturt Highway, were given the lowest possible safety rating by the Australian Road Assessment Program.

Mr Smith said Ridley Road was one of many in his region that need more than a "bandaid" fix.

Paul Smith says Ridley Road is not the only one that needs urgent repairs in regional SA. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

"I can't even go down the freeway in the left-hand lane anymore on the motorbike. The ruts are too bad," he said.

"I've gotten to the stage now where I don't care about our road rules. I will ride on the part of the road that's safe.

"If that means me riding on the wrong side of the road, I'm still going to do it. That's safer than taking our lives in our hands with these potholes."

World.title: Close to a dozen new stations mapped out for Sydney uncovered by opposition
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The locations of close to a dozen new stations have been mapped out as the state government considers potential metro and heavy rail extensions around Western Sydney.

In the north-west, the potential stations include Emerton, Bidwell, Marsden Park and Schofields.

In the south-west, they include suburbs like Maryland, Pondicherry and Oran Park.

The map detailing potential new metro stations was obtained by the state opposition. (Supplied: Sydney Metro)

The map was obtained by the state opposition, as part of a parliamentary order for government documents.

The Minns government has already set aside $40 million for a business case to assess the feasibility of extending the Western Sydney Airport Metro in a northerly direction from St Marys to Tallawong, via Marsden Park and Schofields.

The federal and state governments have also jointly committed $100 million for another business case to assess southerly rail extensions, linking the new airport with Campbelltown and Leppington.

The documents shed new light on the potential routes for each extension. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

While business cases themselves remain confidential, the map released to the opposition sheds new light on the potential routes each extension could take.

Shadow Transport Minister Natalie Ward said she was "excited" to have uncovered the map.

"We've uncovered the document that's been sitting on [Transport Minister] John Graham's desk for months.

" I think he should be excited too and become clear about what his plan is [and] what Labor will do for Western Sydney. "

A mixture of metro and heavy rail

The map shows a northerly extension from St Marys to Tallawong, where the existing metro currently terminates.

It plots out stations at Emerton, Bidwell, Marsden Park and Schofields along the way.

The heavy rail already passes through Schofields, providing an ideal interchange between modes of transport.

In the north-west, the potential stations include Emerton, Bidwill, Marsden Park and Schofields. (Supplied)

In the south-west, potential stations include suburbs like Maryland, Pondicherry and Oran Park. (Supplied)

The map shows a potential southerly extension would connect Bradfield to Campbelltown, with stops at Bradfield South, Maryland, Pondicherry, Oran Park, Narellan, Mount Annan and Macarthur.

Bradfield South could also be connected to Leppington via a heavy rail link, with a single stop at Rossmore.

The suburb of Schofields has been flagged for a potential metro station. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

Sloane vows to 'build another metro'

Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane said Sydneysiders would get another metro, if they elected a Coalition government.

"I will build another metro and I will plan for future infrastructure in our city," she told 2GB.

While she previously vowed to "progress" a new metro in the city's south-west, Ms Sloane said the opposition was still open to the northern extension between St Marys and Tallawong.

"We've got to make a choice about north and south," she said.

"We need to look at the business case and make a decision."

Kellie Sloane has vowed to build another metro. (ABC News: Gavin Coote)

To pay for it, she previously said the Coalition would seek a new "city deal" from the federal government to fund infrastructure.

While speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Ms Ward was asked whether the Coalition would be prepared to privatise a state asset to pay for a metro, should such a deal not materialise.

"We'll be very clear at the election what our commitments are," she said.

Government managing expectations

Transport Minister John Graham said the government would consider the business cases and make its position clear in "future months".

However, he said the government would not announce any transport plans it could not afford.

"If we put a plan to the public, it will be one we can pay for, and it won't have privatisation," he said.

" I'm very unclear as to whether the opposition in its comments today is for or against privatisation. "

John Graham said the government is focusing on infrastructure it can afford. (ABC News: Nick Dole)

He said the government was focused on progressing construction of Sydney Metro West — connecting Westmead with the CBD — as well as the Western Sydney Airport Metro, which would not be ready in time for the first passenger flights in October.

An opening date for the Sydney Metro extension to Bankstown is expected to be announced in the coming weeks.

"We will have room for future transport projects," Mr Graham said.

"But we're not going to do that lightly [and] we're going to not do that quickly. We will step through it in an orderly manner."

World.title: ABC watchdog finds litany of failings at Four Corners
World.content:
Breaking BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing ABC watchdog finds litany of failings at Four Corners Calum Jaspan Updated September 22, 2026 — 5:25pm ,first published 4:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The ABC’s flagship investigative program Four Corners had a culture that favoured limiting knowledge about anonymous sources, fell short on fact-checking and had inadequate upward referral processes, its independent ombudsman has found. The ombudsman’s report into Cocaine Nation and Meth Highway, two episodes fronted by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal, was released on Tuesday afternoon and found the programs failed to meet the ABC’s editorial standards for accuracy, fair and honest dealing and independence and integrity. Mahmood Fazal reporting for the ABC’s Four Corners program in South-East Asia. “The breaches were the result of a combination of factors,” the report reads. “These include management’s failure to properly interrogate, inadequate upward referral, a culture that favoured limiting knowledge about sources given perceived risks, insufficient verification and fact-checking, and a failure to provide the audience with the context necessary to assess the reliability of the information presented.” The two episodes examined by the ombudsman featured the same man who was first depicted as a former drug addict in recovery and then as an active methamphetamine dealer whose identity was hidden from the audience.



Fazal has denied any wrongdoing and insisted that his stories went through the program’s standard editorial checks. “They just keep going on attacking me, my work, my sources, and apparently I’m the one that’s betrayed the ABC?” Fazal said on social media in July. The former bikie turned star reporter was sacked by the ABC in May over a separate incident in which he launched an external podcast which featured online gambling advertising without receiving the proper approvals. The ombudsman was scathing of how Four Corners and Fazal handled information about Aitken. Important information relating to anonymous, disguised and confidential sources involved in criminal activity was either not verified or not disclosed to audiences, the ombudsman said. “As a result, audiences were given a misleading impression of who key contributors were, the basis on which the ABC was relying on them and the level of confidence that could reasonably be placed in their claims,” the ombudsman said.



The ombudsman made a number of recommendations, including implementing stricter standards relating to the use of anonymous sources, improved approval and fact-checking processes and editorial oversight of high-risk stories. Her report called for a further investigation into both programs and their use of anonymous sources, which is already underway. Related Article Inside Story

ABC The artist, the ex-bikie and a scandal at the ABC that won’t end The ABC removed the two episodes in July after its news division conducted its own, separate investigation. A third Four Corners episode fronted by Fazal was later removed along with several other stories, including from investigative audio program Background Briefing. All senior ABC staff in the chain of command above Fazal at the time the episodes aired have since left. New Four Corners boss Joel Tozer overhauled the program’s standards when he took control earlier this year. An ABC spokesperson said the board had requested the ombudsman’s investigation into the two episodes.



“Both programs have now been removed from ABC platforms and the ABC has published a correction, acknowledging that aspects of the programs were materially misleading,” the spokesperson said. “To ensure the ABC’s editorial standards are met in future, the Ombudsman has made a number of recommendations. The ABC accepts the recommendations in full and has begun implementing them. “The ombudsman’s recommendations will strengthen the ABC’s editorial processes.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion.
