World.title: Jetstar staff to stop charging baggage and seat fees in union protest
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Jetstar staff to stop charging baggage and seat fees in union protest Chris Zappone September 22, 2026 — 5:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Weeks after Jetstar unveiled a controversial new fee to slug passengers for access to overhead bins, staff will refuse to charge for extras in an act of protest. The Australian Services Union said that on Wednesday, its members “will waive, or record as zero dollars, a range of sales-related fees that would ordinarily apply, including excess baggage charges, seat changes, late fees and other sales transactions”. Jetstar last month announced a new fee for using overhead baggage bins. The low-cost subsidiary of Qantas will forgo fee revenue during one of its busiest periods of the year, the ASU said, noting that the action coincides with the first week of the Victorian and Queensland school holidays, and days ahead of the AFL Grand Final in Melbourne. The protected industrial action will start at 12.01 am on Wednesday September 23 and continue until midnight on Thursday.



ASU-covered staff will continue to assist passengers as normal during this action, although staff won’t charge extra fees, the union said. Related Article Aviation Jetstar halves number of carry-on items customers are allowed “Our members are still turning up to look after passengers, but they won’t be collecting extra fees on Jetstar’s behalf until Jetstar shows that it is serious about its workforce,” said ASU National Assistant Secretary, Scott Cowen. The action comes less than two months after Jetstar turned heads by announcing a first-in-Australia charge for priority access to overhead bins. A Jetstar spokesperson said the airline continues “to meet with the ASU and are committed to working constructively towards an outcome”.



“We have plans in place so that there will be no impact to our operations as a result of the planned industrial action.” Flying on Jetstar? Wednesday may be a good day to dodge some fees. iStock The ASU is bargaining for wage increases, better morning shift penalties and overtime payments, and improved sick and personal leave, among other things. The new priority carry-on fees would start at $25, ranging from that cost for a one-way Launceston to Sydney flight up to $52 from Cairns to Tokyo. Inspired by European low-cost carrier Ryanair, Jetstar customers paying the new overhead compartment fee also would get priority access by being allowed to board the plane first.



Jetstar’s new policy begins for flights departing after February 2, 2027. Jetstar said it had put a “comprehensive and fair offer” on the table that includes pay increases, better penalty payments and allowances, and rostering flexibility. “This is a great package for our people which also allows us to keep investing in our fleet and grow our network while keeping fares low, despite escalating fuel costs impacting the industry.“ The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: Tech stocks lead ASX higher after Wall Street surge; oil snaps losing run
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets Tech stocks lead ASX higher after Wall Street surge; oil snaps losing run Staff writers Updated September 22, 2026 — 5:10pm ,first published September 22, 2026 — 5:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket advanced on Tuesday, led by tech stocks after an AI-fuelled rally on Wall Street, even as oil prices ended their four-day drop during the session. The S&P/ASX 200 finished 25.90 points, or 0.3 per cent, higher at 8757.80, with seven of its 11 sectors in the green. The gains came after the benchmark index closed flat on Monday. The Australian dollar was steady at US71.16¢. Easing oil prices and bonds yields brought relief to markets. Bloomberg Tech stocks led the session’s gains after America’s tech-focused Nasdaq index hit a record overnight, with chip stocks and other companies in the artificial-intelligence industry leading the way. AI chip giant Nvidia climbed 2.3 per cent and Advanced Micro Devices rallied 9.9 per cent. Tech leaders have recently warned a slowdown is needed in AI’s development for the safety of humanity. Yet even if the industry leans into more measures for safety, some analysts say it will still be hungry for chips to power it all. Early signs of success for Meta’s new artificial intelligence agent Muse underlined the bullishness around demand for the chips needed to power such agents.



Of the local tech names, software giants WiseTech Global and Xero climbed 2.9 per cent and 1.6 per cent, respectively. AI data centre operator NextDC jumped 3.8 per cent, and digital networks operator Megaport gained 4.3 per cent. Family tracking app Life 360 rose 2.9 per cent. Related Article Exclusive

Telecommunications ‘I’d love to see more of it’: Telstra backs data centre boom amid backlash The tech rally extended into real estate investment trusts, where AI data centre landlord Goodman Group, the nation’s largest property stock, climbed 1.4 per cent. The mining heavyweights were also higher, albeit at a more moderate pace. Iron ore and copper giants BHP and Rio Tinto were up 0.7 per cent and 0.1 per cent as the red metal advanced for a sixth day toward a record as falling inventories and pre-Christmas season buying signalled tightening supplies in China’s physical market. WA mineral explorer Global Lithium Resources’ share price soared 49.6 per cent to $1 after the company said it agreed to be taken over by United Arab Emirates-based Titan Lithium for $1.15 a share, valuing it at $333 million.



The ASX’s overall gains continued even as oil ticked higher again after four days of losses, with traders weighing Middle East supply risks against a diplomatic push to end the US-Iran war. Brent rose toward $US102 a barrel after tumbling by nearly 8 per cent over the previous four sessions. While that was much higher than its roughly $US72 price earlier this year, it’s down from the nearly $US110 it touched last week. President Donald Trump is set to address the United Nations General Assembly in New York later on Tuesday EST, and may meet with his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, on the sidelines. In addition, the US president will host a summit with China’s leader Xi Jinping this week. “Investors will be watching for any progress on the diplomatic front as President Trump meets with Presidents Pezeshkian and Xi,” said Hamad Hussain, senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics. However, it is not guaranteed the talks will result in tangible progress given how far apart the US and Iran remain in their demands, he added. Supply risks in the Middle East remain acute, with a tanker reportedly struck in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations. Meanwhile, satellite data has shown Saudi Arabia’s observed loadings from inside the Persian Gulf have jumped, suggesting the kingdom has shifted exports back toward the waterway after the shutdown of a key cross-country pipeline.



Related Article Opinion

Oil ‘Stop the bleeding’? A Trump move to stop the diesel spike could hurt all of us Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The oil rebound had yet to filter into energy stocks, which declined on the back of its four-day slump. Oil major Woodside fell 2.4 per cent and Santos dropped 1.4 per cent, while refiners Ampol and Viva Energy swung into the green and closed up 2.4 per cent and 0.9 per cent, respectively. Airlines still enjoyed a boost from the price reprieve, with Qantas and Virgin Australia both up 1.8 per cent. Amid the renewed risk-on sentiment, defensive sectors such as utilities and consumer staples struggled in Tuesday’s session. Origin Energy slumped 4 per cent and AGL dropped 2.3 per cent. Supermarket chain Woolworths dropped 0.5 per cent and Coles was flat. Discretionary consumer stocks blossomed, with Wesfarmers up 0.8 per cent, pokies maker Aristocrat up 2.3 per cent and fashion jewellery chain Lovisa up 4.5 per cent. The financial sector was mixed, with Commonwealth Bank dropping 0.4 per cent, National Australia Bank down 0.3 per cent and Westpac down 0.1 per cent, while ANZ Bank rose 0.3 per cent.



Overnight on Wall Street, the S&P 500 jumped 1.5 per cent and pulled within 0.4 per cent of its record set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.7 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite leaped 2.3 per cent. While market worries remain about how much oil is available for customers worldwide, ING commodities strategists wrote in a commentary on Monday that profit-taking by investors after the recent jump in oil prices, together with hopes for discussions at this week’s UN General Assembly and at a meeting between China’s and America’s leaders, helped improve optimism. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said following talks on Sunday with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng that the US had “a very successful engagement” with the Chinese side. In Beijing, China’s Foreign Ministry on Monday confirmed that Xi Jinping will pay a state visit to the US between September 23 and 25. Experts and policymakers believe trade, tariffs and AI safety are likely to be discussed. Skydance-owned Paramount fell 2.9 per cent as it reached a settlement in lawsuits brought by 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild trade union challenging its $US110 billion ($154 billion) acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, which jumped 10.8 per cent.



Related Article Petrol prices Pain at the pump: Saudi oil shock sends Australian fuel prices surging The parties worked through the weekend to reach the deal, which includes protections designed to limit the market power and ensure the editorial independence of the media giant, which will control two of Hollywood’s biggest studios, two major subscription streaming services and dozens of TV channels ranging from CBS to HBO. Paramount has promised to release 30 movies a year at the combined studios, a move designed to placate cinema owners and Hollywood talent who believed the merger would reduce film output. Under the terms of the deal, half of those films must be produced by the new company. with AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial as it happened: Former NSW Police officer says he acted in self-defence as trial continues over alleged murders of Jesse Baird, Luke Davies
World.content:
Thank you for reading our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial in the NSW Supreme Court.

The former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Sydney couple Jesse Baird, 26, and Luke Davies, 29, in the eastern suburbs on February 19, 2024. His criminal trial started in the historic King Street court complex on Monday.

Beau Lamarre-Condon (left) is accused of murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies.

The Crown alleges Lamarre-Condon planned to kill Baird after developing an obsessive and jealous infatuation with him following a casual romantic relationship, and killed Davies spontaneously to eliminate a witness to the crime.

Today, Lamarre-Condon’s barrister, John Stratton, SC, outlined the defence case in his opening address.

He said that Lamarre-Condon went to Baird’s home on February 19, 2024, to collect his belongings, including jewellery, and was disguised as an Uber Eats rider because he didn’t want to “go through the embarrassment” of seeing Baird.

Stratton said Lamarre-Condon entered the home when nobody answered his knock at the door and was “surprised by Jesse Baird”, who “understandably did not recognise him because he was still wearing the motorcycle helmet”.

The defence case is that the two men struggled and Lamarre-Condon’s police gun went off twice and fatally wounded Baird.

In the alleged struggle, the gun was “flung into the loungeroom”, Stratton said, and the accused picked up a mobile phone and started ringing Triple Zero.

He encountered a second man, Davies, and “Mr Davies was now holding the gun”, the defence said. Stratton said Lamarre-Condon “grabbed Mr Davies by the arm and pushed the gun away from himself and towards Mr Davies”.

The defence said that in the struggle that followed Davies “pulled the trigger and fatally shot himself”.

Stratton said that Lamarre-Condon had entered Baird’s home on an earlier occasion in August 2023 using a key that Baird had given him. Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to aggravated break and entry to Baird’s home and stealing Baird’s wallet and phone.

Baird’s mother Helen choked back tears on Tuesday afternoon as she gave evidence about her close relationship with her son and his blossoming relationship with Davies.

She said there was a problem with Baird’s vehicle when he visited her in Victoria over Christmas 2023. “It turned out there’d been water poured into the fuel tank,” she said.

The Crown has foreshadowed the court will hear Lamarre-Condon asked a friend “what would happen if someone added water to a diesel engine”.

Baird’s sister Kourtnee testified that Baird told her he was afraid of the accused in December 2023.

“Jesse said that he was fearful that he was a NSW police officer, he had access to a weapon, a gun, he said that he would go on his phone and block contacts from Jesse’s male friends,” she said.

World.title: The day the music died at the NRL grand final? Say it ain’t so
World.content:
CultureMusicNRL grand final Opinion The day the music died at the NRL grand final? Say it ain’t so Robert Moran Spectrum deputy editor September 22, 2026 — 5:00pm

September 22, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This year’s NRL grand final will be as uncomfortably silent as Sunday dinner with your family. For the first time since the NRL’s inception in 1998, the big game – to be held at Accor Stadium on October 4 – will have no pre-game entertainment. What is this, Footloose? How did we get here? Apparently the NRL lowballed their first choice, British pop angel Olivia Dean, and then floundered in their negotiations with local hitmaker Tones and I. Tones and I performing at the 2019 AFL grand final. Getty I guess the thousands of fans who already bought tickets to the game are just supposed to pack their Bluetooth speakers? For the NRL, it’s an embarrassing development. The pre-game show is one of the grand final’s lasting memories. We all remember where we were when Tina Turner belted out The Best at the Broncos-Dragons decider in 1993, or that other year when that other big-name artist and/or band did that other thing (sorry, my memory’s shot from ageing).



Locals like to lampoon American sports’ penchant for over-the-top glitz and glamour, but at least they have the right spirit. It’s a belief that their game is important and worthy of celebrating. Have some pride in your product, NRL! You can’t treat the game’s biggest day with the casual indifference of your 24th wedding anniversary. It’s especially humiliating considering the AFL – a sport where players spend 80 minutes struggling to pick up a ball – has living icon Kylie Minogue opening their grand final at the MCG on Saturday (and G Flip as a reserve), and the NFL just shipped the Jonas Bros all the way to Melbourne for an inconsequential season opener earlier this month. Kylie Minogue will lead the AFL grand final entertainment this Saturday. That the NRL couldn’t book an act despite recently striking a goldmine deal with Nine and Foxtel worth $5.3 billion from 2028 until 2034 is also galling. Where’s all that money going to? Johnathan Thurston’s array of sideline coats? It also feels like a missed opportunity since there’s no shortage of international pop acts touring Australia at the moment. Beyond Dean, the likes of Lily Allen, Hilary Duff, Zara Larsson, even Ben Folds, are in town. Imagine the viral potential of pop-boy Conan Grey (also currently touring) belting Vodka Cranberry, his dramatic anthem of gay yearning, in front of a stadium of frenzied Panthers fans?



Since I’ve also read that NRL chairman Peter V’landys is apparently not a fan of spending money on “entertainment” (not sure what he considers rugby league – art?), it should be noted that there are alternatives to the big-name international headliner. It’s called “supporting Australian music”. At a time when festivals are folding and touring has never been more expensive for up-and-coming acts, where local artists are battling the scourge of AI in music, a platform as large as the NRL grand final is a valuable opportunity. Superstar Australian DJ Dom Dolla is coming to town. Why not give him a call? Think of all the local bands and artists who would benefit from being named as the final’s pre-game headliner, endure weeks of being pilloried by Murdoch media for their “woke agenda” and/or “controversial lyrics”, and come through the other side convincing everyone that “Hey, they weren’t that bad”? It’s a rite of passage for Australian musicians. Unlike V’landys, I won’t give up. There are still a couple of weeks until the big day; surely we can muster something together? Big names like Kevin Parker and Ninajirachi and Dom Dolla are in town and on tour; other brilliant locals like Jem Cassar-Daley, Sidney Phillips, Larissa Lambert and Briggs (now in hardcore version) have just released new albums that could use the promotional push of a grand final slot.

World.title: Beloved author and illustrator Terry Denton dies aged 76
World.content:
CultureBooksVale Beloved author and illustrator Terry Denton dies aged 76 Staff reporter September 22, 2026 — 4:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beloved illustrator and author Terry Denton, famed for the 13-Storey Treehouse series co-written with Andy Griffiths, has died aged 76. In a post to social media his literary agency Curtis Brown and publishers Pan Macmillan shared the news: “Terry died surrounded by his family on Monday [September 21].” Author Terry Denton in his studio in Mornington. Mario Borg Based in Victoria, Denton was best known for his Gasp! series, which was adapted for television, as well as the Treehouse books, co-written with Griffiths – the current Australian Children’s Laureate – over the course of three decades. He also designed the puppets for Australian television series Lift Off, including the iconic EC doll. His work garnered awards across his long career, starting with the Children’s Book Council of Australia Picture Book of the Year Award in 1986 for Felix and Alexander. As an illustrator he worked with other authors including Mem Fox, Paul Jennings, Alison Lloyd and Gillian Rubinstein.



Griffiths, Denton’s frequent collaborator, said: “Working – and playing – with Terry over three decades has been an incredible honour and a pure delight. I’ve never laughed so hard as I did when working with him, whether in the writing room or on stage. He was a true clown and much beloved – both in real life and as a character in the Treehouse series. Jill and I will miss him greatly.” The statement from his agency and publisher included tributes from his children. “Dad gave joy to millions of children around the world and after all those stories and all those live he touched, he always came home to us. “We are so grateful that his stories will continue to live on, bringing wonder, laughter and comfort to generations yet to come – and most especially to his beloved grandchildren, who will grow up knowing him through the magic he left behind.”



Denton is survived by his wife Kristen, his children Max, Imogen and Eve, and his grandchildren Georgia, Lucy, Charlie, Alfie and Felix. The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: ‘We know what’s coming’: Wallabies brace for physical examination against Springboks
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies ‘We know what’s coming’: Wallabies brace for physical examination against Springboks Jonathan Drennan September 22, 2026 — 4:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Wallabies are preparing for world champions South Africa to be at their best this Sunday in Perth despite Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus’ admission that his team are likely to be “a little bit punch-drunk” after a gruelling four Test series against New Zealand. Wallabies forwards coach Tom Donnelly understands that while the Springboks may rotate players, their tactics should remain consistent: seeking to dominate an opposition forward pack physically. Taniela Tupou training with the Wallabies. Getty Images “We know the scrum’s going to be a big part of the game, we know they’re going to maul,” Donnelly said. “No matter who they pick, they’ve got probably two or three packs that are very, very class.



“It’s all just a matter of focusing on ourselves, we know what we need to do to front up and go out there with a bit of an attacking mindset against them ... we know what’s coming. “If we can front up there physically and then be accurate with how we want to execute, then that will give us a chance to match up with them.” Wallabies scrummage against South Africa last August in Johannesburg. AP Wallabies prop Taniela Tupou has faced South Africa nine times, winning five Tests. Having experienced the pleasure and pain of playing the world champions, Tupou understands he cannot shoulder the responsibility of winning the physical battles alone. “It’s not just me, it’s us as a group, as a forward pack. Obviously, I can’t go out there and do it on my own, so I rely on everybody to do their job and myself to do my job. It’s a bit different coming against the Springboks,” Tupou said.



“Ox [Springboks loosehead prop Ox Nche] is such a good scrummager, they’re so strong, so if it’s me or Allan [Alaalatoa] or Zane [Nonggorr] whoever’s at tighthead prop, they have to be at their best because if you don’t, you know what’s going to happen.” On Friday, Erasmus confirmed his players were tired and plans had been made to ensure they could deploy as fresh a team as possible in Perth. Rassie Erasmus and the Springboks have been staying on the Central Coast this week. Getty Images “Anybody who plays four games against New Zealand will be a little bit punch-drunk at the end,” he said. “That’s why prior to the New Zealand series we had the Nations Championship games, we really rotated a lot. And in the Argentinian game we had to gamble a little bit, keeping players behind and we almost lost that match.” If selected on Sunday, Tupou, who plays for French domestic club Racing 92, will play his last game for the Wallabies until the spring tour in November, due to October’s Bledisloe Cup Tests falling outside World Rugby’s regulation 9, which covers the mandatory release of players by clubs for Test rugby.



Another perspective Australian rugby ‘He’s made it look easy’: Springboks rival blown away by Suaalii’s rugby transition Tupou said he hasn’t brought up playing for the Wallabies in November against England, Scotland and Wales, but is hopeful of being available if selected. “As you get a bit older you realise that one of these camps will be your last, it does mean a little bit more to me [to represent the Wallabies],” Tupou said. “I’m just enjoying it and I haven’t spoken to Les [Kiss] about what the future looks like. “I’m hoping this is not the last time, hopefully I’ll see the team in the UK.”



Brumbies back rower Charlie Cale has been replaced in the Wallabies squad by the Force’s Nick Champion de Crespigny after his shoulder partially dislocated in training in Perth. Donnelly is confident Cale can make a full recovery and return to Super Rugby next season. “He’s still a young man, he’s still got a massive future ahead of him,” Donnelly said. “A little bit of a silver lining is if it needs to be repaired [Cale’s shoulder], it can get fixed and he can hit the ground running the Super Rugby next year and give himself a great run in to being available for the World Cup.” South Africa are due to name their team on Wednesday at 6.30pm [AEST] with breakaway Pieter-Steph du Toit and centre Damian de Allende both being rested after playing all four Tests against New Zealand. More to come

World.title: ABC watchdog finds litany of failings at Four Corners
World.content:
Breaking BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing ABC watchdog finds litany of failings at Four Corners Calum Jaspan Updated September 22, 2026 — 5:25pm ,first published 4:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The ABC’s flagship investigative program Four Corners had a culture that favoured limiting knowledge about anonymous sources, fell short on fact-checking and had inadequate upward referral processes, its independent ombudsman has found. The ombudsman’s report into Cocaine Nation and Meth Highway, two episodes fronted by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal, was released on Tuesday afternoon and found the programs failed to meet the ABC’s editorial standards for accuracy, fair and honest dealing and independence and integrity. Mahmood Fazal reporting for the ABC’s Four Corners program in South-East Asia. “The breaches were the result of a combination of factors,” the report reads. “These include management’s failure to properly interrogate, inadequate upward referral, a culture that favoured limiting knowledge about sources given perceived risks, insufficient verification and fact-checking, and a failure to provide the audience with the context necessary to assess the reliability of the information presented.” The two episodes examined by the ombudsman featured the same man who was first depicted as a former drug addict in recovery and then as an active methamphetamine dealer whose identity was hidden from the audience.



Fazal has denied any wrongdoing and insisted that his stories went through the program’s standard editorial checks. “They just keep going on attacking me, my work, my sources, and apparently I’m the one that’s betrayed the ABC?” Fazal said on social media in July. The former bikie turned star reporter was sacked by the ABC in May over a separate incident in which he launched an external podcast which featured online gambling advertising without receiving the proper approvals. The ombudsman was scathing of how Four Corners and Fazal handled information about Aitken. Important information relating to anonymous, disguised and confidential sources involved in criminal activity was either not verified or not disclosed to audiences, the ombudsman said. “As a result, audiences were given a misleading impression of who key contributors were, the basis on which the ABC was relying on them and the level of confidence that could reasonably be placed in their claims,” the ombudsman said.



The ombudsman made a number of recommendations, including implementing stricter standards relating to the use of anonymous sources, improved approval and fact-checking processes and editorial oversight of high-risk stories. Her report called for a further investigation into both programs and their use of anonymous sources, which is already underway. Related Article Inside Story

ABC The artist, the ex-bikie and a scandal at the ABC that won’t end The ABC removed the two episodes in July after its news division conducted its own, separate investigation. A third Four Corners episode fronted by Fazal was later removed along with several other stories, including from investigative audio program Background Briefing. All senior ABC staff in the chain of command above Fazal at the time the episodes aired have since left. New Four Corners boss Joel Tozer overhauled the program’s standards when he took control earlier this year. An ABC spokesperson said the board had requested the ombudsman’s investigation into the two episodes.



“Both programs have now been removed from ABC platforms and the ABC has published a correction, acknowledging that aspects of the programs were materially misleading,” the spokesperson said. “To ensure the ABC’s editorial standards are met in future, the Ombudsman has made a number of recommendations. The ABC accepts the recommendations in full and has begun implementing them. “The ombudsman’s recommendations will strengthen the ABC’s editorial processes.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: Jetstar staff to stop charging baggage and seat fees in union protest
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Jetstar staff to stop charging baggage and seat fees in union protest Chris Zappone September 22, 2026 — 5:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Weeks after Jetstar unveiled a controversial new fee to slug passengers for access to overhead bins, staff will refuse to charge for extras in an act of protest. The Australian Services Union said that on Wednesday, its members “will waive, or record as zero dollars, a range of sales-related fees that would ordinarily apply, including excess baggage charges, seat changes, late fees and other sales transactions”. Jetstar last month announced a new fee for using overhead baggage bins. The low-cost subsidiary of Qantas will forgo fee revenue during one of its busiest periods of the year, the ASU said, noting that the action coincides with the first week of the Victorian and Queensland school holidays, and days ahead of the AFL Grand Final in Melbourne. The protected industrial action will start at 12.01 am on Wednesday September 23 and continue until midnight on Thursday.



ASU-covered staff will continue to assist passengers as normal during this action, although staff won’t charge extra fees, the union said. Related Article Aviation Jetstar halves number of carry-on items customers are allowed “Our members are still turning up to look after passengers, but they won’t be collecting extra fees on Jetstar’s behalf until Jetstar shows that it is serious about its workforce,” said ASU National Assistant Secretary, Scott Cowen. The action comes less than two months after Jetstar turned heads by announcing a first-in-Australia charge for priority access to overhead bins. A Jetstar spokesperson said the airline continues “to meet with the ASU and are committed to working constructively towards an outcome”.



“We have plans in place so that there will be no impact to our operations as a result of the planned industrial action.” Flying on Jetstar? Wednesday may be a good day to dodge some fees. iStock The ASU is bargaining for wage increases, better morning shift penalties and overtime payments, and improved sick and personal leave, among other things. The new priority carry-on fees would start at $25, ranging from that cost for a one-way Launceston to Sydney flight up to $52 from Cairns to Tokyo. Inspired by European low-cost carrier Ryanair, Jetstar customers paying the new overhead compartment fee also would get priority access by being allowed to board the plane first.



Jetstar’s new policy begins for flights departing after February 2, 2027. Jetstar said it had put a “comprehensive and fair offer” on the table that includes pay increases, better penalty payments and allowances, and rostering flexibility. “This is a great package for our people which also allows us to keep investing in our fleet and grow our network while keeping fares low, despite escalating fuel costs impacting the industry.“ The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: Tech stocks lead ASX higher after Wall Street surge; oil snaps losing run
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets Tech stocks lead ASX higher after Wall Street surge; oil snaps losing run Staff writers Updated September 22, 2026 — 5:10pm ,first published September 22, 2026 — 5:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket advanced on Tuesday, led by tech stocks after an AI-fuelled rally on Wall Street, even as oil prices ended their four-day drop during the session. The S&P/ASX 200 finished 25.90 points, or 0.3 per cent, higher at 8757.80, with seven of its 11 sectors in the green. The gains came after the benchmark index closed flat on Monday. The Australian dollar was steady at US71.16¢. Easing oil prices and bonds yields brought relief to markets. Bloomberg Tech stocks led the session’s gains after America’s tech-focused Nasdaq index hit a record overnight, with chip stocks and other companies in the artificial-intelligence industry leading the way. AI chip giant Nvidia climbed 2.3 per cent and Advanced Micro Devices rallied 9.9 per cent. Tech leaders have recently warned a slowdown is needed in AI’s development for the safety of humanity. Yet even if the industry leans into more measures for safety, some analysts say it will still be hungry for chips to power it all. Early signs of success for Meta’s new artificial intelligence agent Muse underlined the bullishness around demand for the chips needed to power such agents.



Of the local tech names, software giants WiseTech Global and Xero climbed 2.9 per cent and 1.6 per cent, respectively. AI data centre operator NextDC jumped 3.8 per cent, and digital networks operator Megaport gained 4.3 per cent. Family tracking app Life 360 rose 2.9 per cent. Related Article Exclusive

Telecommunications ‘I’d love to see more of it’: Telstra backs data centre boom amid backlash The tech rally extended into real estate investment trusts, where AI data centre landlord Goodman Group, the nation’s largest property stock, climbed 1.4 per cent. The mining heavyweights were also higher, albeit at a more moderate pace. Iron ore and copper giants BHP and Rio Tinto were up 0.7 per cent and 0.1 per cent as the red metal advanced for a sixth day toward a record as falling inventories and pre-Christmas season buying signalled tightening supplies in China’s physical market. WA mineral explorer Global Lithium Resources’ share price soared 49.6 per cent to $1 after the company said it agreed to be taken over by United Arab Emirates-based Titan Lithium for $1.15 a share, valuing it at $333 million.



The ASX’s overall gains continued even as oil ticked higher again after four days of losses, with traders weighing Middle East supply risks against a diplomatic push to end the US-Iran war. Brent rose toward $US102 a barrel after tumbling by nearly 8 per cent over the previous four sessions. While that was much higher than its roughly $US72 price earlier this year, it’s down from the nearly $US110 it touched last week. President Donald Trump is set to address the United Nations General Assembly in New York later on Tuesday EST, and may meet with his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, on the sidelines. In addition, the US president will host a summit with China’s leader Xi Jinping this week. “Investors will be watching for any progress on the diplomatic front as President Trump meets with Presidents Pezeshkian and Xi,” said Hamad Hussain, senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics. However, it is not guaranteed the talks will result in tangible progress given how far apart the US and Iran remain in their demands, he added. Supply risks in the Middle East remain acute, with a tanker reportedly struck in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations. Meanwhile, satellite data has shown Saudi Arabia’s observed loadings from inside the Persian Gulf have jumped, suggesting the kingdom has shifted exports back toward the waterway after the shutdown of a key cross-country pipeline.



Related Article Opinion

Oil ‘Stop the bleeding’? A Trump move to stop the diesel spike could hurt all of us Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The oil rebound had yet to filter into energy stocks, which declined on the back of its four-day slump. Oil major Woodside fell 2.4 per cent and Santos dropped 1.4 per cent, while refiners Ampol and Viva Energy swung into the green and closed up 2.4 per cent and 0.9 per cent, respectively. Airlines still enjoyed a boost from the price reprieve, with Qantas and Virgin Australia both up 1.8 per cent. Amid the renewed risk-on sentiment, defensive sectors such as utilities and consumer staples struggled in Tuesday’s session. Origin Energy slumped 4 per cent and AGL dropped 2.3 per cent. Supermarket chain Woolworths dropped 0.5 per cent and Coles was flat. Discretionary consumer stocks blossomed, with Wesfarmers up 0.8 per cent, pokies maker Aristocrat up 2.3 per cent and fashion jewellery chain Lovisa up 4.5 per cent. The financial sector was mixed, with Commonwealth Bank dropping 0.4 per cent, National Australia Bank down 0.3 per cent and Westpac down 0.1 per cent, while ANZ Bank rose 0.3 per cent.



Overnight on Wall Street, the S&P 500 jumped 1.5 per cent and pulled within 0.4 per cent of its record set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.7 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite leaped 2.3 per cent. While market worries remain about how much oil is available for customers worldwide, ING commodities strategists wrote in a commentary on Monday that profit-taking by investors after the recent jump in oil prices, together with hopes for discussions at this week’s UN General Assembly and at a meeting between China’s and America’s leaders, helped improve optimism. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said following talks on Sunday with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng that the US had “a very successful engagement” with the Chinese side. In Beijing, China’s Foreign Ministry on Monday confirmed that Xi Jinping will pay a state visit to the US between September 23 and 25. Experts and policymakers believe trade, tariffs and AI safety are likely to be discussed. Skydance-owned Paramount fell 2.9 per cent as it reached a settlement in lawsuits brought by 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild trade union challenging its $US110 billion ($154 billion) acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, which jumped 10.8 per cent.



Related Article Petrol prices Pain at the pump: Saudi oil shock sends Australian fuel prices surging The parties worked through the weekend to reach the deal, which includes protections designed to limit the market power and ensure the editorial independence of the media giant, which will control two of Hollywood’s biggest studios, two major subscription streaming services and dozens of TV channels ranging from CBS to HBO. Paramount has promised to release 30 movies a year at the combined studios, a move designed to placate cinema owners and Hollywood talent who believed the merger would reduce film output. Under the terms of the deal, half of those films must be produced by the new company. with AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

Locals like to lampoon American sports’ penchant for over-the-top glitz and glamour, but at least they have the right spirit. It’s a belief that their game is important and worthy of celebrating. Have some pride in your product, NRL! You can’t treat the game’s biggest day with the casual indifference of your 24th wedding anniversary. It’s especially humiliating considering the AFL – a sport where players spend 80 minutes struggling to pick up a ball – has living icon Kylie Minogue opening their grand final at the MCG on Saturday (and G Flip as a reserve), and the NFL just shipped the Jonas Bros all the way to Melbourne for an inconsequential season opener earlier this month. Kylie Minogue will lead the AFL grand final entertainment this Saturday. That the NRL couldn’t book an act despite recently striking a goldmine deal with Nine and Foxtel worth $5.3 billion from 2028 until 2034 is also galling. Where’s all that money going to? Johnathan Thurston’s array of sideline coats? It also feels like a missed opportunity since there’s no shortage of international pop acts touring Australia at the moment. Beyond Dean, the likes of Lily Allen, Hilary Duff, Zara Larsson, even Ben Folds, are in town. Imagine the viral potential of pop-boy Conan Grey (also currently touring) belting Vodka Cranberry, his dramatic anthem of gay yearning, in front of a stadium of frenzied Panthers fans?



Since I’ve also read that NRL chairman Peter V’landys is apparently not a fan of spending money on “entertainment” (not sure what he considers rugby league – art?), it should be noted that there are alternatives to the big-name international headliner. It’s called “supporting Australian music”. At a time when festivals are folding and touring has never been more expensive for up-and-coming acts, where local artists are battling the scourge of AI in music, a platform as large as the NRL grand final is a valuable opportunity. Superstar Australian DJ Dom Dolla is coming to town. Why not give him a call? Think of all the local bands and artists who would benefit from being named as the final’s pre-game headliner, endure weeks of being pilloried by Murdoch media for their “woke agenda” and/or “controversial lyrics”, and come through the other side convincing everyone that “Hey, they weren’t that bad”? It’s a rite of passage for Australian musicians. Unlike V’landys, I won’t give up. There are still a couple of weeks until the big day; surely we can muster something together? Big names like Kevin Parker and Ninajirachi and Dom Dolla are in town and on tour; other brilliant locals like Jem Cassar-Daley, Sidney Phillips, Larissa Lambert and Briggs (now in hardcore version) have just released new albums that could use the promotional push of a grand final slot.

World.title: Beloved author and illustrator Terry Denton dies aged 76
World.content:
CultureBooksVale Beloved author and illustrator Terry Denton dies aged 76 Staff reporter September 22, 2026 — 4:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beloved illustrator and author Terry Denton, famed for the 13-Storey Treehouse series co-written with Andy Griffiths, has died aged 76. In a post to social media his literary agency Curtis Brown and publishers Pan Macmillan shared the news: “Terry died surrounded by his family on Monday [September 21].” Author Terry Denton in his studio in Mornington. Mario Borg Based in Victoria, Denton was best known for his Gasp! series, which was adapted for television, as well as the Treehouse books, co-written with Griffiths – the current Australian Children’s Laureate – over the course of three decades. He also designed the puppets for Australian television series Lift Off, including the iconic EC doll. His work garnered awards across his long career, starting with the Children’s Book Council of Australia Picture Book of the Year Award in 1986 for Felix and Alexander. As an illustrator he worked with other authors including Mem Fox, Paul Jennings, Alison Lloyd and Gillian Rubinstein.



Griffiths, Denton’s frequent collaborator, said: “Working – and playing – with Terry over three decades has been an incredible honour and a pure delight. I’ve never laughed so hard as I did when working with him, whether in the writing room or on stage. He was a true clown and much beloved – both in real life and as a character in the Treehouse series. Jill and I will miss him greatly.” The statement from his agency and publisher included tributes from his children. “Dad gave joy to millions of children around the world and after all those stories and all those live he touched, he always came home to us. “We are so grateful that his stories will continue to live on, bringing wonder, laughter and comfort to generations yet to come – and most especially to his beloved grandchildren, who will grow up knowing him through the magic he left behind.”



Denton is survived by his wife Kristen, his children Max, Imogen and Eve, and his grandchildren Georgia, Lucy, Charlie, Alfie and Felix. The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: ‘We know what’s coming’: Wallabies brace for physical examination against Springboks
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies ‘We know what’s coming’: Wallabies brace for physical examination against Springboks Jonathan Drennan September 22, 2026 — 4:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Wallabies are preparing for world champions South Africa to be at their best this Sunday in Perth despite Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus’ admission that his team are likely to be “a little bit punch-drunk” after a gruelling four Test series against New Zealand. Wallabies forwards coach Tom Donnelly understands that while the Springboks may rotate players, their tactics should remain consistent: seeking to dominate an opposition forward pack physically. Taniela Tupou training with the Wallabies. Getty Images “We know the scrum’s going to be a big part of the game, we know they’re going to maul,” Donnelly said. “No matter who they pick, they’ve got probably two or three packs that are very, very class.



“It’s all just a matter of focusing on ourselves, we know what we need to do to front up and go out there with a bit of an attacking mindset against them ... we know what’s coming. “If we can front up there physically and then be accurate with how we want to execute, then that will give us a chance to match up with them.” Wallabies scrummage against South Africa last August in Johannesburg. AP Wallabies prop Taniela Tupou has faced South Africa nine times, winning five Tests. Having experienced the pleasure and pain of playing the world champions, Tupou understands he cannot shoulder the responsibility of winning the physical battles alone. “It’s not just me, it’s us as a group, as a forward pack. Obviously, I can’t go out there and do it on my own, so I rely on everybody to do their job and myself to do my job. It’s a bit different coming against the Springboks,” Tupou said.



“Ox [Springboks loosehead prop Ox Nche] is such a good scrummager, they’re so strong, so if it’s me or Allan [Alaalatoa] or Zane [Nonggorr] whoever’s at tighthead prop, they have to be at their best because if you don’t, you know what’s going to happen.” On Friday, Erasmus confirmed his players were tired and plans had been made to ensure they could deploy as fresh a team as possible in Perth. Rassie Erasmus and the Springboks have been staying on the Central Coast this week. Getty Images “Anybody who plays four games against New Zealand will be a little bit punch-drunk at the end,” he said. “That’s why prior to the New Zealand series we had the Nations Championship games, we really rotated a lot. And in the Argentinian game we had to gamble a little bit, keeping players behind and we almost lost that match.” If selected on Sunday, Tupou, who plays for French domestic club Racing 92, will play his last game for the Wallabies until the spring tour in November, due to October’s Bledisloe Cup Tests falling outside World Rugby’s regulation 9, which covers the mandatory release of players by clubs for Test rugby.



Another perspective Australian rugby ‘He’s made it look easy’: Springboks rival blown away by Suaalii’s rugby transition Tupou said he hasn’t brought up playing for the Wallabies in November against England, Scotland and Wales, but is hopeful of being available if selected. “As you get a bit older you realise that one of these camps will be your last, it does mean a little bit more to me [to represent the Wallabies],” Tupou said. “I’m just enjoying it and I haven’t spoken to Les [Kiss] about what the future looks like. “I’m hoping this is not the last time, hopefully I’ll see the team in the UK.”



Brumbies back rower Charlie Cale has been replaced in the Wallabies squad by the Force’s Nick Champion de Crespigny after his shoulder partially dislocated in training in Perth. Donnelly is confident Cale can make a full recovery and return to Super Rugby next season. “He’s still a young man, he’s still got a massive future ahead of him,” Donnelly said. “A little bit of a silver lining is if it needs to be repaired [Cale’s shoulder], it can get fixed and he can hit the ground running the Super Rugby next year and give himself a great run in to being available for the World Cup.” South Africa are due to name their team on Wednesday at 6.30pm [AEST] with breakaway Pieter-Steph du Toit and centre Damian de Allende both being rested after playing all four Tests against New Zealand. More to come

World.title: Search to continue for missing 1978 plane after inconclusive object found in Lake Moeraki
World.content:
Search crews scouring a South Westland lake for a plane that disappeared in 1978 say an object sighted on Tuesday does not appear to be an aircraft.

The renewed search for flight ZK-EBU has brought relatives of its pilot and six passengers to the shores of Lake Moeraki north of Haast.

Coastguard, police and navy teams used sonar equipment to scan the lakebed on Tuesday, before divers took a closer look at a shape they had detected.

Senior Sergeant Mark Kirkwood, who was in charge of the operation, said it was worth looking at closely, but the divers were not confident it was an aircraft.

"After 47 years, we understand the significance of this moment for the families of the seven people who disappeared, some of whom are here today, and for everyone who has worked to find answers about what happened to them," he said.

"We will take time tomorrow to have a closer look."

Crews would undertake further analysis of sonar imaging on Wednesday and also search further into the lake, he said.

The renewed search followed decades of efforts by volunteer aviation investigators to find the plane, a Piper Cherokee 6.

Using his own sonar equipment, Hastings resident Gavin Grimmer detected an object in the lake earlier this year.

Westland mayor Helen Lash, who was also watching the search on Tuesday, said it was an emotional day for relatives of the people who vanished.

"They're hopeful, but it's a restrained hope because the worst fear is that it's not what we're hoping it might be," she said.

On Tuesday the search team deployed sonar equipment from a Coastguard boat, Katie Todd/RNZ

"If this means finding something that's been missing for some time and giving those families closure, that's amazing."

The plane had 28-year-old pilot Edward "Ned" Morrison, five members of the Dunedin-based Stuart family and 20-year-old David Hogg on board.

In the days after it disappeared, search crews scoured 2.1 million hectares of land but found no trace of the plane.

Fiordland's John von Tunzelman, who was involved in the search, told RNZ it was "most disappointing" to come up empty handed.

World.title: Health NZ reviewing clinics owned by Tararua Health Group after six staff resign in Pahīatua
World.content:
Audio player for " Public meetings held over dire staff of Tararua healthcare " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/health/1523068%2Fhealth-nz-reviewing-clinics-owned-by-tararua-health-group-after-six-staff-resign-in-pahiatua

Public meetings held over dire staff of Tararua healthcare Checkpoint Download MP3 11m

Health New Zealand is reviewing clinics owned by the Tararua Health Group, after staff raised concerns over unsafe workloads and delays.

Six staff at the Pahīatua Medical Centre resigned on Monday from the Tararua Health Group.

Health New Zealand's central region's director planning, funding and outcome Geoff Gwyn said the concerns were being taken seriously.

"I think we all understand that health care workers are passionate about what they do and the care they provide for their community, and I know that it would have been a difficult decision for them to resign."

But he said he still had confidence in the services provided by Tararua Health Group.

"I have confidence in all of the providers that we have working for us until proven otherwise."

As a result, he told Checkpoint, he was waiting on the findings of a review currently underway at Pahīatua Medical Centre to decide what action needed to be taken.

He said issues were most likely to lie in under-staffing and "clinical management".

He said an independent general practitioner and practice manager would deliver their findings by the end of the week.

Another audit, he announced, was being done at Dannevirke Hospital, which Tararua Health Group also ran.

Gwyn said an audit had been done in June, with no critical risks raised.

But he said after concerns raised by clinicians, who said they didn't feel comfortable referring patients there over safety risks, another audit was undertaken on Tuesday.

He denied publicity had influenced the decision.

"It's [because of] the genuine concerns expressed by clinicians around feeling that they are unable to place patients into that facility."

He added that he was not aware of any complaints being made about the services at Dannevirke.

Gwyn said to terminate a contract with a provider there had to be a clear risk to patients.

He said the resulting impacts on services for the community would also have to be considered.

Gwyn said he didn't think there was a conflict of interest with Mark Willis being the PHO's board director - which managed contracts for health providers - as well as the chief executive of OmniHealth, which owned Tararua Health Group.

"Obviously service delivery is often done by private businesses. General practitioners would be a classic example."

World.title: Labour writes to PM with plea to pass modern slavery laws before election
World.content:
The Labour MP backing modern slavery legislation has written to the prime minister to try to get the law passed before the election.

She has also written to the business committee, which decides the order of business at Parliament and is meeting today.

Newsroom has reported a group of charities has banded together to urge Prime Minister Christopher Luxon to push the legislation through Parliament before it rises for the election this week.

Luxon, who in 2022 said modern slavery was the issue he would march in the street over, on Monday said "we won't get time to do it", but committed to returning it to the order paper if National was re-elected to government.

"Frankly, we've had so much filibustering going on through things that have been discussed in depth and in detail in select committees. So that's on the opposition parties too, as to whether we could or couldn't get to it."

The prime minister's office referred RNZ's questions to Leader of the House Louise Upston, who said the bill had been reported back to the House by the select committee "at a time when there were not enough Members' Days left to pass its remaining stages".

"As Leader of the House, I don't have the unilateral ability to create more Members' days or allow Members Bills to be progressed further up the order paper. That is only something the Business Committee can do. The Business Committee was asked to do that, but did not achieve the required 'near-unanimity'.

"I will note that it is exceedingly likely that the Bill will be reinstated in the new Parliament and pass its remaining stages in early 2027. The National Party will still support the Bill in the 55th Parliament."

Labour's Camilla Belich has been championing the bill, working across the aisle with National's Greg Fleming to get a member's bill through in spite of ACT's opposition.

Heading into the party's caucus meeting on Tuesday, she said Luxon's comments "didn't sound particularly positive".

"There are many opportunities that this could have been prioritised as part of the legislative agenda. I do believe that there's some time tomorrow, a couple of hours that could be put aside.

"It's a matter of having the will to prioritise what's important to you as a government."

She said she had written last week to Luxon and the business committee and had not yet heard back.

The bill is yet to have its committee stage and second and third readings, but Belich was confident there was time to pass it.

"I remain open to receiving communication from any member of the National Party, from the leader of the house, from Greg Fleming, who's the co-sponsor of the bill, from the prime minister, from his office, to try and work out a way that we can ensure that this passes this Parliament.

"The parliament could keep sitting until Thursday, but we haven't suggested that ... I don't know what reason they've decided that we have to rise on Wednesday but we've suggested that there is actually time looking at the order paper this Wednesday tomorrow."

Belich said New Zealand was facing pressure to get legislation addressing modern slavery passed.

"The EU is bringing in provisions to make it even more stringent... there's been comments made by the American president... there is a lot of pressure.

"That's not why we're doing it. We're doing it because it's the right thing to do, and we should not be accepting modern slavery in our supply chains."

World.title: 'Get going and move': Southland man hopes to crack cycling world record for his 95th birthday
World.content:
Audio player for " 95 year old Southland man attempting cycling world record " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/community/1522335%2Fget-going-and-move-southland-man-hopes-to-crack-cycling-world-record-for-his-95th-birthday

95 year old Southland man attempting cycling world record Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

A Southland man is attempting to break a cycling world record for his 95th birthday next month.

Peter Grandiek, 94, will attempt to break a cycling distance record for the 95-100 year age group on his 95th birthday in October.

To do this, he would need to do 21.5km in an hour.

Grandiek told Checkpoint, he was already on schedule to do just that and was training twice a week on Tuesdays and Fridays at the Southland Velodrome, along with spending a bit of time at the gym or on his at-home stationary bike on his days off.

Peter Grandiek says setting a new record is "something to do". Supplied

He believed he would be able to achieve the record as he already cycled about 3km more than needed during his training.

Grandiek said he chose to take up cycling in 2007, when he was in his 70s, after finding running was becoming too hard on his joints.

If he gets the record he would need to be drug tested, which included sending down a team from the North Island, as he had been told there was no one in the South Island who could do it.

He would be covering the cost of their air travel.

When asked why he wanted to set a new record, Grandiek said it was "something to do".

"Something to fill in time... I'm trying to keep as mobile as I could possibly be..."

His advice to others was: "Get up and do something... get going and move."

World.title: Dunedin student drinking issues can't be solved by arrests - local police
World.content:
The student drinking issues in Dunedin are "complex" and can not be solved by arrests and prosecutions, says a local community cop.

A person was seriously injured over the weekend after a large student party on Castle Street - reportedly attended by more than 400 people.

The University of Otago said the injured person was not their student.

A doctor who treated the young person told RNZ they had critical head injuries, and that others also had to be treated for alcohol and drug related harm.

The party comes less than a week after a coroner warned students about excessive alcohol consumption, following the death of a 20-year-old who choked on his own vomit at a Dunedin party in 2023.

Otago coastal area prevention manager for community and youth Senior Sergeant Iain Notman told Checkpoint that Dunedin was a "unique environment" with a concentrated area of students, and that the issue was ever evolving.

"Due to a lot of the size of these things, we just have to take a wider approach to some of these things,

"And also I think in the past, trying to arrest or prosecute our ways out of some of these things, and create a bit of a nanny state also isn't often the way either, it is a complex and ever evolving problem for us," he said.

Audio player for " Police faced with youth drinking problems in Dunedin " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/health/1522528%2Fdunedin-student-drinking-issues-can-t-be-solved-by-arrests-local-police

Police faced with youth drinking problems in Dunedin Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Notman said police were focused on partnerships with the university, campus watch and the local council, to provide the safest possible environment for young people.

Asked if that approach was working, he said young people will always be young people, and that youth drinking was not just a Dunedin issue, but a problem nationally and internationally.

Asked if Otago University needed a culture change, Notman said that was a question for the university.

Notman said the lack of monitored student bars in the university area was also a factor to think about.

"Back from my days university, we had 11 odd student bars where people could be monitored with experts and managers and food on site, whereas we're now down to zero for example in our student quarter.

"And that's increased the purchasing and drinking behaviour from off-site establishments, supermarkets and the like - and pushed a lot of the drinking back into the flats," he said.

The University of Otago said in a statement that a significant amount of work took place throughout the year to help students socialise safely and responsibly.

A spokesperson said staff visited student flats to talk about hosting parties safely, and encouraged students to use the "Good One Party Register".

It said it also worked closely with police and student body OUSA, as well as other community partners.

World.title: Tarakihi catch limits reduce to 10 per person nationwide
World.content:
Fisheries Minister Shane Jones says tarakihi catch limits will be reduced, with a nationwide recreational fishing limit of 10 per person.

Commercial limits for the eastern fishery are being reduced by 20 percent, and the western fishery by 55 percent.

Jones said he has considered the latest science and catch information, uncertainty about future stocks of young fish, and the effects of use of the fishery in making the decision.

"These measures will immediately reduce fishing pressure on these tarakihi stocks and put them on more positive trajectories, while allowing a lower level of fishing to continue.

Limits have been increased for snapper and trevally on the North Island's east coast, leatherjacket on the South Island's east and south coast, and frostfish and blue mackerel in deep water.

Fisheries Minister Shane Jones. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Butterfish catch limits have also been reduced, with a five-per-person recreational limit.

Seafood NZ chief executive Lisa Futschek said the quota management system was working as intended.

"This process matters. Sustainable fisheries management isn't about catch limits remaining static; it is about making changes when the evidence shows they are needed."

The company's general manager for inshore fisheries Tiff Bock said they supported decisions to ensure tarakihi stocks continued to rebuild.

"Industry has been actively rebuilding east coast tarakihi since 2018 through catch reductions, avoidance measures, gear changes, improved monitoring and significant investment in research. We remain committed to rebuilding the stocks."

Reduction 'does not cut it'

Benn Winlove, a spokesperson for the LegaSea non-profit marine life advocacy group, said a 20 percent reduction on the east coast "does not cut it" and the government should expect further court cases.

"We have watched the stock fall dramatically, with little intervention from officials or successive fishery ministers. Court cases by Forest and Bird and the Environmental Law Initiative have made the government make bigger reductions, but it's not working.

"On the east coast, tarakihi is at 7.7 percent of its estimated original biomass. This is well below the 10 percent hard limit where closure is an option, and the rebuild plan is clearly not working."

The Environmental Defence Society (EDS) said tarakihi fared better on the West Coast at 29 percent of its unfished biomass - but it was in rapid decline.

Policy director Raewyn Peart said EDS sought a total closure of the fishery, until the stocks recovered. Seafood New Zealand and other commercial fishing interests sought the 20 percent reduction in the harvest that was adopted by the minister.

"Given how depleted tarakihi stocks are, and how important this fish is for New Zealanders, the minister's decision is extremely disappointing," said Peart.

"EDS called for a complete closure of the fishery given its perilous state. But the minister's decision doesn't even mention closure as an option. This is despite the eastern stock being below the hard limit, which is when closure needs to be considered under the Harvest Strategy Standard," she said.

Fisheries New Zealand's analysis indicated that the harvest reductions adopted by the minister would mean the stocks would continue to be overfished, Peart said.

"It is also clear the western stock will continue to decline and the eastern stock will remain at very low biomass levels for an extended period. This brings the risk that any adverse event, such as a marine heatwave, could tip it over the edge so it never recovers."

"EDS is now investigating legal options to challenge the decision," Peart said.

Catch limit changes:

Inshore

Snapper, increase - SNA 2 - East Cape, Hawke's Bay, and Wellington

Trevally, increase - TRE 2 - East Cape, Hawke's Bay, and Wellington

Leatherjacket, increase - LEA 3 - east coast South Island, Southland

East Coast tarakihi, decrease - TAR 1E, 2, 3, 7E - east coasts North and South Island

West Coast tarakihi, decrease - TAR 1W, 7W, 8 - West coasts North and South Island

Stargazer, decrease - STA 7 - West Coast and top of the South Island

Butterfish, decrease - BUT 7 - West Coast and top of the South Island

Shortfin eel, decrease - SFE 13 - Te Waihora (Lake Ellesmere)

Pāua, decrease - PAU 7 - Marlborough

Elephant fish, decrease - ELE 3 and 5 - east coast South Island, Southland, and Sub-Antarctic

Ling, decrease - LIN 1 - Northland, Auckland, Waikato, and Bay of Plenty

Pāua, decrease - PAU 5D - Southland and Otago

Deepwater

Blue mackerel, increase - EMA 7 - west coast North Island, West Coast South Island

Gemfish, increase - SKI 3 - east coast South Island, Chatham Islands

Frostfish, increase - FRO 3 - east coast South Island

Scampi, increase - SCI 3 - east coast South Island, western Chatham Rise

Ling, decrease - LIN 7 - West Coast and Top of the South Island
