World.title: Brooke van Velden uses final speech to defend infamous Parliamentary c-bomb
World.content:
Outgoing ACT MP Brooke van Velden has defended her infamous Parliamentary c-bomb and called for the abolition of the Public Service Commission during her final speech in Parliament.

The party's former deputy - who is the MP for Tāmaki - is leaving politics at the election.

She is also due to have her first baby in early November, but on announcing her pregnancy said that was not the reason for her departure.

Van Velden said she was spurred into Parliament following her work with ACT leader David Seymour on the End of Life Choice Act before she was an MP.

"Working on that law will remain one of the greatest privileges of my life," she said.

"It convinced me to dedicate the past few years to public service, to advance more laws that benefit New Zealanders."

Public office could be tough: "The abuse, the personal attacks, and the concern for safety," van Velden said.

"While I can't control other people's actions, I can control how I respond... Those attacks have been met by turning the other cheek and getting on with the job."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6372778106112

However the clear exception, she said, "was the fateful day of the c-word".

Van Velden used the word in Parliament last year in protest over the slur being directed at her and other female ministers in a newspaper column.

"I'm proud to have stood up to that misogyny - for my colleagues, and for every woman who stays silent out of fear of being labelled the wrong kind of woman," she said.

Van Velden also called for the Public Service Commission to be abolished, saying it did not work for the public or governments.

"It works for the public service to preserve the status quo, enable public servants to shuffle between agencies while leaving the failures of their roles behind with no accountability or meaningful consequences," she said.

Instead, ministers should hire chief executives directly, van Velden said.

"If that were the structure, I believe we'd see better accountability and transparency over decision making, and over where the money goes."

Van Velden said the various causes she advocated for - such as fundraising for the Ukrainian effort and allowing pregnant women to re-enter their own country under Covid-19 restrictions - were underpinned by her belief in freedom, choice and democratic rights.

World.title: Chimney colours unveiled for Norwood SANFL victors amid TV ratings boost
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Norwood Football Club's colours have been unveiled atop the Brickworks chimney to celebrate its SANFL Grand Final win in what was the most-viewed game since a modern rating system began.

The total national television audience on Sunday was up 16 per cent on 2025 numbers to 109,700, which included 93,500 broadcast TV viewers.

It also included 16,100 viewers from broadcaster video on demand (BVOD), which was up 52 per cent.

The VOZ ratings, which started in 2022 and combine both broadcast TV and BVOD, found that 87,500 viewers of broadcast TV viewers were from Adelaide, along with 12,800 of those streaming online.

The Norwood and Sturt colours will stay atop the Hoffman Kiln until the end of season 2027. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

"The broadcast ratings were exceptional, broke every record for the last five years," SANFL executive Darren Chandler said.

"And when you compare those to what's happening in Western Australia and Victoria, we've absolutely blown it off the charts."

SANFL kicking TV goals SANFL crowds are continuing to climb each year after COVID-19 restrictions put a dent in numbers

Football commentator Mark Soderstrom said 71 per cent of South Australian televisions switched on were tuned into the decider between Sturt and Norwood, which drew 38,250 spectators to Adelaide Oval.

The WAFL Grand Final, on the other hand, drew 19,210 people to Perth Stadium, continuing a four-year decline in crowds, while the VFL Grand Final drew just 12,941, the first time the league had attracted more than 8,000 fans in seven years.

A time-honoured tradition

The annual winners and runners-up of the SANFL grand final have been displaying their colours atop the 1913 Hoffman-designed kiln at Thebarton since the start of the decade.

The much-loved ceremony of nearly 70 years had to be moved from its previous home chimney at the West End Brewery after the facility was closed by its owners, Lion, in 2021.

Redlegs supporters came out to celebrate their team's 2026 premiership win. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Redlegs coach Jade Sheedy, who was a premiership player for Sturt in 2002 when he won the Magarey Medal with teammate Tim Weatherald, also coached Woodville-West Torrens in back-to-back premierships in 2020-21.

He told the crowd of Redleg supporters at Thebarton that when the siren blew on Sunday and Norwood beat Sturt 87 points to 73 after a final-quarter comeback, he thought he was "still in a dream for 15 minutes".

"I guess it was two years of building something pretty special, and to come together in the last 30 minutes and to believe in that, and to kick five goals three to one point in the last quarter showed how much the group had grown and that's what I'm most proud of," Sheedy said.

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley and coach Jade Sheedy were still celebrating in Tuesday. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley said the team had not changed "too much structurally" since they lost the preliminary final by two points in 2025 but had "increased the belief in how we play".

"We just fell short in 2025, but we took a lot of learnings from that and a lot of confidence reviewing how we were playing our footy," he said.

Sturt football manager Geoff Riddle played tribute to the Redlegs at the chimney ceremony. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Sturt football manager Geoff Riddle attended the ceremony on behalf of the runners-up.

"I think we can all agree that Sunday was a great spectacle, and it was a great  for the competition and the league across the country," he said.

He said Norwood were "deserved winners" as the "most consistent team all year".

World.title: Live: Lachie Neale's grand final dreams on the line at AFL tribunal
World.content:
(Getty Images)

While there are is a list of players who have been rubbed out for the grand final because of various on-field misdemeanours, in recent times there have been a few fortunate folks who managed to avoid the ban at the tribunal or elsewhere.

In 1996, Sydney Swans full-back Andrew Dunkley was in strife for striking Essendon's James Hird in a famous prelim. He was banned three days before the big game.

The Swans went beyond appeals — they took it to court, and the Supreme Court of Victoria agreed that Dunkley would be denied natural justice if they had to sort the mess out before Saturday. Sydney won an injunction, Dunkley played, the Swans lost and Dunkley eventually got three weeks.

In 1999, Carlton forward Aaron Hamill was banned for dropping a knee into the head of Essendon's Dean Wallis during the Blues' stunning prelim win over the Bombers.

Carlton appealed. In an early example of what is today commonplace, they called a biomechanist to give evidence, and they swayed the appeals board to let Hamill play. The Blues lost to North Melbourne.

In 2005, Sydney made the grand final with a win over St Kilda, but the BBBBH (Big Bad Bustling Barry Hall, as ABC's own Roy and HG referred to him) himself ended up banned for a gut punch on Saints defender Matt Maguire.

The Swans appealed, Hall caught a private jet to Melbourne to appear, and Sydney's legal team convinced the appeals board that the offence was not off the ball (a rather heroic legal stance), downgrading it from level two to level one.

The board took just four minutes to wrap things up, Hall was clear to play, and went on to kick two goals and the co-captain was part of the team's first flag since 1933. Even Hall himself later admitted he should have been banned.

Most recently, Collingwood's Brayden Maynard was sent straight to the tribunal for a high bump on Melbourne's Angus Brayshaw in the 2023 qualifying final.

Facing a season-ending three match ban (at least), Maynard and the Pies produced a biomechanical expert who testified that although Maynard would have been like a "frisbee on legs" after leaving the ground, he could not have foreseen the result of his actions.

Maynard was cleared, and played in the Pies' grand final win over Brisbane — Brayshaw's acute concussion symptoms lingered, and he never played again.

If you're a complete Tribunal tragic, you can look back on all that craziness in our blog from that Maynard hearing here:

World.title: Diamonds name Klau for Constellation Cup squad
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Diamonds netballer Sarah Klau has retained her spot in Australia's Constellation Cup squad after pleading guilty to assault.

Klau was included in the 14-player squad named on Tuesday, less than a week after the goalkeeper was sanctioned by Netball Australia (NA).

The 31-year-old was handed a $5,000 fine and a two-match ban — suspended for 12 months — by the sport's national governing body.

Klau fined after unprecedented assault charge Diamonds defender Sarah Klau is handed a $5,000 fine and a suspended two-game ban after pleading guilty to assault and failing to disclose the incident prior to the Commonwealth Games.

Klau had fronted Downing Centre Court earlier this month, facing a common assault charge.

She had allegedly kicked a security guard in the back outside a pub in Sydney's eastern suburbs when she was denied entry due to being too intoxicated.

The NSW Swifts player had reportedly attended a Sydney Swans AFL match a day after an ongoing leg injury ruled her out of the remainder of the Super Netball season.

Klau, who has represented Australia on 67 occasions since her Diamonds debut in 2019, failed to disclose the matter to NA before the Commonwealth Games in July, resulting in the sanctions.

Sophie Dwyer also retained her spot in the Diamonds squad, looking for a chance to find redemption after missing an after-the-siren shot in the Commonwealth Games semifinal loss to Jamaica.

Constellation Cup First Test: October 18 (Auckland)

Second Test: October 21 (Christchurch)

Third Test: October 25 (Sydney)

Fourth Test: October 28 (Melbourne)

Dwyer was left on the bench in Australia's bronze-medal win over England in Glasgow.

The core of coach Stacey Marinkovich's squad remains the same from the Games, with Jo Weston unavailable for selection.

Jessie Grenvold, Amy Parmenter and Donnell Wallam return to the side after travelling to Glasgow as reserves.

Grenvold is yet to make her Diamonds debut after earning her maiden call-up in May following a breakout season in defence for the Melbourne Mavericks.

The Constellation Cup begins on October 18, with the Diamonds travelling to Auckland to take on the Commonwealth Games champions.

Diamonds squad: Kiera Austin, Courtney Bruce, Sophie Dwyer, Sophie Garbin, Matilda Garrett, Jessie Grenvold, Georgie Horjus, Sarah Klau, Cara Koenen, Kate Moloney, Amy Parmenter, Jamie-Lee Price, Donnell Wallam, Liz Watson

AAP

World.title: How Nick Daicos won the Brownlow Medal
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Coming into the night, the 2026 Brownlow Medal count held little intrigue about who the winner would be.

Few — if any — in the footballing world thought there was anyone who could seriously challenge Nick Daicos for the award.

But there was still one person who was in shock: Daicos, himself.

"I can't believe I'm the Brownlow medallist to be honest," Daicos said at the award ceremony in Melbourne.

The count was close until about the halfway mark, before Daicos pulled away from the pack as the season progressed.

With his 47 votes last night, Daicos has earned more votes in the last four years than any other player has in any five-year period.

Daicos earned more votes than three entire clubs. He collected 63 per cent of Collingwood's votes for the evening.

He racked up record after record: the most votes in one year, most consecutive games with three votes (six), the most games with three votes (13).

It wasn't just a win, it was domination.

With the win, Daicos joins Tom Mitchell, Gary Ablett Jr and Ben Cousins as father-son selections who have claimed the Brownlow Medal (Jobe Watson's 2012 victory was rescinded).

Daicos time

Plenty has been written about what makes Daicos special.

Coaches and opposition players talk about his elusiveness, vision and ability to make something out of what seems like nothing.

And then there is his competitiveness.

"He hates losing," Magpies great Scott Pendlebury said.

"Especially at table tennis. Whenever we travel on the road, he always tries to get a re-match."

That competitive drive is often what turns good into great, and great into legendary.

But words pale into insignificance compared to watching the best of Daicos in full flight.

Players like Daicos stand out due to the highlights they create.

Teams spend more time trying to get Daicos off balance than any other player in the competition.

It hasn't seemed to have an effect yet.

No matter what teams throw at Daicos, he still has an unerring habit of getting the ball and letting his imagination run wild.

That drive was forged from his early days as a player, often being one of the slightest on the field when he played up in age at both the Greythorn Falcons and the Kew Rovers.

When Daicos moved to Carey Grammar for year 10, he was thrust immediately into the first team to compete in the prestigious APS football competition.

His teammates were no slouches either, with Daicos playing alongside the likes of Noah Anderson and last year's Brownlow medallist, Matt Rowell.

No player in the AFL was more important in getting his team in scoring positions than Daicos was this year.

Daicos thrived at winning the ball when no-one had clear control.

He has an innate ability to track the ball before anyone else, working smarter and not harder.

Daicos also has a scary ability to render his direct opponents as traffic cones.

The Magpies look to get Daicos the ball as much as possible, and he repays them with territory.

Few can match his combination of skill, speed and footy intelligence.

Although Collingwood fell short this year, hopes are higher for 2027 with additional reinforcements.

Family zone

Throughout football's history, geography has shaped the make-up of teams to a great extent.

Teams recruited from specific regions. The fortunes of clubs rose and fell based on the growth of different geographic areas.

Urban expansion fuelled Hawthorn's rise, while weak and depopulating zones condemned other clubs to near extinction.

There was one exception to the geography-based dictation of the footy landscape: the sons of former players.

The father-son rule was introduced in 1949 to ensure players such as Ron Barassi could continue on the legacy of their fathers at their clubs regardless of geography.

These days, the role of geography has inverted and it now dictates where all the father-son selections are.

The family zone for Victorian footy now runs through south-east Melbourne.

This was the former recruiting area for Hawthorn, otherwise known as the Family Club.

The ranks of father-son selections are littered with schools and clubs based in the most desirable parts of Melbourne, often far from the origins of their fathers' careers.

For example, the Silvangi and Daicos offspring played their junior footy at the Greythorn Falcons.

That's only a stone's throw from Collingwood captain Darcy Moore's junior club of Ivanhoe.

Nor is it far from where Mitchell or Watson first honed their craft.

The eastern side of Melbourne has increasingly become a powerhouse in junior footy as well, with Sandringham, Oakleigh and the Eastern Ranges dominating the AFL's Talent League in recent seasons.

Brownlow's changing face

A major change took place to the fabric of the Brownlow Medal this year.

Umpires gained access to a select group of 17 statistics before voting. Daicos excelled in several of these measures.

This may rob part of what made the Brownlow so special.

Umpires have a unique perspective. They're also party to the intangibles, such as on-field demeanour, respect and sportsmanship.

This year's votes aligned more closely to the results of the AFL Coaches Association award than ever before, according to Wheelo Ratings.

Coaches pore over key numbers throughout their games and now umpires can rely on some of the same figures to adjudge best afield as well.

Supplying data may condition umpires to discard insights gleaned in the heat of the action, turning them instead into just another spin on the same cold distant observations.

Defenders are already suffering even more than they traditionally do, while midfielders, who often accumulate high "count" stats, get a larger share of the spoils.

Rucks also outperformed their expected output this year, likely benefiting from the inclusion of hit-outs.

This will likely serve to further intensify a growing trend towards vote concentration in disposal-accumulating midfielders.

The leaderboard for career-long average votes is strewn liberally with current players, with previous leaders Haydn Bunton and Graham Moss only playing the prime vote-earning part of their careers in the VFL.

If this trend continues, Daicos will soon break Patrick Dangerfield and Ablett Jr's record for most career votes, at least until the next star enters the scene.

But all of that is for the future.

All that is important now is that the inevitable ascension of Daicos to the pinnacle of the game has taken place.

World.title: Formula 1 agrees to shorter races in 2027
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Formula 1 has approved a 15 kilometre reduction in official race distances starting next season.

The change means the total distance will be cut from 305 to 290 kilometres.

The Formula 1 Commission finalised the decision in London.

"In line with the refinements to the power unit regulations to be introduced in 2027 on fuel flow, a reduction in the total race distance from 305km to 290km was approved, corresponding to a reduction of two or three laps," a statement read.

Aussie F1 GP loses season-opening honour Melbourne's Australian Grand Prix will not have the privilege of opening the 2027 Formula 1 season, but it will boast two races in its biggest weekend yet.

The power unit regulations favour increased engine power over hybrid electrical output.

To better handle rain delays and red flags, the commission has also abolished the strict three-hour overall event cap.

While the two-hour maximum of active racing time remains, the change gives organisers flexibility to complete full race distances.

Another objective ‌is to give spectators the best possible chance ‌to enjoy a full race when disruptions occur.

Practice sessions will also gain added flexibility to extend following stoppages.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Lions 'praying' Neale gets off but confident they will cope if ban stands
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Brisbane Lions players are confident they can cover the potential absence of Lachie Neale in the grand final, with the two-time Brownlow medallist facing a one-match ban.

Neale and the Lions will challenge the suspension at the AFL tribunal on Tuesday evening.

The 33-year-old has been charged with striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in last Saturday night's preliminary final.

Neale facing grand final ban The Lions will contest a one-match suspension handed to Lachie Neale, which would rule the two-time premiership captain out of the AFL grand final.

If the suspension is upheld, Neale will miss Saturday's grand final against Fremantle at the MCG.

Lions teammate Jarrod Berry said it would be a blow to lose Neale.

But he said the Lions were equipped to overcome any adversity.

"One of our best traits is being able to deal with that [adversity]," Berry said.

"We do it well and there's no point putting energy into it until we know the result.

"We'll be sitting tight and praying that he gets off. But if he doesn't, we'll face it when it comes."

Neale's gut punch on Ginnivan was graded as intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact by match review officer Michael Christian.

There is damning vision showing Neale guilty of the behind-play strike and numerous precedents this season of other players being banned for one match for similar incidents.

But the Lions are set to argue the suspension should be downgraded to a fine.

They will cite a fresh clause that allowed Collingwood great Scott Pendlebury to avoid a suspension in March.

Clause that could save Neale The Brisbane Lions will challenge Neale's one-game suspension for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in last Saturday night's preliminary final.

Pendlebury was given a one-match ban for rough conduct for a bump on Adelaide's Josh Worrell.

He was found guilty by the tribunal but the sanction was downgraded to a $3,000 fine due to "compelling and exceptional circumstances", a clause open to the tribunal that will be central to Neale's case.

The relevant clause states: "Players will not automatically receive a reduced sanction for a good record.

"However, if a classifiable offence is contested or referred to the tribunal, a player with an exemplary record may argue that their good record constitutes exceptional and compelling circumstances."

The Magpies successfully argued the clause applied to Pendlebury, who had never previously faced the tribunal in his storied 21-year career.

Neale also has not previously appeared before the tribunal in his 320-match career.

He is also a dual Brownlow medallist and premiership captain, plus a four-time All Australian.

Geelong coach Chris Scott does not agree with the provision.

"Seriously, when we're starting to say, 'There's a rule for you because you've done good things for the game,' it's almost implying that other people haven't done a good job," Scott said on Fox Footy.

But Scott added: "I know his record is exceptional, but aside from that, I just like to see them play.

"I actually think that's going to be hard to defend personally, but my hope is that he does play."

AAP

World.title: Banned Swan falls well short in Brownlow Medal vote
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The AFL has avoided the unwanted scenario of one of Sydney's suspended players winning the Brownlow Medal, with Isaac Heeney finishing outside the count's top five.

The league had a contingency plan in place if Heeney had won the game's highest individual honour.

But Nick Daicos's record-breaking number of votes, and prolific polling from Bailey Smith and Marcus Bontempelli, meant the plan never needed to come into play.

Daicos wins first Brownlow Nick Daicos breaks Patrick Cripps's record in the 3-2-1 voting era by winning the first Brownlow Medal of his career.

Heeney, and Swans teammates Chad Warner and Nick Blakey were among the notable absences from Monday night's awards ceremony.

Along with Riley Bice and James Jordon, they have been absent from Sydney's headquarters since being suspended by the club in August.

The five were stood down for breaching club standards following a post-match incident at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne.

Those suspensions are separate to a police investigation into sexual assault allegations, with Victoria Police flagging an update is not expected until late October.

No charges have been laid and the ABC is not suggesting any wrongdoing on the part of the five suspended players.

Daicos rewrites history with Brownlow win Nick Daicos's stardom has always had an inevitability to it, and his maiden Brownlow Medal triumph is the latest example of him fulfilling his immense promise.

The five players were ruled ineligible for All-Australian honours and were not invited to the Brownlow Medal function in Melbourne.

But they remained eligible for the award.

Brodie Grundy, Charlie Curnow, Dane Rampe, Logan McDonald and Tom McCartin were among those on hand for the Swans.

Once the count started, Heeney was the only player considered a genuine contender.

Heeney did not poll until round four, when he landed two votes, and claimed three votes against Gold Coast in Gather Round.

Warner polled for the first time in round four, while Blakey claimed three votes in round six.

Heeney claimed three consecutive three-vote performances to rise into the top four of the count at one point.

But his best performances were not enough to come close to Daicos's record-setting mark of 47 votes.

Heeney finished equal-eighth on 26 votes, ahead of teammate Errol Gulden (17), who ended the season with five consecutive best-afield performances.

AAP

World.title: Brownlow simply latest chapter as Daicos continues rewriting AFL history
World.content:
When Nathan Buckley's decade-long tenure as Collingwood coach came to an end midway through 2021, there was a silver lining for the club amid the painful exit of the club legend.

Buckley's tenure had seen the Pies flirt with winning a premiership in 2018 and 2019 before ultimately failing, but by the time he wrapped up, Collingwood seemed well out of the premiership window.

The silver lining came in the form of a player who was yet to set foot on an AFL field: Nick Daicos, then a teenager touted as a generational prospect years before he was eligible to be drafted.

Daicos wins first Brownlow Medal and sets new modern-day voting record Nick Daicos breaks Patrick Cripps's record in the 3-2-1 voting era by winning the first Brownlow Medal of his career.

The AFL world was no stranger to the Daicos surname due to the exploits of Nick's famous father, Peter, who was immortalised at Collingwood as a member of the club's 1990 premiership side.

You did not need to be a Collingwood fanatic to know about Nick Daicos. Everyone around the game knew the kid was on his way because of his prolific exploits at the junior levels.

The weight of expectation that comes with the level of hype Daicos had as a draft prospect can prove crippling. Unfortunately, years of evidence support this.

Sometimes even the most hyped prospects can take time to fit into the AFL system, and it makes sense. These are boys coming to a man's game.

The more rigorous training regimes, expanded playbooks, media commitments, dietary requirements, and everything else that comes with being an AFL player can be too much. That is even before we get to the pace of the game being completely different.

Nick Daicos with his parents. (Getty Images / AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

That hasn't been the case with Daicos, who, as an audacious Nike advert claimed on the morning of the Brownlow count, has proven it inevitable from day one.

From his first game, Daicos showed an ability to bend the game to his will in ways not seen in teenagers, and we have all been blessed to witness it.

Daicos's arrival helped catapult Collingwood from second-last in 2021 to fourth in his first season in the AFL.

Collingwood fell one point short of a grand final appearance in Daicos's debut season, but went all the way in his second.

After collecting boatloads of the football across halfback while occasionally dipping his toes in the midfield as a rookie, Daicos supercharged the Pies engine room in 2023, helping them claim the flag, and he has not looked back since.

Daicos helped propel Collingwood to a premiership in just his second season in the AFL. (AFL Photos via Getty Images: Dylan Burns)

From very early on in Daicos's career, the Brownlow win appeared to be a question of when rather than if, but it was the one accolade he was frustratingly made to wait on.

Daicos followed up his premiership by polling a ridiculous 38 votes in 2024, the most by any player in the league's history up until that point, only for that year's winner, Patrick Cripps, to poll 45.

Last year, he was again a seemingly unbackable favourite before being stunned by Gold Coast's Matt Rowell.

Missing out on a Brownlow after being among the favourites for a few years can be something that follows you.

Marcus Bontempelli, despite being widely considered the best player of his generation, has yet to win the prestigious medal.

Bulldogs star Marcus Bontempelli's career is an example of just how hard Brownlow Medals are to come by. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

Buckley was famously made to wait year after year before eventually breaking through in 2003, his 11th season, while Gary Ablett Jr was even denied by his own teammate before his maiden Brownlow triumph. It is almost a rite of passage if you're an all-timer.

Despite Bontempelli, Zak Butters and Bailey Smith all challenging him at various points during the count, Daicos would not be denied this year.

Almost in revenge for the previous two seasons, this year, Daicos turned in an individual season that would ultimately prove impossible to ignore for the umpires.

Daicos broke Cripps's record with 47 votes and set a few more records along the way.

He is now the only player in league history to poll over 30 votes in three consecutive seasons, the only player to put together six straight three-vote games, and the only player to put together 13 three-vote games in a single season.

Daicos celebrates his Brownlow triumph with his parents after the count. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Given the ease with which Daicos has played from his first contest in the AFL four seasons ago, it was surprising to talk about the weight of expectation actually weighing on him after winning his elusive first Brownlow.

You get the sense that the weight of expectation might be the only thing that is capable of slowing him down, because efforts from his AFL counterparts to do so have so far proven futile.

For a player so metronomic and seemingly superhuman on the field, it was refreshing to hear Daicos admit he too deals with nerves and struggles with criticism, just like the rest of us.

Daicos admitted to the Brownlow win being a relief after being denied for so many years as a favourite, even saying he had given up trusting in betting markets.

Daicos is likely to put together more dominant seasons now that the weight of winning a Brownlow is no more. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

Now that the Brownlow box has been ticked off, it is frightening to think of what an unburdened Daicos could potentially achieve.

Still just 23 years of age, Daicos has gone from being the precocious youngster to one of Collingwood's veterans, and he will act as the bridge from one era of Collingwood premiership contention to the next, just as Scott Pendlebury did.

He seems good enough to single-handedly wrench Collingwood's premiership window open for as long as he wants.

Daicos has the chance to eclipse Scott Pendlebury (right) as Collingwood's greatest-ever player. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Adding premierships to his 2023 triumph will be at the top of Daicos's to-do list, and the hope will be that in the process of achieving that goal, his resume ultimately becomes undeniable.

The chance to be Collingwood's greatest player is in play. The chance to be the greatest player in league history is as well, as premature as that shout may seem.

The records Daicos set with his maiden Brownlow win will eventually be just another footnote for a player who is poised to rewrite the game's history books.

Like the commercial said: inevitable.

Tech.title: A cut cable disrupted hundreds of flights across the US
Tech.content:
is a senior editor who has obsessed over headlines and internet speeds since 2011. He previously worked as an advocate for the National Park System.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Hundreds of flights were cancelled or delayed on Monday after construction crews in New Jersey accidentally cut a Verizon fiber cable used for air traffic control.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said that a circuit failure led to the discovery of the severed fiber cable, ABC News reports. The outage hammered airports across the Northeast, causing ground stops at all three major New York City airports.

In a statement to CNBC, Verizon said that it bore “no responsibility for this incident,” putting the blame on “construction contractors working in the area” that “dug up and cut our cable.”

Ironically, it looks like trains make have taken out the planes, but fingers are still being pointed. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said an Amtrak crew accidentally cut the line, but AP reports that Amtrak blames a New Jersey Transit crew for the disruption. “This incident occurred on New Jersey Transit property and involved a New Jersey Transit contractor,” an Amtrak spokesperson told NBC4.

As of Monday evening, Duffy said that “the telecom lines have been repaired, and all airport operations in the Northeast are resuming,” but cautioned that it will take “some time to clear all existing delays.” According to FlightAware, there were over 1,000 canceled flights today in the US

Tech.title: Amazon wants to help the Colorado River, but we still don’t know how much water the company uses
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amazon plans to spend $20 million on water conservation projects along the Colorado River, a crucial but dwindling water supply for 40 million people in the Western US.

The initiative comes as Amazon and other tech companies face mounting scrutiny over how much water their data centers use. Amazon has a goal of becoming water positive — replenishing more water than it uses — by the end of the decade. It recently disclosed some information about its water use, but we still have an incomplete picture of the company’s impact as a whole.

Amazon announced the launch of a Colorado River Basin Collaborative today, with a mission to “create one of the biggest corporate water conservation efforts for a single U.S. watershed.” It expects to raise $100 million over two years — including the $20 million investment from its own coffers — for water conservation efforts.

The Colorado River brings water to 40 million people

Stretching 1,400 miles, the Colorado River brings water to 40 million people across seven states in the Western US and and two states in Mexico. The waterway has faced “unprecedented” drought over the last 26 years, according to the US Bureau of Reclamation. Decades of overuse on top of human-caused climate change have exacerbated the problem. To cope, the US Department of the Interior finalized a plan in August imposing steep water cuts on Arizona, Nevada, and California.

As the first stop for most goods the US imports from Asia, California is home to more Amazon warehouses than any other state. In Orange County, California, Amazon pledged $2.2 million over the next three years to help detect and patch up leaks. That effort is ultimately supposed to conserve 189 million gallons of water each year, according to Amazon.

As part of the newly announced collaborative, other companies can contract independently with conservation projects they choose. The United Nations-backed Water Resilience Coalition will vet projects. Amazon is also joining the Water Resilience Coalition, which includes Microsoft, Meta, and other brands across a range of sectors.

Tech companies are facing waves of resistance against new AI data centers. AI was estimated to use between 312.5 billion and 764.6 billion liters of water in 2025, according to one estimate, about as much water as people consume globally in water bottles. In Arizona, Colorado River water cuts are expected to raise utility rates, and some residents fear data centers could make things worse.

In June, Amazon disclosed that its data centers used 2.5 billion gallons of water globally in 2025, including those it owns, leases, or shares. Data centers Amazon owns and operates directly reduced their water consumption by 2 percent in 2025 compared to the year prior, according to the company. It attributes gains to a 52 percent improvement in water efficiency since 2021. The company says it uses 0.12 liters of water per kilowatt-hour of electricity, claiming that’s about seven times more efficient than the industry average for data centers.

Amazon’s annual sustainability report shares water use per unit of power (l/kwh) for its data centers since 2021, but not the company’s total water use over that time period. Sustainability experts and environmental advocates caution against assessing a company’s sustainability by efficiency measurements alone. The more efficient a technology becomes, the more resources it might ultimately consume as companies start using it more, according to an economic concept called Jevons paradox. That makes it important to track how much water a company is using overall, as well as how much it needs in each place it operates during demand peaks when supply is most limited.

For comparison, Microsoft’s latest sustainability report discloses its data centers’ total water use since 2020, while Google’s report shares water use for global operations since 2021 with a breakdown by location. All three tech giants have had to abandon data center projects after facing community opposition, Reuters reports. Unlike other tech companies, Amazon’s warehouses also have a massive physical footprint that isn’t reflected in the company’s data center disclosures.

A Guardian investigation in 2025 alleges that Amazon obscured how much water the company uses by deciding not to account for how much it takes to generate electricity, considered a “secondary” water use. Concerned about “reputational risk,” executives decided to only address “primary” water use at its facilities when calculating progress toward sustainability goals. The numbers Amazon recently shared about its data center water use also exclude water consumption stemming from electricity generation.

While data centers often use water for cooling systems, a majority of a data center’s water footprint stems from this “secondary use.” Power plants need water to cool equipment and turn turbines using steam, and in 2021, Amazon used 10.5 billion gallons (39.7 billion liters) of water in 2021, according to the Guardian report citing an internal leaked document. That’s about as much as 95,000 US households consume.

In an email to The Verge, Amazon spokesperson Margaret Callahan says the Guardian report “relied on cherry-picked data from an outdated document that misrepresents our water strategy — making the conclusions fundamentally wrong and misleading” and that a “document’s existence doesn’t guarantee its accuracy or finality.”

Callahan didn’t provide more data on how much water Amazon has used in total over the years. She pointed out that the company is 75 percent toward its goal of becoming water positive, returning 3 gallons for every 4 that it used last year.

In its announcement today, Kara Hurst, chief sustainability officer at Amazon, compares the new Colorado River initiative to the company’s previous climate targets.

”Through the Climate Pledge, we’ve seen what happens when companies tackle a problem together: progress accelerates. We’re bringing that same model to the Colorado River because water and climate are deeply connected,” Hurst says.

Amazon’s carbon footprint, however, grew 16 percent in 2025 — a trend happening across the tech industry as companies race to make advances in AI.

Tech.title: California tightens rules on AI data center energy and water use
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed seven bills designed to prevent AI data centers from passing utility costs onto residents, as reported earlier by the Los Angeles Times. The package of laws requires the California Public Utilities Commission to introduce a new rate classification for data centers while forcing them to pay for upgrades to local power grids and water systems.

Other bills included in the package will require proposed data centers to disclose their estimated water use to local governments, along with information about energy efficiency and drought planning. They must also meet certain energy, water, and fuel consumption requirements before qualifying for a streamlined approval process. Last week, Newsom signed an executive order to speed up the creation of an AI “kill switch.”

Related Gavin Newsom is pushing for an AI kill switch

“While the Trump administration moves toward deregulation, communities are left to deal with the consequences — higher electricity demand, grid constraints, water use, and pollution,” Newsom says in the press release. “With these laws, we are ensuring that Californians remain in the driver’s seat — and that those profiting from data centers aren’t doing so at our expense.”

Tech.title: GM can’t ‘bring back’ Apple CarPlay because it never left
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Last week, GM announced a new software experience for its upcoming Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks, including a new look for Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, the popular phone mirroring systems that the automaker made a big deal about removing from its electric vehicles in 2023.

Naturally, this led to some confusion about whether GM was “bringing back” CarPlay and Android Auto to its vehicles. Yahoo Finance reported it that way, calling it an “about-face” by the automaker, while Apple Insider’s headline boasted that GM “cave[d]” on its decision to remove the interface from its gas-powered vehicles. Even The Verge’s own commenters were a bit flummoxed about what was going on.

It’s certainly true that GM has not offered phone projection in any of its electric vehicles for the past three years. That means no CarPlay or Android Auto in the Chevy Equinox, Blazer, Bolt, and Silverado EVs; Cadillac Lyriq, Optiq, Vistiq, and Escalade IQ; or GMC Sierra and Hummer SUV and Truck EVs.

All of those vehicles have Google software products embedded in their systems, like Maps and Gemini. That’s because GM builds its operating system on top of Android Automotive, which is often called Google Automotive Services or GAS when bundled with the full suite of native apps. But if you’re hoping to plug in your phone, or connect wirelessly, and see the familiar app layout on the infotainment screen of a GM electric vehicle, you’ll be sorely disappointed.

The same can’t be said about GM’s many gas-powered trucks and SUVs. GM never disabled phone projection in its best-selling ICE models. Tens of thousands of owners of GM-branded vehicles regularly project their phones’ displays on their vehicles’ infotainment screens without any issue. And now CarPlay and Android Auto are both getting spiffy new picture-in-picture upgrades in the Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra, a sign that perhaps GM is learning to co-exist with phone mirroring.

GM is partly responsible for the confusion. In an October 2025 appearance on Decoder, GM CEO Mary Barra defended the company’s decision to prohibit CarPlay in its electric vehicles and indicated that the policy would eventually extend to GM’s gasoline-powered lineup as well.

Everyone freaked out for a second time. Removing phone projection in EVs was one thing, but many truck and SUV owners were understandably incensed about the prospect of losing the capability in their beloved GM-branded vehicles. But a few days later, GM seemed to walk back that statement, clarifying to a number of outlets that Apple CarPlay and Android Auto would remain available in its gas-powered vehicles “for the foreseeable future.” Last week’s announcement of a new software experience in the Silverado and Sierra trucks would seem to be included in that “foreseeable future.”

Allow me to add some further reporting here. For the Silverado/Sierra announcement, I spoke to Colin McCormick, group product manager for Google built-in, projection, and profiles at GM. Here’s what he had to say about how GM’s position on phone projection has evolved over the years:

And so the way that I look at this is that we were one of the early adopters of CarPlay and Android Auto when it first came out. And we do have a small segment of EVs right now that don’t offer that, but there is a large majority of our vehicles that do offer that. And our big position on this is that it shouldn’t be two competing systems. So as we work together with Apple and Google to provide solutions that we think are best for the customer, this is what we’re representing in this new UI design. So I think we’re landing in a spot where … we don’t have a customer that has to decide, ‘Oh, I’m going to use projection,’ or, ‘Oh, I want to use the native system.’ That’s our sweet spot for us. And that’s where we want to live.

GM most likely realizes that its position on CarPlay and Android Auto isn’t popular. People really like mirroring their phones! It’s clean, it’s familiar, and it’s (mostly) dependable. The same can’t be said for most modern cars’ native software. Even the ones that are really well designed, like Rivian and Tesla, still struggle with some core functions like profile logins and messages. And you can find plenty of owners of both brands that would give their firstborn child for the ability to mirror their phone.

CarPlay and Android Auto aren’t perfect. They have dependability problems and connectivity problems aplenty. But they are worlds better than the majority of the native operating systems in cars today — most of which are just trash. Yes, they’re getting better. And GM is not wrong in thinking it can offer a better experience. But people get testy when you take away their choices.

So GM is finding ways to coexist with CarPlay and Android Auto. It doesn’t want to lose more customers over it, which is why we’re getting this most recent solution that includes picture-in-picture phone projection. GM thinks this solves the “two competing systems” problem, as mentioned by McCormick. But what it really does is get it out of the corner it backed itself into over phone mirroring.

Tech.title: Bungie says it’s ‘not done with Destiny’ and will bring back vaulted content
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Months after seemingly giving up on Destiny 2, Bungie now says it’s planning to restore vaulted content in the game like campaigns, destinations, and raids. The decision reverses the Destiny Content Vault that Bungie created six years ago, controversially removing older content from Destiny 2 that players had paid to access.

“We understand that removing these experiences had a lasting impact on player trust and enjoyment of Destiny,” admits Bungie. “We cannot change the decision we made, but we can acknowledge its impact and do the work to make it right by restoring these important parts of Destiny’s history.“

All Destiny 2 players will get access to the vaulted content, but it’s not a simple switch of a button for Bungie. The developer made big changes to Destiny 2 with the Beyond Light expansion, meaning it has to go back and update lighting, encounters, combatants, and other underlying systems for this older content. “That work will take time, but it is necessary to ensure returning content meets the stability and gameplay standards of Destiny 2 today,” says Bungie.

The decision to return this content to Destiny 2 comes just weeks after a “Sunrise” Destiny 2 offline preservation mod appeared. The mod lets players access older areas in Destiny 2 that had been vaulted, but not the exact campaigns and missions that players had experienced previously.

Bungie now says its own restoration project is the “first step to lay the foundation for how we reforge into new stories and games that you all deserve.” Could that be a Destiny 3 sequel? There’s no mention of such a project, despite fans desperately pleading for a successor to Destiny 2 in multiple high-profile Twitch streams in recent weeks. Bungie is only committing to building a “stronger long-term future for Destiny” right now.

Alongside the Destiny 2 efforts, Bungie is also admitting that Marathon, its extraction shooter, didn’t “reach as many players as we had hoped, and we also know and understand that the game needs to evolve.” That means Marathon will expand deeper into a survival experience. The changes are a little vague right now, but it sounds like Marathon really needs to change and attract more players if it’s to be a sustainable project for Bungie.

Tech.title: Can John Ternus find Apple’s next big thing?
Tech.content:
Today, I’m talking with Mark Gurman, who is the world’s best-sourced Apple reporter — both as Bloomberg’s chief Apple correspondent and the host of the upcoming podcast Power On.

Earlier this month, Apple hosted its annual iPhone hardware event, virtually every detail of which was reported ahead of time by Mark. But this event was special, for a number of reasons.

It was new Apple CEO John Ternus’ first major product launch since he took over for former CEO Tim Cook less than two weeks prior. It was also the debut of the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable smartphone. The timing of those two things was not at all coincidental, as you’ll hear Mark explain. Apple takes these hardware events — and the stories they tell — extremely seriously.

This year’s story actually says a great deal about what’s happening at Apple, how Cook managed in wholesale leadership ranks over the past year, and how all of that might change Apple’s culture. Furthermore, what all that tells about Ternus’ plan to navigate Apple from what you might call the iPhone era into the AI era.

Okay: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman on the future of Apple. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Mark Gurman, you’re the chief Apple correspondent and the managing editor of consumer technology at Bloomberg. Welcome to Decoder.

Good to be here finally. Thanks for having me. And it’s been a while, so it’s good to catch up on all things Apple.

Yeah, I’m really excited to talk to you. Obviously, Apple just had its big event. They announced the iPhone Duo. It was John Ternus’s first event as CEO. This is a Decoder episode, so we’ve got a new CEO, and we’ve got a new org chart inside of Apple.

There’s been a lot of shuffling. You’ve been chronicling them very, very deeply over the past few years. Let’s just start with the event. I have a very basic question for you.

Sure.

Do you ever get nostalgic for a time when you didn’t know what was going to happen at the iPhone event?

Do I ever get nostalgic?

Do you ever wish that you, Mark Gurman, were about to be surprised?

Honestly, I never think about it that way. I’m just fixated on delivering the goods and delivering the news. And people love their Apple. People want to know everything that’s coming down to the last minute, so I’m here to provide it for them.

The thing with me, and I don’t know if most people know this about me, but I hope people know this about me, is that I’m a huge Apple fan through and through, and I’ve always been. And I’m so lucky to be able to cover a company that I love, a company that I am obsessed with, and a company whose products I use. There are so many people who cover companies that they couldn’t care less about. That’s not me.

So I do what I do because I love Apple and I love covering Apple. I love the community around it, and I love talking about it. And it’s always fun to get a peek at the future and help keep not only myself informed, but people informed around me.

That actually leads me to a lot of things because I’ve known you forever. We’ve been working in and around the same spaces forever. You got your start as an Apple blogger at the Apple rumor sites.

There’s a whole culture around Apple that has grown up and changed over the years, and you can trace it to different eras of hardware, to different CEOs, to different sizes of the company. This was the first event with John Ternus as CEO. Apple announced a big new product in the iPhone Duo.

Do you sense that the community is changing? How do you think that community has changed over the years? And do you think Ternus is going to lead to a difference in what that community feels like?

I have to say, this event really didn’t feel much different than a Tim Cook event. They felt pretty interchangeable. It could have been Tim up there introducing it. It could have been Ternus up there introducing it.

The one thing I will say that did feel slightly different is that Ternus came out swinging with a point of view on AI. The first thing he came out with was about the intelligent personal hub. Now, here’s the big difference between Tim Cook and John Ternus in terms of their management style. You’re inside Apple, you’re an executive, you’ll come to him with an idea, you’ll come to him with a viewpoint, a decision, an opinion, and he’ll just pepper you with more questions. He won’t make a singular decision in many cases. It’s very much communal decision-making, collaborative decision-making.

John Ternus, if you come to him and you want him to make a decision, he’ll make a decision. He’ll have an opinion. Now, you may hate his opinion; you may completely disagree with him, but he has a viewpoint. But that’s the big difference between talking to people about Ternus and Tim.

Ternus comes out talking about his view on AI. I may disagree with it. A lot of people may disagree with it. They may think the OpenAI or Anthropic approach is superior, but at least he came out and had a viewpoint.

Apple’s been at this AI game now for two years since they launched Apple Intelligence at WWDC in 2024, and it’s been a mishmash of things. They haven’t really come out with a very strong narrative and viewpoint, and they finally did. So, as I said, whether you agree with it or not, they did do that. And I thought that was a really interesting way to kick off the keynote.

All right, we’re just going to get into the weeds of Apple nerds disagreeing about things.

Okay, let’s do it.

I sat through that event, and I appreciated the same thing that you saw, which is, “Oh, we’re telling a story.” John Ternus is on the stage, and the first thing he’s doing is telling a story about this product and how it fits into the universe of technology. And then I took a beat, and I was like, oh, but they’re also just making sure that he’s successful at his first event by playing Apple’s greatest hits.

Because an “intelligent personal hub” is just a replay of Steve Jobs saying the iMac was the digital hub. At the very end of the event, Ternus said, “There’s one more thing, and it’s the iPhone Duo.”

There was just a part of all of that that, to me, felt like Apple saying, “Look, our new CEO can put on the clothes of the old CEO. He can do this same dance that you’re expecting.” Underneath it, what I felt was, to your point, that I don’t buy the story about the intelligent hub.

No, I don’t buy it either.

Because any of the things we’re seeing AI do are happening in cloud services. It’s the same week that Meta launched Muse, right?

Right.

You can feel what you want about Meta launching Muse, but Mark Zuckerberg is giving everybody 8GB of storage and 8GB of RAM in the cloud, and Muse can go do a lot of things that AI on the iPhone absolutely cannot do at this point in time.

I just felt like there was a part where they were playing it really safe with John by having him basically show up and be the new lead singer of Journey. You can’t get it wrong if you’re going to do “Lights.” If you’re going to show up on stage and do “Don’t Stop Believin’,” you’re going to be fine for a minute. And it’s all the stuff that comes after that’s going to really show his real personality. But it sounds like you thought that that’s his point of view.

Well, it’s a couple of things. At a very high level, Apple’s going to tell a story around what they have. If Apple invented ChatGPT, they would’ve invented ChatGPT, and they would’ve told a good story around that. Apple has gone as far as it’s able to, at least for now, on AI. So it’s telling the story, the best version of that story that they can with what they have to work with, with the bird they have in hand. So that’s the one thing.

I agree with you on the intelligent personal hub, and how that compares to the iMac back in ‘98. And it feels like they’re trying to sell this pivot from the Mac as the center of everything with the peripherals around it; then you got to iCloud in 2011, the center of everything with the peripherals around it. Now, it’s this Intelligence right at the center with everything around it.

But what’s so fascinating is that Apple held a major product launch event in September of the year 2026 and did not introduce a single notable new AI feature. The first 15 minutes or so of the keynote was simply a replay, a re-narrativization of what they introduced over the past two years with Apple Intelligence. And so they tried to just tell that story in a more concrete way.

The other thing is they don’t have any AI devices at the very core, and so they need to prop up the iPhone as their AI device because they don’t have an alternative. But of course they’re only going to do that until they have that killer device, and then they’re going to change that whole narrative.

So it’s a very narrative PR and marketing-driven company. And I’m not saying that to be critical. I mean, if I ran the company, obviously I’m going to tout what I have. I’m not going to veer from that. But it is interesting how they’re playing this. And I agree, they did play it very safe. There’s nothing safer than John Ternus introducing a new iPhone. It’s like the safest thing you can do. No major new AI product, no smart home hub, nothing in the spatial space, just straight down the middle.

Yeah, it seems like that next wave of smart home products, which we’re expecting later this year... I say, “We’re expecting.” I’m expecting it because that is something you have reported.

[Laughs] I am expecting it, yes.

Mark Gurman is expecting new products from Apple. That is the first cut at some truly AI-native devices. Because you have Siri AI and it is functional now in a way that it previously was not functional, you can try some new classes of devices.

There are about a half dozen AI-native devices coming in the next year and a half or so. The first will be the smart home hub, which is basically an Amazon Echo Show but Apple-style. It will have a square screen and an entirely new operating system. The idea is: what would a Siri AI operating system look like? This is that: intercom, video conferencing, proactive intelligence.

So you walk up to it, it recognizes who you are, and it will show content personal to you. It will know who is speaking. Obviously, the Amazon Echo can do that, but Apple’s doing it in its own Apple-y way with AI-based Face ID.

They’re working on a home security system. They’re working on another version of the smart home hub that I just talked about that is attached to a robotic arm. So you put it on your desk, and it can move around. It’s actually a category that’s pretty popping in Asia and in China right now.

Then you’ve got the wearables, the smart glasses. I still believe those are going to be introduced and shipped in 2027, so not too far from now. Trust me, you’ll be wearing them. Within 365 days, you will be wearing them and have video footage of you wearing them at the Steve Jobs Theater. And if that is not the case, either something went horribly wrong for you or something went horribly wrong for Apple.

You’ll also have the AirPods with cameras. That’s an interesting thing that we should talk about, but they’ll have the AirPods with cameras and then a few other wearables that I won’t get into.

So this is what I was talking about when I said there were eras at Apple and people’s relationship with the company really changed. The Steve Jobs era was defined by devices, and in particular, Steve Jobs himself getting up and doing a keynote and famously putting up pictures of all the existing smartphones and saying, “Well, these all suck. And here’s the reason they all suck, and here’s the iPhone and here’s why it’s better.”

That created one kind of relationship between Apple’s enormous community of fans, its leader, and the products. I think that was very successful. I think the Tim Cook era has been meaningfully different. I think it’s largely a story about scale. To some extent, it’s a story about values. To a huge extent, it’s a story about privacy.

Apple has marketed itself as the privacy company. It fought the FBI to keep the iPhone encrypted. There’s a lot there with Tim Cook’s version of the company, but it’s more corporate. Certainly, it’s just a vaster company. It’s safer. It’s not as rough around the edges as Jobs’ Apple, but it wasn’t as device-based.

I don’t think the Vision Pro has the same kind of mainstream cultural impact as even the hockey puck mouse that Jobs put out. There was a thing that he could do with products that Tim Cook Apple could not quite do with products. And that just feels really different to me.

I’m going to correct you on that because every time I put an article or a post out about the Vision Pro being on life support, I get what amounts to basically a notch or two below a death threat from dozens of people. So people are passionate about it.

Dozens? Dozens?

Well, honestly, I think what it is is that people have created businesses around spatial computing and apps, and they’re just pissed off that they’ve invested all this time and money in a category that’s probably going to die out.

And then you have consumers who spent four grand on this product, and they’re like, “I saved up for this thing, I’m living with this thing, and I’m pissed off to hear the realities.” But if you have another hour, we can talk about the Vision Pro.

No, the comparison there is good. People have invested in it. They care deeply about it. The comparison I’m making is that the relationship people have to Apple in the Cook era is as an institution. It’s just like this big thing that spans the globe on a massive scale.

It’s IBM.

Yeah, and in the Jobs era, it was all about really, really innovative new products that redefined categories over and over again. You’re describing a whole bunch of new products that came up in the Cook era that John Ternus is going to launch. How do you expect the culture of Apple to change around its products or its relationship to the culture to change as we go from one CEO to another?

But think about what they did. You’ve got the coolest new iPhone and Apple product in maybe 10, 20 years introduced one week after Tim Cook steps down. And then for the next 12 to 18 months, you’ve got, I don’t know, six or seven new product categories. Maybe you have 25 pretty breakthrough things.

So Tim Cook made a decision that, even though his tenure at a product company was pretty limited in major new things, the Apple Watch turned out to be a success, even though it started as a complete dud, as you remember. The AirPods are a unique beast in that they’re an accessory, but it’s not a platform on its own yet. It’s going to get there. And the Vision Pro is a failure.

Tim Cook could have ended his tenure as CEO with the iPhone Duo. He could have just waited. Typical transitions at Apple happen mid-October or mid-April; they happen on January 1st. It was a specific decision that was made for John Ternus to be the one to introduce the iPhone Duo. It was a specific decision made for John Ternus to be the one to introduce this whole new product roadmap. Even though, as you know, because of the length of hardware development cycles and R&D, these things were in the oven for five to 10 years.

So it’s really interesting that this decision was made to let Ternus be the face of this whole new era of products rather than allow Tim Cook to take the credit for it. And I think that’s to your point where they’re trying to draw the line in the sand of this new era. If Cook is already going to step down in the next three years, let’s just do it now and let Ternus take the credit for everything.

Take me inside that. You’ve obviously done a lot of reporting. I think you were the first to break the news that Cook would be searching for a successor. You were, I think, among the very first to break that it would be Ternus. Tell me about that process.

This is a big decision; Cook is going to play a huge role at the company. He has a massive compensation program tied pretty much to having to talk to Xi Jinping and Donald Trump. It seems like that’s his job: to just manage that relationship.

For $47 million a year, I would talk to Trump and Xi Jinping on the phone every day.

[Laughs] I would need at least 50, but that’s just me. That’s his job: to go do politics much the same way that Eric Schmidt at Google was in charge of governments after Larry Page became CEO. There’s a whole pattern here.

Brad Smith at Microsoft, even though he wasn’t CEO, but yeah.

He’s the president of the company. Yeah, there’s a parallel here. Tell me about this decision of Tim Cook wanting to elevate his position to something like that, and of making John Ternus the face of the product side of the company in this new role.

So 2023 rolls around and Tim Cook starts every executive team meeting, all high-level meetings with people at Apple at the executive levels, with, “We need to start taking succession seriously. We need to start thinking about who the next people are.” At that time, there was a really strong realization that many of the people at the top of Apple either had half a billion dollars in the bank or were already billionaires, and that this era would start to age out really quickly.

And so Tim Cook knew that he wanted to take a step back. Jeff Williams, the number two as the COO, knew he wanted to retire. The CFO, Luca Maestri, wanted to retire, too. The general counsel, Kate Adams, also wanted to retire. They were all about the same age, give or take a few years. So they basically came up with this plan that would go one by one over the next few years.

It started with the CFO. Luca retires at the very end of 2024, and he’s replaced by the new CFO, Kevan Parekh. Then 2025 rolls around, and Jeff Williams, the COO, retires and is replaced by his deputy, Sabih Khan. Then in 2026, they had the transition for the general counsel, and they got a great replacement for her from Meta, Jennifer Newstead. And then at the end of 2026, the big one: Tim Cook to John Ternus. So they played this out very, very slowly.

What Tim Cook has done, and I do think this is going to change in the Ternus era as we progress here, is that he came up with this strategy that I call “Hotel California.” You never want to leave. Tim Cook, he’s staying around as executive chairman. The general counsel had her stay around an extra six to nine months to run government affairs. Jeff Williams stayed around three to four months after stepping down as COO to just oversee the design team, the watch team, and the health teams as part of a transition.

For CFO Luca Maestri, the vast majority of his responsibilities went to his successor, but he kept three things. He kept oversight of information systems and technology. The big Decoder trope is that the structure of a company is connected directly to its culture. If you tell me how your company is roughly organized, I can tell you where about 80 percent of your problems are and where the other 20 percent of the magic is.

Every now and again, I get pushback on this from a CEO who says, “No, no, it doesn’t matter. It’s all about the people.” I feel like Apple is both, right? The structure of Apple has been the same for a long time. Steve Jobs used to call it the world’s biggest startup. And then you just had these people who had been there forever. They’re just the same cast of characters under Cook as they were under Jobs.

You could probably shuffle them any way you wanted, but it was the same people, and so, of course, the culture persisted. You’re describing a wholesale turnover at the top. And then it also seems like there are some structural changes happening underneath John Ternus, right? Jony Ive was the chief design officer of the company, which always felt to me like part of that Hotel California strategy.

Oh, that was its own... That was like Hotel Cupertino. I mean, that was its own level.

But they were afraid of him leaving because he was so tied to the Jobs era, and then they managed to work him out of the company. We can talk about OpenAI in a bit. But Johny Srouji is the chief hardware officer now. That’s not a title Apple has ever had before. That also feels like potentially a transitional title.

Can we talk about that? Can we talk about Srouji for a minute?

So it’ll be interesting to see how quickly that happens, I think in a year or two. I think about what came to be known as the Cook Doctrine, where Tim Cook would often say, “We want to own and control every foundational technology that goes into our phones.” This is really just a statement of Apple’s own paranoia about being chained to Intel for a long time or whatever it might be. I think the models are getting commoditized to a point where they could fast-follow and have a very effective product. It just seems like this next generation of devices involves some kind of ambient listening that we are not ready for as a society. People are really mad about Meta glasses. What are you going to do about it?

They soiled the water for Apple and a lot of other companies. Meta being the first mover on this created an industry-wide problem. And I think even though Apple has such a strong privacy stance, there are people who don’t believe them. There are people who don’t care what they have to say. There are people who are going to be angry about the Apple glasses and whatnot.

I think Apple, to some extent, is on such a high horse with its privacy message that it came away surprised that there would be some backlash to Apple doing this. They think, I believe, that people are overblowing it when it comes to Apple and everyone should just be focused on Meta. And just because Meta has done a poor job protecting people’s privacy doesn’t mean we’re going to. So we’ll see what happens.

One thing: when I talk to the folks there, they never make the connection between Apple and Meta in the sense that Meta’s apps run on Apple’s phones. People are mad about Meta, and they still think the phones, Apple’s phones, are listening to them, and they can’t quite make that connection because it undoes a lot of their own messaging. If you believe your iPhone is listening to you, that’s not just Meta’s problem. It is also Apple’s problem.

They kind of have to actively ignore that relationship because otherwise everything else falls apart. And I think that’s why there’s this blind spot. If people’s watches start generating transcripts, it’s exactly the same relationship as “my iPhone is listening to me, and that’s why I saw an ad for a vacation that I only talked to my friend about.”

I’m curious what they’re going to do. I have a feeling they’re just going to bulldoze their way through it. They’re going to just try to tell a good story. They’re going to do a ton of PR briefings about it. They’re going to do a ton of white papers about it, and get as nerdy and in-depth as they can on this stuff.

You know what they’re going to do? They’re going to throw out a lot of comparisons. I even heard Ternus do this in one of the interviews, in Apple’s statement on some of these features. I could totally imagine them saying, “Why is it any different recording from smart glasses if you could just hold your phone up and record people?” With the audio intelligence feature, one thing I didn’t even think of is the Apple Watch-

It’s very funny you just mentioned that because that is exactly what Mark Zuckerberg just said to our friend Alex Heath.

Oh, that’s funny.

“How is it different from a phone?” This is the industry’s approach. I think the answer is that people are like, “Yeah, I can see you doing that, and I feel very comfortable telling you to stop.” There’s something different about that.

I didn’t even realize this. Someone pointed this out to me the other day. It’s like your Apple Watch has had the Voice Memos app for, I don’t know, eight years at this point. Who stopped anyone from recording their whole day with the Voice Memos app on the Apple Watch anyway? This is just a more privacy-centric version of that. So Apple’s solving a problem here. They’re not creating one. So it just depends on how you look at these things. I think they’ll bulldoze their way through it. It’s going to be a problem, but I think they’ll be fine.

All right. Last two before I let you get out of here. We’ve talked around the iPhone Duo a lot. We’ve mentioned it a lot. It’s the thing that just came out. We haven’t talked about it. What do you think of it?

I think it’s incredible. I think, and this is a bold take, that foldables will become the new normal within a decade. If you look at the market share of smartphones at the end of 2006, smartphones had like 6 percent of the market. Now they have 85 percent of the market. It went over 50 percent of the market after five to six years.

The iPhone itself was not the source of that, but the iPhone got everyone into the smartphone game. I think the iPhone Duo is going to do the same for the phone market. I think it’s going to become the new normal.

Even though Apple is a late mover to foldables?

Yeah. I think the Apple brand is that strong, really. I really do. I think the fit and finish, the software integration, is going to get people really excited about this category. I think that the Apple Upgrade program, the leasing program, will eventually expand internationally. I think that’s going to get people in it.

I think that at some point they’re going to stop advertising sticker prices and focus on the monthly prices, and they’re going to get people locked into this thing. They’re going to have a family of iPhone Duos over time. You’ll see every phone maker just transitioning, transitioning to foldables. Samsung: half the line is already foldables. Very soon the candy bar style is going to become legacy.

That’s a big prediction. Although I will say their iPhone handoff feature, where you can move a number between phones, seems to point to a future where I, for example, have the folding phone for work and then a much smaller, lighter phone for the weekends with the family. You can see that vision taking shape only because it’s now easy to port a number between devices, just whenever you want, which I think is incredible.

Last question. We’ve talked a lot about Apple, its culture, and its set of products. What do you think its biggest challenges are in the new era under John Ternus, and what do you think its biggest opportunities are?

I would say that I think the biggest challenge and the biggest opportunity are the same thing. Ternus’ Apple for the next three to five years is still Tim Cook’s Apple, right? That’s just the reality. He’s still going to be there in the background. He’s still going to loom large, and the product pipeline is still going to be coming out of an era that started under Tim Cook.

But in five years from now, they are going to need to start thinking of what actually replaces the iPhone as the next thing. We went from the Mac to iCloud to AI as the center. What is Apple’s new thing after the phone? What is Apple’s new thing after the current generation of AI? And Ternus’ tenure as CEO, I think, will go down as a success if he’s able to find that next new centerpiece. He’s got a few years before he needs to start cooking on that, but I’m talking about something that can be in development for 5 to 10 years.

Tim Cook never had the opportunity to have his new centerpiece of the company. He never had the opportunity to put his stamp on products at the company for two reasons. Both things that he tried to do as his centerpiece failed spectacularly. Obviously the Vision Pro, but the car — the car, that was Apple’s multi-trillion-dollar market cap opportunity, and they just blew it. Ternus will need to successfully hit that.

I’d actually put a third thing on that list. It was the very beginning of the Cook era, with Jobs literally on his deathbed, and he said he’d figured out TV.

Oh, yes.

He had to spend however long pretending he knew what that meant because I don’t think it had been solved. And so there was this first wave of “Apple’s going to redefine TV” because the last page of the Isaacson biography had a Jobs quote on it.

They haven’t even done a new Apple TV box in four years.

That’s a long time. It’s funny because you don’t need one. It never occurs to me that I need to upgrade this thing, but maybe there’s going to be some AI feature.

Well, Siri AI. They’ve been waiting for the Siri AI update. This could be a whole other podcast, but Siri AI has been the gate to all of these new product categories. The AirPods were supposed to be out already, the Apple TV, the HomePod, the smart home hub… all these devices were supposed to come out. Apple couldn’t do any of them until Siri AI. Now Siri AI is here, so the floodgates are open.

All right. Well, Mark, we’re going to have to have you back on the show to talk about those floodgates and all these new products very soon. I can’t believe you haven’t been on until now. Thank you so much for being on Decoder.

Yeah. And obviously I’d love to have you on my new podcast, Power On Podcast, launching very shortly. So thanks in advance.

Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!
